NCCN
The **National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN)** is an alliance of leading cancer centers and medical experts dedicated to improving oncology care, treatment outcomes, and patient education. The organization develops and publishes authoritative, research-based clinical practice guidelines and recommendations trusted by healthcare providers and patients alike to guide decisions across the continuum of cancer prevention, screening, diagnosis, treatment, supportive care, and survivorship. 

NCCN provides extensive patient-focused educational resources, most notably the *NCCN Guidelines for Patients* series, which translates complex medical recommendations into accessible guidance to help individuals navigate treatment options and disease staging. These resources are

Basal Cell Skin Cancer
A form of skin cancer that can recur or metastasize to lymph nodes or distant body parts, requiring diagnosis through physical exams, biopsies, and imaging.<SEP>Basal cell skin cancer, also known as basal cell carcinoma (BCC), is the most common type of skin cancer, arising from abnormal basal cells in the epidermis, primarily caused by UV radiation.

Skin Cancer
A category of malignancy identified as the most common cancer in American men, ranking ahead of prostate cancer.<SEP>A malignant cancer of the skin mentioned as one of the types of cancer screened by healthcare providers.<SEP>Skin cancer is a broad disease category comprising malignancies that develop in the layers of the skin, most frequently in the epidermis.<SEP>Skin cancer is a distinct form of cancer that develops from skin cells, distinguished from cutaneous lymphomas which develop from abnormal lymphocytes.

Squamous Cell Skin Cancer
A category of cutaneous malignancy that includes cancer of the vermilion border of the lip, addressed in specific NCCN patient guidelines.<SEP>A common type of skin cancer (also referred to as cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma or CSCC) that can develop locally, regionally, or metastasize to distant body parts.<SEP>A common type of skin cancer, also known as cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), originating in the squamous cells of the epidermis.<SEP>A type of skin cancer (also referred to as CSCC) treated using surgical options, radiation, and various forms of systemic therapy.<SEP>A type of skin cancer originating in squamous cells, also known as CSCC, which can arise from lesions, old wounds, or burns and may spread to other parts of the body.<SEP>Squamous cell skin cancer (also referred to as cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma or CSCC) is a form of skin cancer that can be treated with topical therapies, excision, Mohs surgery, or lymph node procedures.<SEP>Squamous cell skin cancer is a category of skin cancer that originates in the squamous cells located in the upper part of the epidermis.

Melanoma
A form of skin cancer associated with inherited mutations in genes like BRCA1 or BRCA2.<SEP>A less common but more aggressive type of skin cancer that originates in melanocytes.<SEP>A severe form of skin cancer associated with inherited germline mutations such as those found in BRCA1 and BRCA2.<SEP>Melanoma is a type of skin cancer that develops in melanocytes, the cells responsible for producing melanin in the epidermis.

Epidermis
The outermost layer of the skin that acts as a waterproof barrier and houses squamous cells, basal cells, and melanocytes.<SEP>The outermost layer of the skin that provides a waterproof barrier, produces melanin, and contains basal cells, squamous cells, and melanocytes.

Dermis
The middle layer of the skin composed of connective tissue, blood vessels, oil and sweat glands, nerves, and hair follicles.<SEP>The middle layer of the skin containing connective tissue, hair follicles, and sweat glands.

Hypodermis
The deepest layer of skin, also called subcutis, composed primarily of fat and connective tissue.<SEP>The deepest tissue layer of the skin consisting of fat and connective tissue.

Basal Cells
Cells located in the lower epidermis that continuously divide to form new cells and can mutate to cause basal cell skin cancer.<SEP>Cells located in the lower epidermis that divide continuously and mature into squamous cells.

Squamous Cells
Flat cells located in the upper section of the epidermis that are continuously replaced by dividing basal cells.<SEP>Thin, flat cells resembling fish scales located in the upper layer of the epidermis as well as other organs such as the lungs, thyroid, and esophagus.

Melanocytes
Cells found in the epidermis that produce melanin to provide skin pigmentation and protect against ultraviolet radiation.<SEP>Specialized cells in the lower part of the epidermis that produce melanin to provide skin color and protection from ultraviolet rays.

UV Radiation
Ultraviolet radiation from sunlight or tanning beds that damages cellular DNA and represents the primary cause of basal cell skin cancer.

Surgery
**Surgery** is a conventional, invasive operative medical intervention widely utilized as a primary cancer treatment modality

Radiation Therapy
**Radiation Therapy** is a conventional localized cancer treatment modality overseen by radiation oncologists and delivered by radiation therapists. It utilizes high-energy beams and ionizing radiation—including x-rays, gamma rays, photons, electrons, and protons—to damage cancer cell DNA, destroy malignant cells, shrink tumors, and provide palliative symptom and pain relief. 

The therapy encompasses multiple specialized modalities and delivery techniques, such as External Beam Radiation Therapy (EBRT), Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy (SBRT), brachytherapy, whole-brain radiation, and focused palliative radiation. Treatment schedules often involve delivering radiation in small fractions over several weeks, typically five days per week. It can be applied across various phases of management, including induction, consolidation, or as a post-surgical (adjuvant) therapy to eradicate residual microscopic disease. It also serves as an effective primary alternative when surgical resection is not feasible, or it may be deferred in select low-risk scenarios, such as certain early-stage prostate cancers. Additionally, radiation therapy is frequently combined with chemotherapy or systemic therapies to enhance therapeutic efficacy.

Systemic Therapy
**Systemic therapy** is a broad category of pharmacological cancer treatments that circulate throughout

Immune Suppression
A medical condition characterized by a weakened immune system, often resulting from organ transplants or autoimmune diseases, that elevates skin cancer risk.

Full Skin Exam
A routine clinical examination conducted by a doctor at least once a year following cancer treatment to monitor for recurrence or new lesions.

Adrenal Tumors
A disease category involving growths in the adrenal glands, for which patient management guidelines and specific imaging tests are provided.<SEP>Abnormal growths located on the adrenal glands, evaluated using hormonal and molecular imaging tests.<SEP>Tumors that form in one or both adrenal glands, categorized as benign, functional, or malignant.

Adrenocortical Carcinoma
A rare malignancy starting in the adrenal cortex that can be functioning or nonfunctioning and primarily affects children under 5 and adults in their 40s and 50s.<SEP>A very rare malignant adrenal tumor originating in the adrenal cortex, which can be functioning or nonfunctioning.

Neuroblastoma
A rare cancerous adrenal tumor that predominantly affects infants and children aged 5 and under, with the ability to spread to other parts of the body such as bones.<SEP>A rare, cancerous type of adrenal tumor that primarily affects infants and children aged 5 and under.

Cushing Syndrome
A medical condition caused by an adrenal adenoma that produces excessive amounts of the hormone cortisol.

Aldosteronoma
A type of adrenal adenoma that secretes excessive amounts of the hormone aldosterone.

Adrenal Glands
Paired endocrine glands located on top of each kidney that produce hormones regulating metabolism, blood pressure, immune response, and stress.

Endocrine System
A system of glands and tissues in the human body that secrete hormones into the bloodstream to regulate cellular and organ function.<SEP>The biological bodily system composed of hormone-producing glands and tissues, including the adrenal glands, responsible for regulating various physiological processes.

Adrenal Cortex
The outer layer of the adrenal gland responsible for producing steroid hormones such as cortisol, aldosterone, and DHEA.

Adrenal Medulla
The inner region of the adrenal gland that synthesizes catecholamines, including epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine, mediating the stress response.

Benign Adrenal Tumors
Non-cancerous tumors of the adrenal gland that do not metastasize, often discovered incidentally during imaging tests.

Functional Adrenal Tumors
Adrenal tumors that synthesize and release excess hormones, often causing distinct endocrine symptoms.

Malignant Adrenal Tumors
Rare cancerous neoplasms of the adrenal glands, diagnosed in 300 to 500 individuals annually.

Adenoma
A benign epithelial tumor in the adrenal gland that can overproduce specific hormones like aldosterone or cortisol.<SEP>A category of benign polyp arising on the colon inner lining that carries potential to develop into invasive cancer over time.<SEP>An adenoma is a common type of benign polyp in the lining of the colon and rectum that carries the potential to progress into invasive cancer over time.<SEP>An adenoma is a common type of non-cancerous polyp forming on the inner lining of the colon and rectum that can develop into invasive adenocarcinoma.<SEP>An adenoma is the most common type of colon polyp and has the potential over time to develop into invasive colon cancer.<SEP>An adenoma is the most common type of polyp found on the rectal wall, capable of developing into invasive cancer over several years.<SEP>The most common type of adrenal gland tumor, also known as adrenocortical adenoma, which is noncancerous and may be functioning or nonfunctioning.<SEP>The most common type of non-cancerous polyp found in the colon and rectum that has the potential over time to develop into invasive cancer.

Imaging Tests
**Imaging Tests** are a broad category of medical diagnostic and radiological procedures that produce detailed visual

Adrenal Gland Cancer
A rare cancer affecting approximately 1 to 2 people per million, originating in one or both adrenal glands.

Pheochromocytoma
A tumor originating in the adrenal medulla that can cause high blood pressure, headaches, rapid heartbeat, and sweating; most are benign but can be cancerous.

Beckwith-Wiedemann Syndrome
A hereditary genetic condition linked to an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors and kidney tumors.

Carney Complex
A genetic condition identified as a hereditary risk factor for adrenal tumor development.<SEP>Carney complex is an inherited syndrome identified as a risk factor for the development of thyroid cancer.

Familial Adenomatous Polyposis
A hereditary condition that can elevate the risk of developing adrenal tumors.<SEP>An inherited genetic disorder category characterized by the development of numerous polyps that significantly elevate the risk of colon cancer.<SEP>An inherited genetic disorder causing hundreds to thousands of precancerous polyps to develop in the colon and rectum, often leading to cancer.<SEP>Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is a rare inherited cancer syndrome characterized by the growth of hundreds to thousands of polyps in the colon and rectum.<SEP>Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is an inherited condition recognized as a syndrome related to an increased risk of thyroid cancer.

Hereditary Paraganglioma-Pheochromocytoma Syndrome
A genetic condition predisposing individuals to pheochromocytomas and adrenal tumors.

Li-Fraumeni Syndrome
A hereditary cancer predisposition syndrome associated with an elevated risk of adrenal tumors.<SEP>A hereditary health condition linked to an increased risk of developing pancreatic cancer.

Lynch Syndrome
A genetic hereditary condition that increases the risk of developing certain tumors, including adrenal tumors.<SEP>A hereditary genetic condition associated with increased susceptibility to ovarian cancer and other malignancies.<SEP>An inherited cancer syndrome caused by genetic mutations in mismatch repair genes, significantly increasing the risk of colon, endometrial, and ovarian cancers.<SEP>An inherited cancer syndrome that is tested for when rectal tumors demonstrate mismatch repair deficiency (dMMR) or high microsatellite instability (MSI-H).<SEP>An inherited genetic condition that increases the risk of cancers in the urinary tract, including bladder cancer.<SEP>An inherited genetic disorder that predisposes individuals to colon, uterine, ovarian, and other cancers.<SEP>An inherited genetic disorder that significantly increases the risk of developing various cancers, including upper urinary tract and bladder cancer.<SEP>An inherited genetic syndrome associated with a higher likelihood of pancreatic cancer.<SEP>An inherited genetic syndrome category associated with an increased hereditary risk for developing colorectal cancer.<SEP>Lynch syndrome is an inherited cancer syndrome caused by mutations in mismatch repair (MMR) genes that places individuals at higher risk for colorectal, endometrial, and ovarian cancers.

Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1
A hereditary syndrome that predisposes individuals to tumors in endocrine glands, including adrenal tumors.

Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2
A genetic disorder that increases the risk of developing endocrine tumors, including adrenal tumors.

Neurofibromatosis Type 1
A hereditary condition predisposing patients to the development of adrenal tumors.

Von Hippel-Lindau Syndrome
A genetic condition that predisposes individuals to both adrenal and kidney tumors.

Kidney Cancer
A disease category involving neoplasms originating in the kidneys, including renal cell carcinoma (RCC) subtypes.<SEP>A general category of cancers that originate in the tissues of the kidneys, predominantly comprising renal cell carcinomas.<SEP>A type of cancer associated with some of the same hereditary genetic risk factors as adrenal tumors.

Adrenal Tumor
An abnormal growth of cells located in one or both of the adrenal glands, which may be benign or malignant, and functioning or nonfunctioning.

Functioning Tumor
A classification of adrenal tumor that produces hormones, leading to diverse systemic symptoms such as weight gain, high blood pressure, or hormonal changes.

Nonfunctioning Tumor
A classification of adrenal tumor that does not produce excess hormones and typically causes symptoms only if it grows large enough to press on adjacent organs.

Blood Tests
**Blood Tests** refer to a broad category of diagnostic laboratory evaluations performed on blood samples to assess overall patient health, evaluate organ function, analyze blood cell populations, and detect specific biological markers and disease indicators. These evaluations encompass a wide range of standard panels and specialized assessments, including complete blood counts (CBC), comprehensive metabolic panels (CMP), blood chemistry profiles, alkaline phosphatase (ALP), kidney and liver function tests (LFTs), hormone level evaluations, and tumor markers. 

Clinically, blood tests serve as vital tools across all stages of medical care, particularly in oncology and endocrine management. They are routinely utilized prior to, during, and after therapy to establish baseline health, guide and refine treatment plans, monitor therapeutic response, and check for disease progression or recurrence. Specifically, blood tests play essential roles in diagnosing, managing, and monitoring conditions such as acute myeloid leukemia (AML)—where they track cell and blast counts—chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, and adrenal conditions, including detecting signs of hormone hypersecretion.

Genetic Tests
Diagnostic tests that detect inherited gene mutations linked to hereditary cancer syndromes and elevated cancer risks.<SEP>Laboratory tests that analyze DNA to identify inherited mutations, diagnose cancer, and guide clinical treatment planning.<SEP>Medical diagnostic tests that evaluate DNA to identify hereditary mutations associated with an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors.<SEP>Tests used to detect inherited genetic mutations that heighten the risk of prostate cancer.

General Health Tests
A baseline category of clinical assessments, including vital signs, physical checks, and history taking, used to gauge overall patient health.<SEP>A diagnostic category covering broad physical assessments used to gauge overall patient baseline health before and during cancer care.<SEP>A diagnostic evaluation category encompassing medical history assessments, nutritional assessments, and medication reviews used to guide cancer treatment selection.<SEP>A group of baseline clinical tests and evaluations administered to determine a patient's overall health prior to treatment.<SEP>An overarching category of foundational clinical evaluations, encompassing medical histories and routine screenings, used to understand patient baseline health.<SEP>Baseline clinical evaluations including performance status, medical history, and cardiac assessments used to guide cancer treatment.<SEP>Comprehensive baseline evaluations, including medical history and physical health assessments, conducted prior to oncologic therapy.<SEP>Evaluations of a patient's overall health conducted alongside cancer assessments to aid treatment planning.<SEP>Foundational diagnostic assessments including medical history, family health history, and physical examinations.<SEP>Routine medical examinations and diagnostic assessments conducted to evaluate the overall health status of a patient undergoing tumor evaluation.

Care Team
The **Care Team** is a multidisciplinary, collaborative group of healthcare providers, medical specialists, and clinical staff—including physicians, oncologists, surgeons, nurses, therapists, social workers, and allied health professionals—responsible for coordinating, managing, and delivering comprehensive patient care. 

In diagnostic and evaluative capacities, the Care Team collects patient medical histories, assesses physical well-being and performance status, orders and conducts diagnostic testing and imaging (such as scans and X-rays),

Medical History
A clinical assessment gathering records of past illnesses, surgeries, treatments, symptoms, and medications to inform patient treatment plans.<SEP>A clinical assessment record of past illness, injury, symptoms, medications, and supplements used to guide treatment decisions.<SEP>A clinical evaluation record category covering lifetime illnesses, prior treatments, medications, supplements, and previous infections like H. pylori.<SEP>A comprehensive clinical consultation where the care team reviews a patient's illnesses, family health history, lifestyle, and symptoms.<SEP>A comprehensive clinical record documenting past illnesses, treatments, symptoms, supplements, and prescription medications to evaluate treatment options.<SEP>A comprehensive lifetime record of illnesses, injuries, prescription medicines, OTC drugs, and supplements used to guide clinical care.<SEP>A comprehensive record of a patient's past health issues, illnesses, injuries, prescription medicines, OTC drugs, and supplements used to guide cancer treatment.<SEP>A comprehensive record of a patient's past illnesses, treatments, injuries, symptoms, and medications used to determine optimal treatment plans.<SEP>A comprehensive record of an individual's past and present health issues, treatments, medications, supplements, and symptoms.<SEP>A medical history is a comprehensive record of a person's prior health issues, illnesses, injuries, treatments, and medications used to determine optimal treatment.<SEP>A record of past illnesses, injuries, medications, and treatments used to assist care teams in determining appropriate cancer treatment.<SEP>A structured clinical assessment capturing a patient's lifelong health issues, treatments, symptoms, prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, and supplements.

Family Health History
A record of health conditions and diseases present among biological relatives to evaluate genetic and hereditary risks.

A diagnostic imaging procedure utilizing radio waves and strong magnetic fields to obtain detailed images of prostate cancer, pelvic lymph nodes, and bones.<SEP>A diagnostic imaging test using strong magnets to produce images of the inside of the body without radiation, available in closed or open formats.<SEP>A magnetic resonance imaging scan that uses radio waves and powerful magnetic fields rather than x-rays to create detailed images of internal body structures.<SEP>A magnetic resonance imaging scan that utilizes powerful magnetic fields and radio waves without radiation to produce detailed images of internal tissues.<SEP>A magnetic resonance imaging scan that utilizes powerful magnets and radio waves without x-rays to capture internal body images.<SEP>A magnetic resonance imaging scan used to visualize tumors and lesions in the brain and spinal column in suspected or diagnosed central nervous system lymphoma.<SEP>A magnetic resonance imaging test that utilizes radio waves and strong magnetic fields rather than x-rays to create detailed internal images.<SEP>A magnetic resonance imaging test using radio waves and strong magnets rather than x-rays to visualize internal tissues and cancer spread.<SEP>A medical imaging scan used to determine the exact size and dimensions of the prostate for diagnostic calculations.<SEP>An MRI scan is a diagnostic imaging procedure that utilizes radio waves and powerful magnetic fields rather than radiation to image internal body structures.<SEP>Magnetic resonance imaging scans of the prostate used to detect lesions and combined with ultrasound for targeted sampling.<SEP>Magnetic resonance imaging, an imaging procedure using radio waves and magnets to provide detailed pictures of soft tissues, the prostate, and nearby structures.

FDG-PET/CT Scan
A combined diagnostic scan utilizing a radioactive glucose tracer (18-fluorodeoxyglucose) to identify rapidly metabolizing cancer cells in adrenal tumors.<SEP>A hybrid imaging technique utilizing a radioactive glucose tracer (18-fluorodeoxyglucose) to evaluate cellular metabolic activity and tumor aggressiveness.<SEP>An advanced imaging modality combining fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography and computed tomography, scanning from neck to mid-thigh.

Contrast Materials
Substances (oral or intravenous) used during imaging procedures like CT or MRI to enhance and clarify pictures of internal organs and structures.

Heart Disease
A cardiovascular condition tracked within personal and family medical histories to assess hereditary health risks.<SEP>A category of cardiovascular health conditions assessed as part of a patient's comprehensive family health history.<SEP>A category of cardiovascular illnesses documented as part of family health history to identify hereditary risks.<SEP>A chronic cardiovascular condition tracked as part of family medical history to evaluate hereditary and overall health risks.<SEP>A chronic cardiovascular condition tracked as part of personal and family health histories.<SEP>A group of cardiovascular medical conditions documented during family health history evaluations.

Diabetes
A chronic metabolic condition screened as part of a patient's medical and family health history.<SEP>A chronic metabolic condition tracked as part of personal and family health histories.<SEP>A chronic metabolic disorder recorded in family health histories to identify hereditary health risks.<SEP>A chronic metabolic disorder tracked in patient and family medical histories.<SEP>A chronic metabolic health condition identified as a risk factor for pancreatic cancer.<SEP>A metabolic condition evaluated during medical and family history collection.<SEP>A metabolic health condition recorded during the patient's family health history review.

Cancer
A broad category of diseases characterized by the uncontrolled growth and proliferation of abnormal cells.<SEP>A broad category of malignant diseases, including AML, that is tracked in patient medical and family histories.<SEP>A broad group of diseases involving abnormal cell growth that can run in families and requires specialized tracking, imaging, and treatments.<SEP>A major disease category involving abnormal cell proliferation that can run in families and affect various organs.

Stroke
A serious medical cerebrovascular event documented as part of personal and family health histories.

High Blood Pressure
A common chronic health condition evaluated during physical exams and recorded in health histories.

High Cholesterol
A chronic metabolic condition recorded when gathering family health history.

SSTR-PET Scan
A specialized somatostatin receptor positron emission tomography scan used in patients with neuroendocrine and adrenal tumors.

Basal Cell Carcinoma
The most common type of skin cancer, arising from basal cells in the lower epidermis, grouped with squamous cell cancer as nonmelanoma skin cancer.

Nonmelanoma Skin Cancers
A classification of skin cancers that includes basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, also referred to as keratinocyte carcinomas.

Sun Exposure
Ultraviolet radiation from sunlight, recognized as a primary risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma.

Indoor Tanning
The use of artificial tanning devices such as booths and beds, representing a major risk factor for developing skin cancers.

Environmental Toxins
Harmful environmental agents, including tobacco smoke, vehicular exhaust, and arsenic, that induce skin damage and raise the risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma.<SEP>Harmful pollutants including tobacco smoke, vehicle exhaust, and arsenic that can induce skin damage and malignancy.

Neuroendocrine Tumors
Neuroendocrine tumors are a specific category of lung carcinomas distinct from non-small cell lung cancer.<SEP>Tumors that can be evaluated for aggressiveness and progression using metabolic and receptor-targeted imaging scans.

SSTR-PET/CT Scan
An imaging scan utilizing a tracer targeted to somatostatin receptors on cell surfaces to evaluate certain tumors.

Biochemical Tests
Diagnostic evaluations measuring hormones and substances in blood, urine, or saliva to assess adrenal tumor activity.

PET/MRI
A hybrid diagnostic imaging technique combining positron emission tomography and magnetic resonance imaging to detect cancer cells.

18-Fluorodeoxyglucose
A radioactive glucose tracer utilized in FDG-PET imaging that is consumed rapidly by active cancer cells.

Somatostatin
A regulatory hormone in the body that controls the release and activity of other hormones.

Somatostatin Receptors
Cell-surface proteins (SSTRs) found on various cells that bind somatostatin and serve as targets for SSTR-PET imaging.

Skin
The largest human organ, providing protection against microbes, regulating temperature, and mediating sensation across three distinct layers.

Melanin
A biological pigment produced by melanocytes that determines the color of skin, hair, and eyes, and protects tissue from UV damage.

Ultraviolet Rays
Electromagnetic radiation from sunlight and indoor tanning beds that damages skin and drives cutaneous carcinogenesis.

Scars and Chronic Wounds
Persistent dermatological injuries, ulcers, and burns that predispose tissue to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.

Marjolin Ulcer
A form of squamous cell carcinoma that develops from chronic nonhealing wounds, scars, or burn sites.

cells lining the nasopharynx.<SEP>The most common histological subtype of nasopharyngeal cancer, developing in the thin, flat cells of the nasopharyngeal mucus membranes.<SEP>The most common histological type of anal cancer, starting in squamous cells found on skin and tissue surfaces.<SEP>The most common histological type of cervical cancer.<SEP>The most common type of cervical cancer, often considered for ovarian transposition prior to radiation therapy.<SEP>The most common type of mouth cancer, arising from the stratified squamous cells of the oral mucosal epithelium.<SEP>The most common type of mouth cancer, forming in the thin, flat cells of the mucous membranes of the mouth.

Actinic Keratoses
Actinic keratoses are pre-cancerous skin lesions that can be managed with photodynamic therapy, cryotherapy, or topical therapy.<SEP>Pre-cancerous skin lesions that frequently occur in the same area as Bowen’s disease and are treatable with superficial therapies.<SEP>Scaly or rough precancerous skin lesions caused by long-term sun exposure that carry a risk of progressing to squamous cell carcinoma.

Marjolin’s Ulcer
A form of squamous cell skin cancer that develops in old wounds, burns, or scars, which can be harder to treat.<SEP>A type of squamous cell carcinoma that develops within chronic, non-healing wounds, ulcers, burns, or scarred skin.

Xeroderma Pigmentosum
A genetic disorder that elevates sensitivity and cancer risk from radiation, contraindicating radiation treatment.<SEP>A genetic syndrome characterized by the body's inability to repair DNA damage caused by ultraviolet light, significantly elevating skin cancer risk.

Recessive Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa
A rare, inherited disorder that causes severe skin fragility and blistering, placing affected individuals at high risk for skin cancer.

Weakened Immune System
An immunocompromised health status resulting from medications or conditions like HIV, lymphoma, or leukemia that increases vulnerability to skin cancer.<SEP>An immunocompromised physical state caused by factors like organ transplants, HIV/AIDS, or corticosteroid use, increasing CSCC incidence and recurrence.

Organ Transplantation
A medical procedure requiring recipients to take immunosuppressive medications, which impairs the immune response and elevates skin cancer risk.

Skin Biopsy
A biopsy procedure that takes a small tissue sample of inflamed skin on the breast.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure involving the removal of a small skin tissue sample for pathological evaluation to identify squamous cell skin cancer.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure where a sample of skin lesion tissue is removed and microscopically analyzed for cancer.<SEP>A general diagnostic procedure involving the extraction of a skin sample to test for malignancies such as cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.<SEP>A medical diagnostic procedure involving the surgical removal of skin lesion tissue for microscopic examination to definitively diagnose cancer.<SEP>A medical procedure where a sample of inflamed breast skin is excised to diagnose inflammatory breast cancer.

Arsenic
A toxic environmental contaminant found in soil, water, and air that can lead to skin damage and squamous cell carcinoma.

Lymphoma
A broad classification of cancer that arises from the uncontrolled proliferation of lymphocytes.<SEP>A category of cancer characterized by the abnormal overgrowth of white blood cells known as lymphocytes.<SEP>A general category of cancer that originates when white blood cells known as lymphocytes grow uncontrollably.<SEP>A type of blood cancer whose presence can compromise the immune system and increase the risk of anal cancer.<SEP>Cancer of the lymph nodes that compromises the immune system and increases an individual's susceptibility to squamous cell skin cancer.

Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia
A cancer of the white blood cells in bone marrow that weakens the body's immune defenses and elevates skin cancer risk.<SEP>A hematologic malignancy identified as an immunocompromising risk factor for developing anal cancer.<SEP>A slow-growing type of blood cancer occurring in lymphocytes, characterized by an oversupply of abnormal B cells.<SEP>Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a cancer of the blood characterized by elevated white blood cell counts and managed through biomarker testing, staging, and targeted treatments.<SEP>Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a type of blood and bone marrow cancer involving abnormal B cells, characterized by changes in the bone marrow and lymph system.

HIV/AIDS
Human immunodeficiency virus infection and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, conditions that severely weaken immunity and raise the risk of squamous cell carcinoma.

Immunosuppressants
Anti-rejection medications administered following organ transplantation that dampen immune response and reduce the ability to clear HPV.<SEP>Pharmaceutical drugs taken after organ transplantation to prevent organ rejection by diminishing immune function, which in turn elevates skin cancer risk.

Skin Cancer Screening
Routine clinical evaluations recommended for high-risk and immunocompromised individuals to detect suspicious skin lesions and skin cancer early.

Dermatologist
A medical specialist trained in evaluating, diagnosing, and managing skin disorders, precancerous lesions like actinic keratoses, and skin cancers.

Pathologist
A pathologist is a medical doctor and diagnostic laboratory specialist who examines cells, tissues, bodily fluids,

Skin Shave Biopsy
A diagnostic procedure performed superficially or deeper using a razor-like tool to remove the epidermis and part of the dermis for cancer evaluation.

Skin Punch Biopsy
A diagnostic procedure where a small circular piece of skin and connective tissue is excised using a hand-held tool to test for cancer.<SEP>A diagnostic skin-sampling procedure performed to detect inherited genetic variations and evaluate leukemia predisposition syndromes.<SEP>A diagnostic surgical technique that extracts a small core of skin and connective tissue using a circular hand-held instrument.<SEP>A skin punch biopsy is a diagnostic medical procedure where a small piece of skin and connective tissue is removed to test DNA unaltered by AML for inherited cancer syndromes.<SEP>A skin punch biopsy is a medical procedure in which a small sample of skin and connective tissue is collected to obtain non-leukemic DNA to test for inherited genetic conditions.

Excision Biopsy
A surgical diagnostic procedure where all or part of a suspicious skin lesion is removed, often performed in an office or hospital setting.<SEP>A surgical procedure in which all or part of a suspicious skin lesion is removed for laboratory examination.

Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma
A common form of skin cancer arising from squamous cells, also referred to as squamous cell skin cancer or CSCC, with varying levels of risk and treatment paths.<SEP>A form of skin cancer (CSCC) that can present as local, regional, or metastatic, requiring risk assessment and tailored medical interventions.<SEP>A type of skin cancer that can affect the vermilion border of the lip where the skin and lip meet.<SEP>Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) is a common form of skin cancer that can be classified into risk levels such as low, high, or very high risk.<SEP>Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) is the second most common type of skin cancer, commonly found on sun-exposed skin, highly treatable, and capable of local or regional spread.

Actinic Keratosis
Actinic keratosis is a precancerous skin condition marked by thick, rough, or abnormal skin growths often treated with topical medications, cryotherapy, or curettage.<SEP>Actinic keratosis is an area of scaly or rough skin with a higher probability of progressing into squamous cell skin cancer.

Marjolin's Ulcer
Marjolin's ulcer is a variant of squamous cell skin cancer that develops in old wounds, burns, or scars and can be more difficult to treat.

Local Squamous Cell Skin Cancer
Local squamous cell skin cancer refers to CSCC that has not spread beyond the primary site to nearby lymph nodes.

Regional Squamous Cell Skin Cancer
Regional squamous cell skin cancer refers to CSCC that has spread to nearby lymph nodes, also known as nodal disease.

MRI
A diagnostic imaging study with or without contrast performed to evaluate the primary tumor and neck structures.<SEP>A diagnostic scan utilizing radio waves and strong magnetic fields to obtain detailed images of soft tissues, the bladder, pelvis, and nearby organs without radiation.<SEP>A magnetic resonance imaging diagnostic procedure performed with contrast to evaluate suspicious neck lymph nodes.<SEP>Magnetic Resonance Imaging, an advanced imaging technique used for diagnostic evaluation and guiding breast biopsies.<SEP>Magnetic Resonance Imaging, an advanced imaging technique used to visualize the prostate gland and identify tumor locations.<SEP>Magnetic resonance imaging is a diagnostic procedure using radio waves, magnetic fields, and computers to produce detailed internal bodily images.<SEP>Magnetic resonance imaging is a radiation-free diagnostic scan used to detail pelvic soft tissues and check for cancer spread in the brain and surrounding organs.<SEP>Magnetic resonance imaging using radio waves and powerful magnets to provide detailed cross-sectional pictures and evaluate potential cancer spread.<SEP>Magnetic resonance imaging, a diagnostic imaging technique used to detect cancer in the spine and central nervous system.<SEP>Magnetic resonance imaging, a diagnostic scan featuring open or closed magnet designs to examine internal body structures.<SEP>Magnetic resonance imaging, a non-invasive medical diagnostic modality that utilizes magnetic fields to generate internal body pictures in closed or open formats.<SEP>Magnetic resonance imaging, a type of diagnostic imaging test used alongside mammograms to evaluate breast tissue.<SEP>Magnetic resonance imaging, an advanced diagnostic imaging procedure utilizing magnetic fields and radio waves to produce detailed images of soft tissues such as the brain.<SEP>Magnetic resonance imaging, an advanced medical imaging technique used to visualize the brain and central nervous system to detect tumor masses.

Needle Biopsy
A diagnostic procedure that collects a small tissue sample from a lymph node using a needle, performed when other biopsies are not safe.<SEP>A medical procedure where a needle is used to extract a sample from enlarged lymph nodes to detect cancer spread.

Doctor
A **doctor** is a licensed medical physician, clinician, and healthcare provider responsible for assessing

Hospital
A medical healthcare facility that provides clinical trials, supportive therapies, counseling, integrative medicine, and multidisciplinary treatment to cancer patients.<SEP>A medical institution where diagnostic imaging, excision biopsies, and surgical cancer treatments are conducted.

Head-to-Toe Skin Exam
A thorough physical screening conducted by a doctor after a CSCC diagnosis to check the body for additional skin lesions.

Lymph Node Exam
A physical examination where a doctor palpates lymph nodes to detect swelling or signs of metastatic nodal disease.

PET/CT Scan
A combined diagnostic imaging procedure that pairs positron emission tomography with computed tomography to accurately pinpoint cancer locations.<SEP>A combined diagnostic procedure pairing positron emission tomography with computed tomography to visualize metabolic cancer activity alongside anatomy.<SEP>A combined diagnostic procedure using a radioactive tracer and CT imaging to locate cancer cells and evaluate whether cancer has spread outside the bladder.<SEP>A diagnostic whole-body imaging technique used to locate cancer and assess the extent of disease in the body.<SEP>A dual-modality diagnostic imaging procedure that combines positron emission tomography and computed tomography to map cancer in the prostate and pelvic lymph nodes.<SEP>A hybrid diagnostic imaging method combining positron emission tomography with computed tomography.<SEP>A hybrid diagnostic imaging modality combining positron emission tomography and computed tomography to generate detailed structural and functional images.<SEP>A hybrid diagnostic imaging procedure combining positron emission tomography with computed tomography.<SEP>A hybrid diagnostic procedure that merges PET and CT imaging to provide detailed structural and metabolic views of prostate cancer and metastasis.<SEP>A hybrid imaging modality that combines positron emission tomography and computed tomography, often utilizing fluorodeoxyglucose.<SEP>A hybrid whole-body imaging examination combining positron emission tomography and computed tomography to locate systemic cancer spread.<SEP>A medical imaging procedure combining a positron emission tomography scan with computed tomography for enhanced diagnostic clarity.

Nodal Disease
A clinical classification referring to the presence and involvement of cancer cells in regional lymph nodes, noted as rare in bone cancers.<SEP>A clinical condition in which cancer cells spread through the lymphatic system and cause lymph node enlargement.

Contrast Dye
A liquid contrast agent injected into a vein to make organs and deep tissues clearer on CT scans and MRI imaging.

Radioactive Tracer
A radiopharmaceutical drug injected through an IV that concentrates in metabolically active cells to reveal cancer on PET scans.<SEP>A radiopharmaceutical substance introduced into the bloodstream to bind to cancer cells or bone tissue, visualizing them during PET and bone scans.

Bowen’s Disease
The earliest superficial form of squamous cell skin cancer that affects only the top layer of the skin.

Superficial Treatments
A classification of cancer treatments that target only the top layer of skin, including photodynamic therapy, cryotherapy, and topical therapies.

Photodynamic Therapy
A superficial cancer treatment utilizing a light-sensitive drug activated by light exposure to destroy cancer cells.<SEP>A therapeutic procedure utilizing light and photosensitizing chemical agents, indicated as a treatment option for actinic keratoses.

Cryotherapy
A medical procedure using extreme cold to destroy abnormal or pre-cancerous tissue, used in the management of actinic keratoses.<SEP>A superficial treatment modality that freezes and destroys precancerous and cancerous cells using extreme cold, typically liquid nitrogen.<SEP>Cryotherapy is a procedure that destroys abnormal and cancerous skin cells using extreme cold via liquid or a cold instrument.

Topical Therapies
Prescription creams and medications applied directly to the skin to treat precancerous lesions and early forms of squamous cell skin cancer.<SEP>Topical therapies are non-invasive medications applied directly to the skin, including 5-fluorouracil, calcipotriene, imiquimod, and tirbanibulin, used to treat actinic keratoses and superficial skin cancer.

Cancer Care Team
A multidisciplinary group of medical specialists and the patient that coordinates personalized treatment planning and clinical decisions.<SEP>A multidisciplinary team of medical professionals, specialists, and nurses who coordinate and provide comprehensive care to cancer patients.<SEP>A multidisciplinary team of oncology healthcare providers responsible for treatment planning, risk evaluation, and referrals for patients with cancer.

Dermatologists
Medical doctors specializing in the diagnosis, examination, and treatment of skin conditions and skin cancers.

Mohs Surgeons
Specialized dermatologists trained in micrographic Mohs surgery and post-surgical reconstructive procedures.

Surgical Oncologists
Surgeons specialized in diagnosing and surgically removing tumors, including cancers that have spread beyond the skin.

Medical Oncologists
Physicians specializing in the treatment of cancer using medications such as chemotherapy and systemic therapies.

Pathologists
Doctors who analyze biopsy tissue and cell samples under a microscope to diagnose and stage cancerous tumors.

Plastic Surgeons
Doctors trained in tumor removal, tissue reconstruction, and repairing deep surgical wounds.

Radiation Oncologists
Physicians trained in using various types of radiation therapy to treat cancer.

Oncology Nurses
Specialized nurses who administer systemic therapies, manage patient care, and assist patients in navigating side effects.

Head And Neck Surgeons
Specialized surgeons trained to treat cancerous and noncancerous conditions located in deeper structures of the head and neck, including ears, nose, and throat.

Pharmacists
Healthcare professionals trained to prepare, dispense, and explain medications and their side effects, with some specializing in cancer treatments.

Geneticists
Medical doctors specializing in hereditary traits and genetic disorders who provide counseling and diagnostic evaluation for patients and families.

Clinical Trials
**Clinical trials** are medical research studies coordinated by healthcare research teams and conducted in sequential phases—typically

Lymph Node Biopsy
A diagnostic procedure performed to examine lymph node tissue when the BPDCN subtype of AML is suspected.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure performed to extract and test lymph node tissue when blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm is suspected.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure performed to test lymph node tissue for metastasis when cancer spread through blood or lymph fluid is suspected.

5-Fluorouracil
5-fluorouracil (5-FU) is a topical chemotherapy medication applied directly to the skin to treat actinic keratoses.<SEP>A topical chemotherapy prescription cream (known by brands such as Carac, Efudex, Fluoroplex) applied directly to the skin to treat early CSCC and actinic keratoses.

Imiquimod
A topical prescription cream (marketed as Aldara) applied directly to the skin to treat early cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma and actinic keratoses.<SEP>Imiquimod is a topical immune response modifier cream that stimulates the immune system to eliminate abnormal skin cells.

Calcipotriene
A topical vitamin D derivative cream (brand names Sorilux, Dovonex) that activates the skin's immune system, often co-administered with 5-fluorouracil.<SEP>Calcipotriene (sold under brand names Sorilux and Dovonex) is a topical vitamin D analog that activates the skin's immune system, often combined with 5-fluorouracil.

Mohs Surgery
A specialized surgical technique and form of PDEMA used to treat local CSCC, particularly if high-risk features are present or initial margins are positive.<SEP>A specialized surgical technique that removes cancerous tissue in stages while examining margins, often used for low-risk and preferred for very high-risk CSCC.<SEP>Also referenced with PDEMA, a specialized surgical procedure used to remove squamous cell skin cancer by precisely checking tissue margins microscopically.<SEP>Mohs surgery is a specialized surgical procedure and the most common form of PDEMA, allowing real-time microscopic evaluation of margins to completely remove skin cancer while sparing healthy tissue.

data.content:
Peripheral and Deep En Face Margin Assessment
Peripheral and deep en face margin assessment (PDEMA) is a surgical approach commonly used on sensitive anatomical areas to completely examine surgical margins and spare normal tissue.

Curettage and Electrodesiccation
A surgical procedure (C&E), often combined with shave excision, recommended for early, small, low-risk cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.<SEP>Curettage and electrodesiccation (C&E) is a two-step dermatologic procedure involving scraping visible tumor tissue and cauterizing the base, used for early cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.

Standard Surgical Excision
A conventional surgical procedure involving cutting out the cancer along with a margin of healthy surrounding tissue.<SEP>A surgical treatment involving the removal of the tumor along with margins of surrounding tissue, applied in both low-risk and high-risk CSCC cases.<SEP>A surgical treatment option recommended for removing local CSCC lesions along with margins of healthy tissue.<SEP>Standard surgical excision is a procedure in which a tumor and a surrounding margin of normal skin are surgically removed with a scalpel and evaluated pathologically.

Lymph Node Dissection
A surgical procedure involving the excision of pelvic lymph nodes to evaluate and prevent the spread of cancer cells.<SEP>A surgical procedure performed to remove cancerous lymph nodes, either during an APR or as a standalone surgery.<SEP>A surgical procedure, also called lymphadenectomy, in which lymph nodes are removed and tested to check for the spread of cancer cells.<SEP>Lymph node dissection is an extensive surgical procedure performed under general anesthesia to remove multiple lymph nodes when cancer has spread.

Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy
A diagnostic procedure (SLNB) using dye and radioactive tracers to locate and evaluate the first lymph nodes where cancer may have spread.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure performed to test the first lymph nodes to which cancer cells are likely to spread from a primary tumor.<SEP>A diagnostic surgical procedure performed to check whether cancer cells have spread to the first receiving lymph nodes.<SEP>A sentinel lymph node biopsy is a surgical procedure that identifies and removes the primary draining lymph nodes to examine them for cancer metastasis.<SEP>A surgical diagnostic procedure involving the injection of a dye or radioactive tracer into the cervix to identify, excise, and test the lymph nodes most likely to contain cancer.<SEP>A surgical procedure in which sentinel lymph nodes are identified, removed, and analyzed to determine whether cancer has spread.<SEP>A surgical procedure in which the sentinel lymph nodes are removed and tested to determine if cancer cells have spread from the primary tumor.<SEP>A surgical procedure to identify and remove the initial lymph node or nodes where cancer cells are most likely to spread from a primary tumor.

Mohs Surgeon
A Mohs surgeon is a specialized dermatologic surgeon trained to excise skin cancer layers and immediately examine the tissue margins under a microscope.

Tirbanibulin
Tirbanibulin (sold as Klisyri) is a topical microtubule inhibitor applied to the face or scalp for 5 consecutive days to kill rapid-growing abnormal skin cells.

Hyperkeratosis
Hyperkeratosis is a condition characterized by thickening of the outer layer of the skin, often seen in rough actinic keratoses.

Topical Tazarotene
Topical tazarotene is a retinoid medication related to vitamin A used to treat thickened or hyperkeratotic actinic keratoses.

Topical Keratolytics
Topical keratolytics, including urea, lactic acid, and salicylic acid, are agents used to soften and break down hyperkeratotic skin layers.

Topical Diclofenac
Topical diclofenac is an agent used as a therapy for actinic keratoses.

Chemical Peels
Chemical peels using substances such as trichloroacetic acid are skin-resurfacing treatments applied to actinic keratoses.

Resurfacing Techniques
Resurfacing techniques, such as laser treatment and dermabrasion, are physical procedures used to treat actinic keratoses.

Surgeon
A medical doctor who performs surgical operations, including lumpectomies, mastectomies, and the localization and removal of sentinel lymph nodes.<SEP>A medical doctor who performs surgical procedures including tumor excision, sentinel lymph node biopsy, and wound reconstruction.<SEP>A medical doctor who performs surgical procedures such as lobectomy, total thyroidectomy, and lymph node dissections based on intraoperative findings.<SEP>A medical specialist who performs surgical procedures; it is recommended that an experienced surgeon perform the diagnostic biopsy for bone cancer at the treatment center.<SEP>A medical specialist who ultimately diagnosed the nurse patient with inflammatory breast cancer following multiple prior visits.<SEP>A physician responsible for performing surgical operations such as thyroidectomies to excise thyroid tumors.<SEP>A specialized medical professional responsible for performing cancer operations such as mastectomies and sentinel lymph node biopsies.<SEP>A specialized physician who performs transabdominal resections, decides on bowel reattachment timing, and creates colostomies.<SEP>A surgeon is a medical professional who performs colon surgeries such as colectomies, removes abnormal lymph nodes, and determines surgical reconnection feasibility.<SEP>A surgical doctor who uses imaging guidance to excise tissue samples from the prostate gland.<SEP>A surgical specialist who performs tumor resections, Mohs surgery, and sentinel lymph node biopsies.

Radiation Oncologist
A doctor specializing in the therapeutic use of ionizing radiation for treating malignancies like anaplastic thyroid cancer.<SEP>A medical doctor specializing in oncology who devises radiation treatment plans and oversees radiation therapy.<SEP>A medical physician specialized in prescribing and administering radiation therapy to treat cancer.<SEP>A medical specialist who oversees radiation therapy for the treatment of cancer.<SEP>A physician specialized in prescribing and overseeing radiotherapy regimens for breast cancer treatment.<SEP>A physician specializing in radiation treatments who evaluates patients, conducts radiation therapy, and discusses potential risks and side effects.<SEP>A radiation oncologist is a cancer specialist who prescribes and plans radiation therapy treatments.<SEP>A specialized doctor who evaluates patients and administers radiation therapy treatments.<SEP>A specialized medical physician responsible for formulating the radiation treatment plan, dosing, and session scheduling.

Mohs Procedure
A surgical excision technique used to remove cancerous skin tissue, often followed by wound repair or reconstruction.

CSCC
Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, a type of skin cancer treatable by surgery, radiation therapy, and systemic therapies.

External Beam Radiation Therapy
A cancer treatment in which a large machine directs high-energy radiation beams at the tumor and surrounding lymph nodes in fractional doses.<SEP>A class of radiation therapy delivered from outside the body via a linear accelerator to target tumors conformally.<SEP>A classification of radiation therapy where a machine directs radiation beams toward the tumor site.<SEP>A common cancer treatment modality (EBRT) that uses radiation, which can cause ovarian damage and cessation of hormone production.<SEP>A form of radiation therapy (EBRT) administered externally in sessions over multiple weeks, frequently given concurrently with chemotherapy or sequentially before brachytherapy.<SEP>A form of radiation therapy (EBRT) utilized for aggressive, anaplastic, recurrent, or metastatic thyroid cancers that cannot be excised surgically.<SEP>A form of radiation therapy (EBRT) where a large machine directs high-energy radiation beams directly at the cancer site.<SEP>A form of radiation therapy delivered from outside the body, used alone or as part of chemoradiation following surgery or when surgery is not feasible.<SEP>A radiation oncology procedure targeting pelvic and abdominal tissue to eliminate cervical cancer cells, often combined with chemotherapy.<SEP>A radiation therapy approach (EBRT) recommended post-surgery or for individualized treatment of cancer recurrences and metastatic growths.<SEP>A radiation therapy technique delivering high-energy rays from outside the body to target cervical tumors.<SEP>A specific form of radiation therapy that directs high-energy radiation beams from a machine outside the body directly at the bladder tumor area.<SEP>A therapeutic treatment using high-energy x-rays or particles delivered from outside the body to destroy cancer cells and relieve symptoms.<SEP>A type of radiation therapy (EBRT) that utilizes a linear accelerator outside the body to deliver radiation to breast tissue and regional lymph nodes.

Brachytherapy
A localized radiation therapy modality used as a treatment option for pelvic cancer recurrence, either alone or alongside other therapies.<SEP>A radiation therapy category where a radioactive source is placed in or near the tumor for a defined period.<SEP>An internal radiation procedure delivering localized radiation directly to the cervix or vagina, recommended after or alongside EBRT.<SEP>An internal radiation therapy technique delivering radiation directly into or near the tumor in cervical cancer treatment.<SEP>An internal radiation therapy technique involving placement of radioactive material inside or adjacent to the tumor in the body to deliver targeted high doses of radiation.<SEP>An internal radiation therapy technique involving radioactive material placed inside the body to deliver high radiation doses directly to the tumor.<SEP>Internal radiation therapy delivered directly into or near the tumor site.

Adjuvant Therapy
A category of treatment administered after primary surgery to destroy remaining cancer cells and reduce recurrence risk.<SEP>Postoperative systemic drug treatment administered following surgery to eliminate remaining microscopic cancer cells.

Chemotherapy
**Chemotherapy** is a major category of conventional, systemic, or localized cancer

Basal Cell Nevus Syndrome
A genetic condition that increases the risk of radiation-induced skin cancers, contraindicating radiation therapy.

Lupus
A connective tissue disease that may make the administration of radiation therapy medically inappropriate.<SEP>A specific autoimmune disease category cited as an example of a condition that affects immune system regulation.

Scleroderma
A connective tissue disorder that can complicate or contraindicate the use of radiation therapy.

Head And Neck
Anatomical region where cutaneous tumors frequently develop and where radiation therapy can be particularly effective.

Scalp
Anatomical site where cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma can occur; tissues here are prone to poor healing if operated on after previous radiation therapy.

Secondary Intention Healing
A wound healing method in which surgical wounds are left open without stitches to heal and close naturally over several weeks.

Linear Closure
A surgical wound closure technique where surrounding skin is altered into an elliptical shape and stitched closed along a line.

Skin Graft
A reconstructive technique involving the surgical removal of a patch of skin from one body area and transplanting it to repair an open wound.

Flapping
A reconstructive surgical technique involving the rearrangement of local tissue to cover a wound and reduce scarring.

Surgical Excision
The surgical removal of cancerous tissue, serving as a primary treatment for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.

PDEMA
A specialized surgical procedure for cancer tissue removal and margin assessment, often followed by reconstructive wound repair.<SEP>Peripheral and deep en face margin assessment (PDEMA) is a specialized surgical margin evaluation technique, often considered alongside Mohs surgery for treating cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.<SEP>Peripheral and deep en face margin assessment, a surgical excision technique evaluated alongside Mohs surgery for the treatment of CSCC.

General Anesthesia
A medically induced state of deep sleep utilized during extensive cancer operations and sentinel lymph node biopsies.<SEP>A state of full sedation and unconsciousness administered during examinations of the bladder and bowel to prevent pain and awareness.

Electron Beam Radiation
A subtype of external beam radiation therapy utilizing electrons to treat superficial tumors.

Photon Beam Radiation
A subtype of external beam radiation therapy using high-energy x-rays to treat deeper, invasive tumors.

Protons
Charged particles utilized as an intense energy beam option within radiation therapy to destroy cancer cells.

Platinum Chemotherapy
A class of chemotherapy agents administered concurrently with external beam radiation therapy during chemoradiation regimens.<SEP>A class of chemotherapy drugs administered concurrently with external beam radiation therapy in chemoradiation protocols.<SEP>A class of chemotherapy medications containing platinum compounds used to treat squamous cell skin cancer.<SEP>A subcategory of chemotherapy drugs containing platinum, such as cisplatin and carboplatin, utilized to treat squamous cell skin cancer and other malignancies.

Cisplatin
A chemotherapy drug used in combination with 5-FU alongside radiation to treat anal cancer.<SEP>A platinum-based chemotherapy drug associated with an increased risk of hypersensitivity reactions with repeated administration.<SEP>A platinum-based chemotherapy drug that serves as the preferred standard agent in chemoradiation for cervical cancer, known for potential nephrotoxic and ototoxic side effects.<SEP>A platinum-based chemotherapy medication used to treat various forms of cancer, including ovarian cancer.<SEP>A specific platinum-based chemotherapy drug administered intravenously to treat cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma and other malignancies.<SEP>An intravenous chemotherapy agent administered on the first day of continuous 5-FU infusions in an alternate anal cancer regimen.

Carboplatin
A platinum-based chemotherapy drug commonly prescribed in combination with paclitaxel for the treatment of ovarian cancer.<SEP>A platinum-based chemotherapy drug that carries a risk of life-threatening hypersensitivity reactions with repeat use.<SEP>A platinum-containing chemotherapy medication used alone or in combinations to target advanced squamous cell cancer.<SEP>An alternative platinum-based chemotherapy medication used when cisplatin is contraindicated or considered too harsh.

Targeted Therapy
-targeted).
        *   Primary central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma.

Immunotherapy
**Immunotherapy** is a category of biological, non-hormonal cancer treatment that stimulates,

U.S. Food and Drug Administration
A federal agency responsible for evaluating and approving investigational medical treatments and clinical trials.<SEP>A federal regulatory agency responsible for evaluating clinical trial data and approving safe and effective medical drugs and therapies.<SEP>The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is a regulatory agency responsible for approving safe and effective cancer drugs, devices, and treatment approaches tested through clinical trials.<SEP>The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is a regulatory agency responsible for evaluating and approving safe and effective medical drugs, devices, and cancer treatment approaches tested through clinical trials.<SEP>The federal regulatory agency responsible for evaluating and approving drugs, medical devices, and treatment methods proven safe and effective in clinical trials.

EGFR Inhibitors
A class of targeted therapy drugs that inhibit the epidermal growth factor receptor protein on cancer cells to halt cell growth and division, exemplified by cetuximab.

PD-1 Inhibitors
A class of immune checkpoint inhibitors that block the programmed death ligand 1 pathway, including cemiplimab and pembrolizumab, used in cancer immunotherapy.

Immune-Related Adverse Events
A specific category of adverse side effects triggered by immunotherapy and immune checkpoint inhibitors.

Phase 1 Trials
Early-stage clinical trial events designed to evaluate the safety, dosage, and side effects of an investigational drug or treatment approach.<SEP>The initial phase of clinical trials evaluating the dosage, safety profile, side effects, and early therapeutic signs of an investigational treatment.

Phase 2 Trials
A clinical research trial phase focused on assessing the efficacy of an investigational treatment against a specific type of cancer.<SEP>A stage of clinical research evaluating how effectively a drug or therapeutic approach works against a specific type of cancer.<SEP>Mid-stage clinical trial studies evaluating how effectively a new drug or treatment approach works against a specific type of cancer.

Phase 3 Trials
A comparative clinical trial phase that evaluates an investigational treatment against standard treatments to support potential FDA approval.<SEP>A stage of clinical research comparing a new drug or approach against a standard treatment to establish efficacy for regulatory approval.<SEP>Late-stage clinical trial studies testing investigational treatments directly against standard treatments to support regulatory approval.

Phase 4 Trials
A stage of clinical research conducted after regulatory approval to monitor long-term safety and therapeutic benefits.<SEP>Post-approval clinical studies monitoring the long-term safety and ongoing benefits of an FDA-approved cancer therapy.<SEP>Post-approval clinical trials designed to assess the long-term safety, benefits, and optimal use of an FDA-approved drug.

Research Team
A group of clinical experts responsible for managing clinical trials, reviewing study details, risks, and benefits with participants, and overseeing informed consent.<SEP>A group of medical experts responsible for managing clinical trials, guiding participants, and conducting informed consent procedures.<SEP>A medical team responsible for collecting research data and coordinating patient care within clinical trials.<SEP>A multidisciplinary group of clinical experts responsible for managing clinical trials, reviewing protocols, and securing informed consent from patients.<SEP>A specialized clinical trials team that collects data, coordinates patient enrollment, and monitors individuals participating in clinical research.<SEP>A specialized group of experts responsible for conducting clinical trials, patient eligibility screening, and informed consent procedures.

NCCN Cancer Centers
A network of leading cancer institutions across the United States providing specialized care and clinical trials through NCCN.<SEP>NCCN Cancer Centers is a network of cancer centers providing resources and directories to help patients find clinical trials.<SEP>NCCN Cancer Centers is a network of cancer institutions offering cancer care and clinical trial access in the United States.<SEP>NCCN Cancer Centers is an alliance of leading cancer centers providing clinical care and cancer trial resources.<SEP>NCCN Cancer Centers is an organization in the United States that offers information and resources for locating cancer clinical trials.<SEP>NCCN Cancer Centers is an organization providing cancer care resources and clinical trial opportunities in the United States.

National Cancer Institute

A clinical category where indolent follicular lymphoma converts into an aggressive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

Head and Neck Cancer
A broad category of cancers originating in various anatomical structures of the head and neck, including the oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, and sinuses.<SEP>A category of cancers arising in the head and neck region, encompassing oral cavity and mouth cancers.<SEP>A group of cancers affecting the head and neck region, including structures like the oropharynx, throat, jaw, teeth, and gums, requiring multidisciplinary pretreatment assessments.<SEP>A group of cancers that affect the mouth, neck, throat, jaw, and adjacent structures, strongly associated with tobacco and nicotine use.<SEP>A group of malignancies affecting the head and neck region, with risk and treatment outcomes significantly influenced by smoking and vaping.<SEP>A group of malignancies affecting the oral and pharyngeal areas linked to human papillomavirus infection.<SEP>Head and neck cancer is a category of malignancies affecting areas such as the oral cavity, throat, and related structures, requiring comprehensive multi-disciplinary pre-treatment evaluations.<SEP>Head and neck cancer refers to a group of cancers affecting the head and neck anatomical structures, with treatments that can impair hearing, airway, and swallowing function.

Mouth Cancer
A form of cancer that develops in parts of the oral cavity and is classified as a subtype of head and neck cancer.<SEP>A form of head and neck cancer that arises in the oral cavity, addressed in patient educational materials.<SEP>A specific form of cancer occurring in the oral cavity for which molecular testing currently provides limited targeted treatment options.<SEP>A subtype of head and neck cancer arising in the oral cavity.<SEP>A type of cancer that develops in the tissues of the oral cavity, categorized under head and neck cancers.<SEP>Also known as oral cavity cancer, it is a subcategory of head and neck cancer that develops in the tissues and structures of the mouth, most commonly starting in squamous cells.<SEP>Mouth cancer is a specific malignancy located in the oral cavity, staged using TNM scores and clinical assessments to determine prognosis and treatment.

B Symptoms
A clinical group of systemic lymphoma symptoms including fever, night sweats, fatigue, and unexplained weight loss.<SEP>A group of disease-related symptoms including unexplained fevers, drenching night sweats, and unexpected weight loss associated with CLL.

Bone Marrow Aspirate and Biopsy
A diagnostic medical procedure removing tissue and cell samples from bone marrow to confirm a diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia.<SEP>A specialized diagnostic procedure sampling marrow tissue used to stage and evaluate follicular lymphoma progression.

Immunophenotyping
A diagnostic process using antibodies to detect the presence or absence of specific white blood cell antigens and biomarkers.<SEP>A laboratory diagnostic process that uses flow cytometry to identify specific immune and surface markers on cells.<SEP>A laboratory test category that analyzes antigens and markers expressed by cells to identify lymphoma types.<SEP>Immunophenotyping is a laboratory testing method used to analyze biomarkers and cellular characteristics in cutaneous B-cell lymphoma diagnosis.<SEP>Immunophenotyping is an analytical process that uses antibodies to identify specific white blood cell antigens or biomarkers on or inside cells.

Health Care Team
A group of medical professionals who provide care, perform diagnostic examinations, evaluate patient symptoms, and offer emotional and clinical support.<SEP>The multidisciplinary group of physicians, nurses, and medical professionals collaborating to diagnose, treat, and monitor lymphoma patients.

Cancer Center
A specialized healthcare facility where oncology imaging tests, such as PET-CT scans, are conducted.<SEP>A specialized medical facility equipped with technology to conduct PET/CT scans and other cancer assessments.<SEP>A specialized medical facility or hospital dedicated to treating cancer patients and providing expertise in specific AML subtypes.<SEP>A specialized medical facility or institution where cancer diagnosis, imaging, and treatments are conducted.<SEP>Specialized medical institutions responsible for diagnostic evaluations, staging, and individualized treatment regimens for lymphoma patients.

Head And Neck Cancer
A broad group of cancers arising in the head or neck region, including the oral cavity, oropharynx, nasopharynx, hypopharynx, larynx, nasal cavity, and paranasal sinuses.<SEP>A broad group of cancers including throat cancer and nasopharyngeal cancer that can impact overall health and oral health including teeth, jaw, and gums.<SEP>A broader category of cancers affecting the head and neck region, influenced by risk factors such as tobacco and alcohol use.<SEP>A group of cancers occurring in the throat, larynx, or oropharynx, often evaluated using endoscopic tools.<SEP>A group of cancers occurring in the throat, mouth, or neck that can be caused by human papillomavirus infection.<SEP>A group of cancers that arise in the head or neck area, generally not inherited, with tobacco and alcohol as key risk factors.<SEP>Head and neck cancer is a broad group of cancers affecting the head and neck region, including throat cancer, which can impact oral health, teeth, jaw, and general body function.<SEP>Head and neck cancer is a category of cancers affecting the head and neck region, with treatments that can impact the jaw, teeth, gums, and regional lymph nodes.<SEP>Malignancies affecting the head and neck areas that can be triggered by long-term HPV infection.<SEP>Malignancies arising in the head and neck region, monitored with CT imaging and strongly linked to smoking or vaping.

Nasopharyngeal Cancer
A form of cancer originating in the nasopharynx, which is the upper part of the throat near the nasal cavity.<SEP>A form of head and neck cancer occurring in the upper part of the throat near the nasal cavity.<SEP>A type of head and neck cancer occurring in the nasopharynx that can specifically affect the eyes and related cranial structures.<SEP>Nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC) is a cancer of the nasopharynx that is predominantly EBV-related and staged using TNM scores to determine prognosis and treatment.

High-Volume Center
A specialized hospital or medical facility with significant clinical experience and case volume in treating head and neck cancers.<SEP>A specialized medical facility or hospital with extensive clinical experience and a high patient caseload in diagnosing and treating complex conditions such as pancreatic cancer.<SEP>Specialized hospitals or medical treatment centers with high patient volume and clinical experience in treating specific head and neck cancers.

Oropharyngeal Cancer
A form of throat cancer affecting the oropharynx, including the soft palate, tonsils, back walls of the throat, and the base of the tongue.<SEP>A subtype of head and neck cancer that develops in the middle part of the throat near the mouth (oropharynx).<SEP>A type of head and neck cancer that arises in the middle part of the throat near the mouth.

Hypopharyngeal Cancer
A type of head and neck cancer located in the lower part of the throat near the voice box.

Laryngeal Cancer
A form of throat and head and neck cancer that affects the larynx (voice box), distinct from nasopharyngeal cancer.<SEP>A type of head and neck cancer occurring in the voice box (larynx).

data.entity_name: Nasal Cavity And Paranasal Sinus Cancer
data.content:
Nasal Cavity And Paranasal Sinus Cancer
A type of head and neck cancer originating in the space behind the nose and the surrounding air cavities.

Oral Cavity
The anatomical region comprising the lips, buccal mucosa, front of the tongue, gums, floor of mouth, hard palate, and retromolar trigone.<SEP>The anatomical structure representing the first part of the digestive and respiratory systems, consisting of lips, gums, tongue, palate, and lining mucosa.

Respiratory System
The anatomical system responsible for breathing, for which the mouth serves as an entry and pathway.

Depth Of Invasion
A pathological measurement assessing how deeply a tumor has invaded through the layers of the oral mucosa.

Local Hospital
Community healthcare facilities that offer cancer care, medical appointments, and patient support groups.

Support Groups
Community or hospital-based groups composed of people diagnosed with cancer, offering shared support and experiences across various stages of care.<SEP>Organizations or community groups offering emotional and social support to individuals undergoing cancer diagnosis and treatment.

Family History
A clinical record of health conditions and cancer diagnoses among biological relatives used to assess hereditary risk factors.<SEP>A clinical risk-assessment category detailing diseases such as cancer, heart disease, and diabetes among biological relatives across generations.<SEP>A diagnostic information category documenting illnesses, cancers, age of onset, and genetic test results among biological relatives to evaluate hereditary risk.<SEP>A family history is a medical record of health conditions, such as cancer, heart disease, and diabetes, occurring in blood relatives.<SEP>A genealogical medical record detailing diseases such as cancer, heart disease, and diabetes among blood relatives to evaluate hereditary risk.<SEP>A medical risk factor indicating the occurrence of bladder cancer or hereditary conditions in relatives.<SEP>A record of health conditions affecting blood relatives, such as cancer, heart disease, and diabetes, to identify potential genetic risk factors.<SEP>A record of health issues and conditions such as cancer, diabetes, and heart disease in blood relatives, collected during cancer treatment planning.<SEP>A record of medical conditions and diagnoses among blood relatives used to evaluate genetic cancer risks and context.<SEP>An inquiry into the medical conditions and cancer diagnoses of blood relatives to evaluate potential hereditary patterns and genetic risk.<SEP>The health record of medical conditions among relatives; having close family members with prostate or related cancers significantly increases disease risk.

Tobacco And Alcohol Use
Established behavioral lifestyle risk factors that increase the likelihood of developing head and neck cancer and negatively affect treatment efficacy and patient survival.<SEP>Known behavioral risk factors that increase the risk of head and neck cancers and negatively impact treatment efficacy and survival.

Dental Exam
A clinical evaluation and cleaning recommended prior to certain cancer treatments to assess and protect the jaw, teeth, and gums.<SEP>A dental checkup and cleaning procedure conducted prior to cancer therapy to prevent and manage complications affecting the jaw, teeth, and gums.<SEP>A specialized examination and cleaning of the oral cavity and teeth required to prevent and manage complications caused by head and neck cancer therapies.<SEP>A specialized oral examination and imaging procedure to evaluate teeth, gums, and jaw health before cancer therapy.<SEP>An examination including x-rays (Panorex) or CT scans performed before cancer therapy to evaluate and optimize oral and dental health.

Endoscopy With Examination Under Anesthesia
A scoping procedure performed under anesthesia to visually examine the airway and throat structures for treatment planning.<SEP>A specialized diagnostic evaluation performed under anesthesia to inspect the upper aerodigestive tract for cancer staging.

Chest CT
A computed tomography imaging study of the chest used to evaluate disease spread or staging in head and neck cancer patients.

FDG-PET/CT
A combined functional and anatomical imaging scan used to detect distant cancer metastases in patients with nasopharyngeal carcinoma.<SEP>A hybrid functional and anatomical imaging scan used to detect leukemia occurring outside of the blood and bone marrow.<SEP>A specialized diagnostic scan combining PET and CT using fluorodeoxyglucose to detect cancer in lymph nodes and distant body sites.<SEP>A specific PET/CT imaging test that utilizes the radiotracer fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) to identify cancerous lesions.<SEP>A specific combined PET/CT scan that utilizes the radiotracer fluorodeoxyglucose to image metabolic activity and cancer cells.<SEP>An advanced hybrid metabolic and anatomical imaging scan used for treatment planning and cancer staging.<SEP>An advanced imaging modality combining PET and CT scans using fluorodeoxyglucose to detect cancer in lymph nodes and distant anatomical sites.<SEP>An advanced imaging modality used as needed to evaluate tumor metabolic activity and staging.<SEP>An advanced imaging scan used to detect extramedullary leukemia occurring outside the blood and bone marrow.<SEP>An advanced imaging scan utilizing the F-18 fluorodeoxyglucose radiotracer to identify cancer across primary, nodal, and distant sites.

Depression Screening
A psychosocial evaluation conducted to assess patient mental health and provide emotional care during cancer treatment planning.

Hepatitis B Screening
A medical test administered as needed during pre-treatment planning to screen for viral hepatitis infection.

Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group
