The Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) is a cancer research organization that established the ECOG performance status scale used to evaluate patient fitness and daily functioning.<SEP>The Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) is a clinical oncology organization known for establishing a standardized performance status scale used to evaluate patients' general fitness and ability to perform daily tasks.<SEP>The Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) is a clinical oncology organization that established the ECOG Performance Status scale to assess patients' functional capabilities.<SEP>The Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) is a clinical research organization known for establishing the ECOG performance status scale used to assess patient functional status.<SEP>The Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) is a medical research organization that established the ECOG Performance Status score, used to assess a patient's overall health and ability to tolerate treatments.<SEP>The Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) is a medical research organization that established the performance status scale used by clinicians to assess patient functional capability.<SEP>The Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) is an organization that developed a widely used performance status scale to assess a patient's level of functioning and fitness.

Fertility Preservation
A category of medical interventions and procedures undertaken to protect a patient's ability to have biological children before undergoing cancer treatment.<SEP>A category of medical interventions and procedures—such as sperm banking, egg freezing, and ovarian tissue banking—designed to preserve reproductive capabilities before cancer treatment.<SEP>A clinical consideration and set of strategies addressing how cancer treatments affect reproductive function and how patients can preserve fertility.<SEP>A medical and reproductive care category focused on maintaining a patient's ability to have children prior to systemic cancer treatments.<SEP>Clinical consultation and medical interventions undertaken prior to systemic cancer treatment to protect a patient's ability to have children.<SEP>Fertility preservation encompasses clinical measures and interventions taken prior to cancer therapy to protect a patient's ability to have biological children.<SEP>Fertility preservation encompasses medical options and planning discussed with the care team to address fertility risks associated with rectal cancer treatment.<SEP>Fertility preservation encompasses medical techniques such as sperm banking, egg freezing, ovarian tissue banking, and ovarian transposition to protect reproductive ability from gonadotoxic cancer therapies.<SEP>Fertility preservation encompasses options and procedures discussed with specialists to maintain reproductive capability prior to cancer treatments like chemotherapy.<SEP>Interventions and consultations undertaken before cancer treatment begins to safeguard reproductive capabilities against therapy-induced impairment.<SEP>Medical and family planning procedures and counseling offered to patients facing fertility risks from cancer therapies like chemotherapy and radiation.<SEP>Medical options, consultations, and actions taken before cancer therapy to preserve the patient's future reproductive potential.<SEP>Medical procedures and consultations, such as freezing sperm or eggs, undertaken to protect the ability to have children prior to receiving cancer therapies.<SEP>Medical procedures and options—such as sperm banking, egg freezing, and ovarian tissue banking—utilized to safeguard reproductive potential before cancer treatment.

Distress
Distress is a multifaceted negative psychological, emotional, physical, and spiritual experience commonly screened for and managed during cancer care.<SEP>Distress is a multifaceted unpleasant experience of psychological, social, or spiritual nature that cancer patients may encounter throughout their diagnosis and treatment.

Complete Head and Neck Exam
A physical examination event where a health care provider evaluates the head, neck, oral cavity, and throat using palpation and specialized instruments.

Distress Screening
A clinical evaluation assessing psychological and emotional distress in patients diagnosed with cancer.<SEP>A clinical evaluation category designed to identify emotional, psychological, and social distress in patients undergoing cancer testing and treatment.<SEP>A clinical evaluation conducted by the care team to measure a patient's emotional, mental, physical, and spiritual stress following a cancer diagnosis.<SEP>A psychological and clinical evaluation method used to assess patient emotional, mental, and social well-being during diagnosis and care.<SEP>A psychological and emotional assessment tool used during cancer workup to evaluate patient distress and provide psychosocial support.<SEP>A routine clinical assessment conducted by the care team to evaluate and monitor psychological and emotional distress in cancer patients.<SEP>An evaluation conducted by cancer treatment teams to screen for psychological, emotional, social, or spiritual distress such as anxiety and depression.<SEP>An evaluation process to assess emotional, physical, social, or spiritual distress resulting from a cancer diagnosis.

Endocrine Tests
Blood tests that evaluate hormone levels and function of glands like the thyroid and pituitary, which may be affected by head and neck radiation therapy.<SEP>Diagnostic blood evaluations conducted before and after radiation therapy to check hormone levels and thyroid or pituitary gland function.

Hearing Test
A diagnostic evaluation, often generating an audiogram, used to detect and characterize hearing loss caused by head and neck tumors or their treatment.<SEP>An audiogram test conducted as needed to evaluate hearing health prior to potential ototoxic cancer therapies.<SEP>An audiological evaluation that produces an audiogram to assess potential hearing loss caused by head and neck tumors or their treatments.<SEP>An auditory assessment resulting in an audiogram to evaluate potential hearing impairment caused by head and neck tumors or their treatment.

Nutrition Assessment
A clinical consultation conducted before cancer therapy starts to evaluate dietary needs and prevent treatment-related malnutrition and weight loss.<SEP>A clinical evaluation category measuring patient nutritional status and dietary needs during cancer diagnosis and treatment.<SEP>A clinical evaluation performed by a dietitian or nutritionist to establish nutritional adequacy prior to starting cancer treatment.<SEP>A pretreatment evaluation by a nutritionist or dietitian to establish an adequate and sustained nutrition and hydration plan.

Speech and Swallowing Assessment
A functional clinical evaluation conducted by a speech or swallowing therapist before and after cancer treatment.<SEP>A functional clinical evaluation conducted by a therapist before and after cancer treatment to assess swallowing and speaking capabilities.

Cancer Diagnosis
The formal identification and staging of cancer in a patient, which triggers multidisciplinary care assessments and potential psychological distress.

Pregnancy Test
A clinical screening administered to patients with ovaries before initiating cancer treatment to avoid harm to a developing baby.<SEP>A diagnostic evaluation performed prior to initiating cancer treatment for patients who can become pregnant to prevent fetal exposure to therapy.<SEP>A diagnostic medical test administered to individuals before cancer therapy to ensure treatments will not harm an unborn baby.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure required prior to starting cancer treatment for patients who have ovaries and are capable of becoming pregnant.<SEP>A diagnostic test administered to individuals capable of pregnancy prior to initiating cancer therapies.<SEP>A screening test performed before starting cancer therapies on individuals with ovaries to ensure pregnancy is not present.

Social Worker
A mental health and support professional available to assist cancer patients and their families in managing anxiety, depression, and distress.<SEP>Healthcare support professionals who assist cancer survivors in navigating mental health services and financial resources.

Nutritionist or Dietitian
A clinical dietary expert who evaluates patient nutritional needs and advises on foods and fluids before cancer treatment begins.

Speech or Swallowing Therapist
A specialized therapist who tests and helps manage speech and swallowing function before and after cancer therapy.

Fertility Specialist
A healthcare professional consulted before treatment to address fertility preservation for patients undergoing bone cancer therapies.<SEP>A healthcare professional specializing in reproductive medicine consulted by patients wishing to preserve fertility prior to initiating endocrine therapy.<SEP>A medical professional specializing in reproductive health who assists cancer patients with fertility preservation options prior to treatment.<SEP>A reproductive healthcare professional who counsels and assists cancer patients in preserving their ability to conceive children.<SEP>A reproductive medicine professional who consults with patients regarding options and procedures for fertility preservation prior to cancer treatment.<SEP>A reproductive medicine specialist who consults with cancer patients on preservation options prior to gonadotoxic treatments.<SEP>Reproductive medicine practitioners who counsel cancer patients on reproductive risks and strategies to preserve fertility prior to initiating therapy.

Barrier Methods
Barrier methods represent a category of non-hormonal contraception, including condoms, diaphragms, cervical caps, and contraceptive sponges, used to prevent pregnancy during treatment.<SEP>Non-hormonal contraceptive devices and methods, such as condoms, diaphragms, cervical caps, and contraceptive sponges, used to prevent pregnancy during cancer therapy.<SEP>Non-hormonal contraceptive devices including condoms, diaphragms, cervical caps, and contraceptive sponges recommended to prevent pregnancy during treatment.<SEP>Non-hormonal contraceptive devices, such as condoms, diaphragms, cervical caps, and sponges, used to prevent pregnancy.

Contraception
A category of birth control methods, including non-hormonal barrier methods and IUDs, used to prevent pregnancy during and after cancer treatment.<SEP>Birth control measures necessary during and following cancer treatment to prevent pregnancy due to potential damage to sperm, eggs, or developing fetuses.<SEP>Birth control measures, such as condoms, used to prevent pregnancy during and after cancer treatment due to potential sperm damage.<SEP>Methods of birth control, including barrier methods and intrauterine devices, recommended to prevent pregnancy during and immediately after cancer therapy.<SEP>Pregnancy prevention measures, such as intrauterine devices (IUDs), recommended during cancer treatment to avoid harm to damaged reproductive cells.

Ultrasound
A diagnostic imaging modality referenced as a complementary breast examination alongside mammograms and breast MRIs.<SEP>A diagnostic imaging test that uses sound waves to generate pictures of internal organs, recommended every six months for liver cancer screening.<SEP>A diagnostic imaging test using sound waves via transabdominal or transvaginal probes to visualize pelvic organs and determine tumor characteristics.<SEP>A medical imaging test utilizing sound waves to examine internal breast structures and assist in clinical diagnosis.<SEP>A non-invasive diagnostic imaging modality that typically serves as the primary radiological evaluation for suspected ovarian cancer.<SEP>A non-invasive diagnostic imaging procedure utilizing sound waves to visualize the size, shape, and structure of thyroid nodules and neck lymph nodes.<SEP>A non-invasive diagnostic imaging technique using sound waves to visualize internal structures, including the prostate.<SEP>A non-invasive imaging category utilizing sound waves to visualize internal organs, encompassing tests such as echocardiograms.<SEP>A painless diagnostic imaging technique that uses high-energy sound waves and a handheld transducer to produce images of internal body structures.<SEP>A painless diagnostic imaging tool that uses high-energy sound waves to produce images of internal tissues, frequently used on the breast and armpit.<SEP>A painless imaging procedure using high-energy sound waves rather than x-rays to create pictures of internal tissues and guide biopsies.<SEP>A painless imaging technique using high-energy sound waves to capture images of internal organs and guide needle biopsies without using radiation.<SEP>An imaging examination technique used to visualize and guide needle placement during a lymph node biopsy.<SEP>An imaging technique employed to visualize internal structures and guide lymph node biopsies.<SEP>An imaging technique utilizing sound waves to visualize the prostate and guide needle placement during a biopsy.<SEP>An initial diagnostic imaging technique commonly used when ovarian cancer is suspected.<SEP>Ultrasound is the primary diagnostic imaging technique used to examine the thyroid gland and neck for abnormal nodules or cancer.

Panoramic Dental X-Ray
A low-dose radiation imaging technique capturing the entire mouth, including the teeth and jaw structures, in a single image.<SEP>A low-dose radiation imaging test that captures the entire mouth, jaw, and teeth in a single image to assist in dental and oral surgical planning.<SEP>A low-radiation dental imaging examination that captures the full mouth, teeth, jaws, and surrounding structures in a single image.

Contrast Material
A diagnostic substance administered orally or intravenously to enhance the clarity and quality of CT and MRI images.<SEP>A substance administered during diagnostic imaging scans (such as CT and MRI) to enhance and sharpen images of internal organs and structures.<SEP>A temporary substance administered intravenously to enhance organ and tissue clarity on CT and MRI scans.<SEP>Contrast material is a category of chemical substances administered during imaging procedures like CT and MRI scans to enhance image clarity.<SEP>Contrast material is an oral or intravenous substance administered during imaging scans to enhance the quality and clarity of the pictures.<SEP>Specialized medical imaging substances administered to enhance and clarify pictures of internal organs during CT and MRI evaluations.<SEP>Substances administered before imaging tests such as CT or MRI to enhance and clarify pictures of internal body organs and structures.<SEP>Substances administered prior to imaging tests like CT and MRI to improve clarity and enhance images of organs and structures.<SEP>Substances used to improve and enhance diagnostic imaging pictures of internal organs and structures during CT and MRI scans.

Cancer Treatment
A category of medical therapies, including chemotherapy, used to treat cancer that can impact fertility and require preventative health measures.<SEP>The therapeutic regimen administered to treat cancer, which can impact fertility, reproductive organs, and patient performance status.<SEP>Therapeutic medical interventions for cancer that can temporarily or permanently impair fertility and cause fetal harm if pregnancy occurs during treatment.<SEP>Therapies and interventions designed to treat malignancy, which can impact fertility, wound healing, and reproductive health.

Technologist
A healthcare specialist who operates imaging equipment such as MRI scanners and screens patients for metal implants and safety risks.<SEP>A medical imaging professional who operates MRI equipment, verifies patient safety regarding metal implants, and collects scans.<SEP>A medical imaging technician who operates MRI machinery and collects scan images from the patient.<SEP>A medical imaging technician who operates scanning machinery such as MRI equipment and collects diagnostic images.<SEP>A medical professional who operates MRI equipment, prepares patients, and collects diagnostic images.<SEP>A medical professional who operates imaging equipment such as the MRI scanner and screens patients for metal.<SEP>A specialized medical technician who operates imaging equipment such as MRI scanners and ensures patient safety around magnetic fields.

Dentist
A dental healthcare practitioner who performs panoramic dental x-rays and coordinates oral care before or during treatment.<SEP>A dental healthcare practitioner who routinely performs panoramic dental x-rays to plan oral treatments such as dentures and braces.<SEP>A dental healthcare professional responsible for monitoring and caring for teeth, jaw, and gum health before, during, and after cancer treatments.<SEP>A dental healthcare professional who monitors and treats teeth, jaw, and gum health before, during, and after head and neck cancer therapy.<SEP>A dental healthcare provider responsible for conducting oral cleanings and evaluations before head and neck cancer treatments begin.<SEP>A dental healthcare provider who regularly performs panoramic dental x-rays to evaluate teeth and plan patient treatments.<SEP>A dental professional who performs cleanings, checkups, and necessary dental work prior to cancer treatment to prevent oral health complications.<SEP>An oral health professional responsible for monitoring and caring for teeth, gums, and jaws before, during, and after cancer therapy.

Oral Surgeon
A specialized dental clinician who uses panoramic dental x-rays for planning surgical interventions like extractions and implants.<SEP>A specialized surgeon who performs surgical dental procedures and utilizes panoramic dental x-rays for procedural planning.<SEP>A surgical dental specialist involved in everyday oral evaluations and surgical treatment planning.<SEP>A surgical dental specialist who conducts panoramic dental x-rays to prepare for procedures including tooth extractions and implants.

Medical Binder
A personal organizational system used by cancer patients to store medical records, imaging results, insurance cards, and appointment notes.

Patient Portal
A secure digital healthcare access system used to deliver medical reports and imaging results directly from providers to patients.<SEP>An online digital access system that enables patients to view test results, imaging reports, and medical records electronically.

Bone Scan
A bone scan is a diagnostic imaging procedure that utilizes a radioactive tracer to detect whether cancer has metastasized to the skeletal system.<SEP>A bone scan is a nuclear imaging diagnostic procedure using a radiotracer to identify areas of bone damage, tumors, or other skeletal abnormalities.<SEP>A diagnostic imaging study used to detect bone conditions and bone metastases that may be superseded by FDG-PET/CT.<SEP>A diagnostic imaging test that uses an injected radiotracer and a special camera to identify areas of bone damage or cancer.<SEP>A diagnostic nuclear imaging procedure performed when symptoms suggest that cancer has metastasized to the bones.<SEP>A diagnostic nuclear imaging study used to identify cancerous lesions and abnormalities within the skeletal system.<SEP>A nuclear imaging procedure that utilizes a radiotracer to detect bone metastases or abnormalities.<SEP>A nuclear imaging test used to detect abnormalities in the bones, which may be replaced by sodium fluoride PET-CT or FDG PET-CT.<SEP>A nuclear imaging test used to evaluate potential cancer spread to the skeletal system.<SEP>A nuclear imaging test utilizing radioactive tracers to detect bone damage and metastasis resulting from prostate cancer.<SEP>A specialized diagnostic imaging procedure used to evaluate bone health and detect potential skeletal cancer spread.<SEP>A specialized diagnostic imaging test used to evaluate whether cancer has metastasized to the skeletal system.<SEP>A specialized imaging test used to evaluate whether prostate cancer has metastasized to the bones.

Sodium Fluoride PET/CT
A specialized PET/CT scan modality used to identify bone malignancy, which may not be necessary if FDG-PET/CT findings are conclusive.<SEP>A specialized diagnostic scan used to evaluate bone involvement and metastatic cancer.<SEP>An imaging test utilizing a sodium fluoride tracer to examine bone metastasis, which may be superseded by FDG-PET/CT.

Smoking And Vaping
Inhalation of nicotine products that increases cancer incidence, hinders cancer treatment efficacy, and prevents wound healing.

Closed MRI
A capsule-like magnetic resonance imaging machine where the magnet completely surrounds the patient; more common than open MRI.<SEP>A closed MRI is an imaging machine configuration with a capsule-like, enclosed design where magnets surround the patient.<SEP>A common type of magnetic resonance imaging system where the magnet completely surrounds the patient.<SEP>A magnetic resonance imaging configuration featuring a capsule-like, enclosed cylindrical bore surrounding the patient during examination.<SEP>A type of MRI scanner featuring a capsule-like design where the magnetic coils completely surround the patient.<SEP>An MRI machine with a capsule-like design where the magnet fully surrounds the patient during scanning.<SEP>An enclosed capsule-like magnetic resonance imaging device configuration.

Open MRI
A magnetic resonance imaging machine with an open top and bottom, accommodating individuals who experience claustrophobia.<SEP>A type of MRI scanner designed with openings on each end to accommodate patients with claustrophobia.<SEP>A type of magnetic resonance imaging system featuring a magnetic top and bottom with open ends, suitable for individuals with claustrophobia.<SEP>An MRI scanner with magnetic top and bottom plates and open sides, designed for patients with claustrophobia or discomfort in enclosed spaces.<SEP>An alternative magnetic resonance imaging machine with an open structure on both ends, designed to accommodate patients with claustrophobia.<SEP>An open MRI is an imaging scanner configuration featuring an open side design with magnetic top and bottom panels.<SEP>An open-sided magnetic resonance imaging design that accommodates individuals with claustrophobia.

Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Therapy
A type of immunotherapy that targets proteins such as PD-1 and PD-L1 to empower the immune system to fight cancer cells.<SEP>An immunotherapeutic treatment class that activates the body's immune cells against cancer, prescribed based on PD-L1 expression levels.<SEP>Immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy is a class of immunotherapy that targets proteins such as PD-1 and PD-L1 to assist the immune system in fighting cancer cells.

Cannabis Use
The consumption of cannabis, which can alter the amount of anesthesia required by a patient during surgical procedures.

Nicotine
An addictive chemical compound present in tobacco and vaping products that drives dependency and complicates cessation.<SEP>The addictive chemical found in tobacco products that causes withdrawal symptoms and urges to continue smoking or vaping.

Ear, Nose, and Throat Doctor
A specialist (ENT or otolaryngologist) consulted for evaluation and diagnosis of abnormalities in the neck, glands, tongue, or mouth.

Fine-Needle Aspiration
A biopsy procedure (FNA) that uses a thin needle to withdraw fluid or cell samples from a suspected tumor or lymph node.<SEP>A biopsy technique using thin needles to extract fluid or cell samples from a suspicious area.<SEP>A diagnostic biopsy procedure that uses a thin needle to extract fluid or tissue from thyroid nodules, often performed under ultrasound guidance.<SEP>A diagnostic needle biopsy procedure that samples thyroid tissue, capable of suggesting but not definitively diagnosing follicular or oncocytic carcinoma.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure using a thin needle to extract a tissue sample from suspicious or enlarged lymph nodes for testing.<SEP>A minimally invasive biopsy technique (FNA) utilizing fine needles to extract tissue or fluid samples from tumors or lymph nodes.

MSI-H/dMMR Mutation
A genetic alteration characterized by microsatellite instability or deficient mismatch repair, preventing the normal correction of DNA errors.<SEP>A genetic biomarker state featuring high microsatellite instability or deficient mismatch repair, indicating repair defects in DNA.

PD-L1 Testing
A biomarker diagnostic test that measures the expression of programmed death ligand 1 protein on cancer cells to determine candidate eligibility for immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy.<SEP>A diagnostic test that assesses programmed death-ligand 1 protein expression via combined positive score (CPS) to determine eligibility for immunotherapy.<SEP>A specialized laboratory assay calculating the Combined Positive Score (CPS) of programmed death ligand 1 to direct immunotherapy selection.

Tumor Mutational Burden-High
A biomarker profile (TMB-H) identified by 10 or more mutations per million base pairs of tumor DNA, indicative of eligibility for immune checkpoint inhibitors.<SEP>Tumor mutational burden-high (TMB-H) is a genomic classification defined by ten or more mutations per million base pairs of tumor DNA, often treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors.

American Joint Committee On Cancer
The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) is an organization that developed a widely used staging system to evaluate the extent, location, and subtype of cancer.<SEP>The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) is an organization that established a standardized cancer staging system to classify the extent, location, and subtype of cancer.

TNM Staging System
A cancer staging classification created by the AJCC assessing tumor depth (T), lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M) to assign cancer stages from 0 to IV.<SEP>A cancer staging framework based on tumor size/extent (T), regional lymph node involvement (N), and metastasis (M), ranging from stage 0 to stage 4.<SEP>A cancer staging system developed by the AJCC based on tumor size and invasion (T), lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M).<SEP>A standard cancer staging classification system based on tumor size (T), regional lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M) used to describe breast cancer progression.<SEP>A standard cancer staging system based on tumor size (T), lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M), evaluated both clinically and pathologically.<SEP>A standardized cancer classification system based on tumor size (T), lymph node involvement (N), and metastasis (M).<SEP>A standardized medical cancer staging classification assessing tumor size, lymph node involvement, and metastasis.<SEP>A standardized medical staging system categorizing tumor extent (T), lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M).<SEP>The TNM staging system is a classification framework used to stage throat and nasopharyngeal cancer by measuring primary tumor size (T), regional lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M).<SEP>The TNM staging system is a standardized cancer classification framework used to evaluate tumor extent, such as for squamous cell carcinoma of the nasopharynx.<SEP>The TNM staging system is an anatomic and prognostic cancer classification system that evaluates tumor size (T), lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M).<SEP>The TNM system is a cancer classification framework based on tumor size and depth (T), lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M).

Clinical Stage
A cancer staging category assigned prior to treatment based on physical exams, biopsies, and imaging tests.<SEP>A cancer staging classification determined prior to treatment, derived from physical examination, biopsy, and imaging evaluations.<SEP>A staging designation determined prior to definitive treatment based on physical exams, biopsies, and imaging tests, designated with the prefix 'c'.<SEP>Clinical stage is a cancer staging category assigned prior to treatment, based on physical examination, biopsy, and imaging results.<SEP>Clinical stage is a cancer staging classification assigned prior to treatment based on physical examinations, imaging, and biopsy results.<SEP>The cancer stage rating assessed before any treatment begins, designated as cTNM based on clinical evaluations.

Pathologic Stage
A cancer staging classification established after surgical resection through laboratory examination of tumor tissue and regional lymph nodes.<SEP>A surgical cancer staging classification determined through microscopic examination of tissue removed during surgery.<SEP>A surgical staging category determined through laboratory examination of tissue removed during surgery, designated with the prefix 'p'.<SEP>Pathologic stage is a surgical staging classification determined by pathological examination of tissue and lymph nodes removed during surgery.<SEP>Pathologic stage, or surgical stage, is a cancer staging category determined through the examination of tissue removed during surgery.<SEP>The surgical stage determined by microscopic examination of tissue removed during surgery, designated as pTNM.

Anatomic Staging
A cancer staging category determined strictly by tumor size, lymph node status, and distant metastatic spread.<SEP>A classification of cancer extent based strictly on tumor size (T), regional lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M).<SEP>A staging method based purely on the physical extent of cancer, determined by tumor size (T), regional lymph node status (N), and distant metastasis (M).

Prognostic Staging
A cancer staging category that integrates anatomical TNM factors and standard-of-care assumptions to predict disease outcomes.<SEP>A comprehensive staging category incorporating anatomic TNM, tumor grade, and biomarker status (HER2, ER, PR) assuming standard-of-care treatment.<SEP>A staging method that combines anatomic TNM data with other factors such as Epstein-Barr virus levels and standard-of-care assumptions, subdivided into clinical and pathologic stages.

Locoregional Disease
A classification of cancer describing a tumor that has extended into local tissues, organs, or regional lymph nodes near the oral cavity.<SEP>A classification of cancer spread, also termed local metastasis or locally advanced disease, involving adjacent structures such as the axillary lymph nodes.<SEP>A clinical classification referring to cancer that has spread to nearby tissue, organs, or lymph nodes within the head and neck region.

Metastatic Disease
A severe disease classification describing cancer that has spread to distant organs, such as the lungs or liver, or distant lymph nodes.<SEP>An advanced classification of cancer where malignant cells have spread to distant organs, such as the lungs or liver.

Numbered Cancer Stages
A cancer classification framework ranking severity from Stage 0 to Stage 4 based on combined TNM diagnostic scores.

Acute Myeloid Leukemia
A fatal type of blood cancer starting in the stem cells of bone marrow, characterized by the accumulation of abnormal, immature white blood cells known as myeloblasts.<SEP>A form of leukemia characterized by genetic abnormalities like core binding factor (CBF) or FLT3 mutations, treated with targeted agents and chemotherapy.<SEP>A type of hematologic cancer starting in the bone marrow that is associated with blasts in the blood and coagulopathy.<SEP>Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a blood cancer characterized by abnormal myeloid blasts that fail to mature properly, resulting in a buildup in the bone marrow and blood.<SEP>Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a blood cancer characterized by the buildup of immature white blood cells (myeloblasts) in the bone marrow and blood, preventing normal blood cell production.<SEP>Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a cancer of the blood and bone marrow characterized by abnormal blood cell production, specific cellular markers, and genetic mutations.<SEP>Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a category of cancer that originates in the bone marrow and requires specialized diagnostic procedures like bone marrow biopsies and flow cytometry.<SEP>Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a form of blood and bone marrow cancer characterized by specific chromosomal and genetic abnormalities.<SEP>Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a form of blood cancer characterized by abnormal white blood cells, distinct cellular biomarkers, and specific genetic mutations.<SEP>Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a form of cancer that originates in blood stem cells within bone marrow, leading to the rapid proliferation of abnormal myeloblasts.<SEP>Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a type of blood cancer requiring specialized multidisciplinary treatment and evaluation through various diagnostic tests.<SEP>Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a blood cancer that begins in the bone marrow's stem cells and presents with various adult subtypes.<SEP>Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a type of blood cancer that starts in the bone marrow stem cells and leads to a buildup of immature myeloblasts.<SEP>Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is an aggressive cancer of the blood and bone marrow involving excessive immature white blood cells, representing a rare serious complication of cancer therapy.

data.entity_name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma Of The Mouth
data.content:
Squamous Cell Carcinoma Of The Mouth
A form of mouth cancer originating in the epithelial squamous cells lining the inside of the mouth and lip mucosa, staged using TNM criteria.

Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia
A specific subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) characterized by distinct genetic and clinical features.<SEP>Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL) is a rare subtype of Acute Myeloid Leukemia defined by the presence of the abnormal fusion gene PML::RARA.<SEP>Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a rare subtype of AML defined by the presence of the abnormal PML::RARA fusion gene.

Blastic Plasmacytoid Dendritic Cell Neoplasm
A rare hematologic neoplasm discussed alongside acute myeloid leukemia subtypes.<SEP>A rare subtype of leukemia related to AML, often prompting lymph node or skin lesion biopsies for confirmation.<SEP>Blastic Plasmacytoid Dendritic Cell Neoplasm (BPDCN) is a specific subtype category of AML that may necessitate lymph node or skin lesion biopsies.<SEP>Blastic Plasmacytoid Dendritic Cell Neoplasm (BPDCN) is an aggressive cancer subtype related to AML that can manifest in blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes, or skin.<SEP>Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm (BPDCN) is an aggressive subtype or related hematologic neoplasm affecting the blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes, and skin.

Head And Neck Cancers
A broader category of cancers that encompasses cancers of the throat and oropharynx.<SEP>A category of cancers affecting the head and neck region, often spreading to regional cervical lymph nodes.<SEP>A group of cancers that arise in the head or neck region of the body, whose treatment is determined by tumor location.

Resectable Tumor
A surgical classification denoting a tumor that can be completely removed through surgical intervention.<SEP>A tumor classification indicating that the cancerous mass can be completely removed through surgical intervention.<SEP>A tumor classification indicating the malignant growth can be safely and entirely excised through surgical intervention.

Unresectable Tumor
A surgical classification indicating a tumor that cannot be safely or completely removed surgically, often due to involvement of major blood vessels or vital structures.<SEP>A tumor classification indicating that the mass cannot be safely or completely removed surgically, often due to involvement of critical veins, arteries, or structures.<SEP>A tumor classification indicating the growth cannot be completely removed surgically due to involvement of critical structures such as blood vessels.

Extranodal Extension
A condition where malignant tumor cells penetrate the capsule of a lymph node and invade the surrounding soft tissues.

Blood
A specialized biological tissue composed of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets that transports oxygen, nutrients, and waste while supporting immunity.

Myeloid Blasts
Immature white blood cells produced in the bone marrow whose maturation arrest leads to acute myeloid leukemia.<SEP>Immature white blood cells whose abnormal presence in the bone marrow or blood (typically 20% or more) serves as the primary diagnostic criterion for AML.<SEP>Myeloid blasts are immature white blood cells that normally mature into granulocytes but accumulate abnormally in bone marrow and blood during AML.

Diagnostic Tests For AML
A group of clinical procedures and laboratory assessments, including blood tests, bone marrow aspirate and biopsy, and genetic testing, used to detect, confirm, and evaluate AML.

Hematopoietic Stem Cells
Early blood-forming cells located in bone marrow that continuously self-renew and differentiate into mature blood cells.<SEP>Hematopoietic stem cells are early blood-forming cells in the bone marrow capable of self-renewal and differentiating into all types of blood cells.<SEP>Hematopoietic stem cells are immature blood-forming precursor cells situated in bone marrow that give rise to all specialized blood cell lineages.<SEP>Immature blood-forming cells originating in bone marrow capable of developing into red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.<SEP>Primitive blood-forming stem cells residing within the bone marrow that differentiate into all mature blood cell lineages.

Myeloblasts
Immature blood cells formed from myeloid progenitor cells that develop into non-lymphoid blood cells.<SEP>Immature blood cells formed from myeloid progenitor cells, referred to alongside lymphoblasts as blasts in leukemia.<SEP>Immature white blood cells that normally mature into infection-fighting granulocytes, but proliferate abnormally as leukemia blasts in AML.<SEP>Myeloblasts, or myeloid blasts, are immature white blood cells that build up in the bone marrow and blood in patients with AML instead of maturing.

Bone Marrow Aspirate And Biopsy
A bone marrow aspirate and biopsy is a diagnostic medical procedure where samples of solid bone and liquid marrow are collected to test for leukemia and genetic abnormalities.<SEP>A core diagnostic procedure used to extract bone marrow fluid and tissue to evaluate blast percentage, biomarker status, and genetic mutations.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure performed to sample bone marrow for AML biomarker assessment and genetic testing.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure used to extract and examine bone marrow cells to guide AML diagnosis and treatment decisions.<SEP>Bedside medical procedures where liquid bone marrow and a small bone specimen are extracted, typically from the hip, to diagnose and analyze AML.<SEP>Diagnostic clinical procedures used to extract and examine bone marrow tissue for blast percentage, chromosome abnormalities, and biomarker mutations.

Complete Blood Count
A complete blood count (CBC) is a general diagnostic blood test that measures white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets.<SEP>A complete blood count is a diagnostic laboratory procedure that measures levels of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.<SEP>A core diagnostic laboratory test that measures red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets, hemoglobin, and blast cells to assess health and disease state.<SEP>A diagnostic blood test measuring levels of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets to evaluate patient health and organ function during cancer assessment.<SEP>A routine blood test that measures red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets to evaluate general health and treatment readiness.<SEP>A routine laboratory blood test measuring cellular components including RBCs, WBCs, and platelets to evaluate hematologic health and disease.<SEP>A standard blood test (CBC) that measures levels of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets to check overall health.<SEP>A standard blood test measuring white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets to evaluate overall health and detect underlying complications.<SEP>A standard blood test that measures red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets to evaluate general health prior to treatment.<SEP>A standard diagnostic blood test (CBC) that measures levels of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, often paired with a differential to identify blasts.<SEP>A standard laboratory blood test (CBC) recommended to assess blood health and aid treatment planning.<SEP>A standard laboratory blood test category that measures components including hemoglobin, platelets, absolute neutrophil count, and white blood cell differential.<SEP>A standard routine blood test (CBC) recommended during initial medical evaluations for colorectal cancer.

AML Specialist
A medical oncologist or hematologist specializing in the diagnosis and management of acute myeloid leukemia.<SEP>A physician specializing in hematologic malignancies and specifically trained in diagnosing and treating acute myeloid leukemia.<SEP>An AML specialist is a medical professional with expertise in diagnosing, managing, and treating acute myeloid leukemia.

AML
Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a cancer of the blood and bone marrow characterized by abnormal blood cell production, requiring comprehensive diagnostic testing, monitoring, and treatment.<SEP>Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a type of cancer characterized by leukemic blasts, for which chemotherapy is the standard of care.<SEP>Acute Myeloid Leukemia, a cancer originating in the bone marrow characterized by the abnormal proliferation of myeloid blasts throughout the blood and bones.

Comprehensive Metabolic Panel
A blood chemistry profile evaluating the functional status of vital organs such as the kidneys and liver.<SEP>A blood test assessing chemicals, proteins, and substances in the blood to evaluate organ function such as the kidneys and liver.<SEP>A category of blood tests that evaluates kidney and liver function, electrolytes, creatinine, and blood urea nitrogen levels.<SEP>A comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) is a blood test measuring chemicals and proteins to evaluate liver and kidney function, assisting in cancer treatment planning.<SEP>A comprehensive metabolic panel (chemistry profile) is a blood test evaluating how well the liver, kidneys, and other organs function.<SEP>A comprehensive metabolic panel is a blood screening test measuring up to 14 chemicals to evaluate kidney and liver function.<SEP>A comprehensive metabolic panel is a diagnostic blood testing procedure that measures substances related to kidney function, liver health, and calcium levels.<SEP>A diagnostic blood panel evaluating blood sugar, calcium, electrolytes, and the function of the liver and kidneys.<SEP>A diagnostic blood panel measuring up to 14 chemicals in the blood to evaluate kidney and liver function.<SEP>A diagnostic blood test (CMP) that evaluates 14 substances in blood plasma to assess liver and kidney function.<SEP>A diagnostic blood test that evaluates kidney and liver function, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and electrolyte balance.<SEP>A routine blood panel (CMP) used in the AML workup to check organ function, particularly of the liver and kidneys, alongside electrolyte balance.

Lumbar Puncture
A diagnostic procedure performed to examine cerebrospinal fluid, commonly utilized in leukemia staging and evaluation.<SEP>A lumbar puncture, or spinal tap, is a diagnostic procedure performed to sample cerebrospinal fluid from the spinal column to check for malignant cells.<SEP>A lumbar puncture, or spinal tap, is a medical procedure in which a needle is inserted into the lower back to extract spinal fluid to check for leukemia cells.<SEP>A medical procedure performed to evaluate cerebrospinal fluid, utilized when central nervous system involvement is suspected.<SEP>A medical procedure, also known as a spinal tap, where a needle is inserted into the lower back to sample spinal fluid to check for leukemia cells.<SEP>A procedure that removes cerebrospinal fluid to examine it for the presence of cancer cells in primary CNS lymphoma patients.<SEP>A specialized diagnostic procedure included in AML workups to check for leukemic involvement in the central nervous system.

Liver Function Tests
A clinical testing category that assesses liver health and bile duct patency by measuring chemicals made or processed by the liver.<SEP>A group of blood tests (LFTs) measuring liver-produced chemicals to determine liver health or detect cancer spread.<SEP>A set of diagnostic blood tests assessing liver health by measuring chemicals made or processed by the liver.<SEP>Blood tests that evaluate enzymes and chemicals synthesized or processed by the liver to detect organ impairment or metastatic spread.<SEP>Blood tests that measure liver enzymes to detect liver damage or possible cancer spread, often performed with a blood chemistry profile.

Blood Clotting Tests
A series of laboratory diagnostic tests designed to evaluate the blood's ability to form clots and identify bleeding risks in AML patients.<SEP>Laboratory tests that evaluate the coagulation system to assess bleeding and clotting risks during AML diagnosis and treatment.

Human Leukocyte Antigen Typing
A specialized genetic and immunological test performed to match patients with potential donors for bone marrow or stem cell transplants.<SEP>A specialized genetic blood test (HLA typing) used to identify matching donors for potential stem cell or bone marrow transplantation.

Brain CT Without Contrast
A non-invasive computed tomography brain scan conducted when bleeding in the central nervous system is suspected.

Brain MRI With Contrast
A contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging scan of the brain performed to evaluate suspected leukemic meningitis.

Heart Tests
A category of cardiac evaluations conducted to evaluate heart performance and monitor for potential treatment-induced side effects.<SEP>A group of diagnostic evaluations used to determine cardiac function and detect side effects before and during cancer treatments.<SEP>Cardiovascular examinations performed as part of the AML diagnostic workup to evaluate heart function before leukemia treatment begins.<SEP>Diagnostic cardiovascular examinations performed to evaluate cardiac health and ensure the heart can tolerate leukemia therapy.

Genetic Testing
A category of testing used to evaluate inherited genetic mutations received from birth parents, distinct from tumor-only somatic testing.<SEP>A diagnostic blood analysis recommended for all individuals diagnosed with ovarian cancer to detect inherited germline BRCA mutations.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure assessing hereditary and familial cancer risks and genetic alterations in patients with ovarian cancer.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure encompassing hereditary germline testing and somatic tumor testing to detect harmful mutations in DNA.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure performed on blood, saliva, cheek swab, or tumor tissue to identify germline or somatic genetic mutations.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure performed to detect mutations and genetic alterations associated with specific cancers and tumors.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure used to find abnormal gene mutations, distinguishing between inherited germline mutations and acquired somatic mutations.<SEP>A medical diagnostic test performed on individuals or relatives to identify inherited mutations and risk factors for diseases such as cancer.<SEP>Diagnostic tests that analyze genes to guide medical decisions and determine tailored cancer treatment options.<SEP>Genetic testing is a diagnostic medical procedure used to identify specific inherited or acquired gene mutations associated with cancer risk.<SEP>Molecular analysis performed on biopsy tissue samples to assist in diagnosing thyroid cancer types.<SEP>Molecular and genetic laboratory analyses performed on bone marrow or blood to detect mutations and risk factors in leukemia and family history.<SEP>Specialized medical laboratory tests that detect inherited gene mutations to evaluate hereditary disease risks and guide targeted cancer therapies.

Central Nervous System Bleed
A serious medical complication involving intracranial or spinal hemorrhage that necessitates emergency brain imaging.

Leukemic Meningitis
A complication characterized by the spread of leukemic cells into the meninges and central nervous system, evaluated by brain MRI.<SEP>A complication of leukemia involving infiltration of the central nervous system membranes, requiring brain MRI assessment.<SEP>A medical complication involving swelling and leukemic infiltration of the membranes surrounding the brain.<SEP>Leukemic meningitis is a neurological complication where leukemia cells infiltrate and cause swelling in the outer lining of the brain.

Extramedullary Leukemia
A clinical presentation where acute myeloid leukemia cells accumulate outside the bone marrow and peripheral blood.<SEP>A condition where leukemic cells proliferate outside the bone marrow and peripheral blood, assessed via PET/CT imaging.

Leukemia
A blood cancer that originates in the bone marrow and can disseminate to lymph nodes, liver, spleen, skin, and central nervous system.<SEP>Leukemia is a general category of blood and bone marrow cancers that impairs normal blood cell production and clotting mechanisms.

Hematopoietic Cell Transplant
A therapeutic procedure and treatment category utilized in managing acute myeloid leukemia.<SEP>An allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant is a medical treatment event involving donor cell infusion that requires close HLA matching between donor and recipient.<SEP>Hematopoietic cell transplant is a specialized medical treatment option used in the management and treatment of AML.

HLA Typing
A diagnostic blood test category that identifies a patient's human leukocyte antigen markers to evaluate donor compatibility for transplants.<SEP>HLA typing is a diagnostic testing procedure performed to identify tissue antigens and establish compatibility between a patient and a potential donor prior to transplantation.

Bone Marrow Aspirate
A bedside procedure using a hollow needle to draw liquid bone marrow from the hip bone for cytological and laboratory testing.<SEP>A bone marrow aspirate is a bedside diagnostic procedure in which liquid bone marrow is drawn with a needle to assess cellular composition.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure using a hollow needle and syringe to extract liquid and cells from the bone marrow, typically from the pelvis.

Bone Marrow Biopsy
A bedside procedure using a wide needle to extract a small core of solid bone and marrow tissue from the pelvis for pathological analysis.<SEP>A bone marrow aspirate and biopsy is a diagnostic procedure that extracts bone marrow tissue and cells to confirm an AML diagnosis and evaluate blast percentage.<SEP>A bone marrow biopsy is a diagnostic procedure using a specialized needle to remove a small piece of bone marrow for histopathological evaluation.<SEP>A clinical procedure that extracts a core sample of bone marrow from the hip bone to evaluate disease status and confirm cancer diagnoses.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure in which a needle is used to extract bone marrow to check whether lymphoma has spread to the bones.<SEP>A procedure using a wider needle to remove a core solid sample of bone marrow tissue, often performed alongside an aspirate.

Coagulation Panel
A group of diagnostic blood clotting tests, also referred to as a disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) panel, that checks coagulation factors.<SEP>A standardized group of blood clotting tests, also referred to as a DIC panel, used to assess coagulation factors and detect clotting dysfunction.

Flow Cytometry
A laboratory method using light-sensitive dyes and light beams to count, analyze, and detect specific markers on blood and bone marrow cells.<SEP>A specialized laboratory diagnostic procedure used to analyze cellular surface proteins and confirm CLL.<SEP>A specialized laboratory procedure that utilizes dyes and light beams to count, analyze, and detect specific surface markers on cells from blood or bone marrow aspirates.<SEP>A specialized laboratory testing method used to detect patterns of proteins on cell surfaces to determine their immunophenotype for cancer diagnosis.<SEP>Flow cytometry is a laboratory diagnostic method used on blood or bone marrow aspirate samples to detect subtle cellular differences and identify immune cell markers.

Skin Lesion Biopsy
A diagnostic procedure performed to test skin lesion tissue in cases of suspected BPDCN.<SEP>A surgical or punch removal of skin lesion tissue to test for specific AML variants such as blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm.

Coagulopathy
A bleeding or clotting disorder resulting from an impaired coagulation process, commonly observed in leukemia patients.<SEP>A category of blood clotting disorder characterized by impaired coagulation, bleeding, bruising, or clot formation, commonly found in leukemia.

Karnofsky Performance Status
A clinical scale and scoring system used to assess a patient's functional capacity and ability to perform daily activities.<SEP>A clinical scoring system (KPS) used alongside ECOG to evaluate a patient's overall functional ability and guide cancer treatment decisions.<SEP>A standardized clinical rating scale used to quantify a patient's general well-being and ability to carry out everyday activities.<SEP>A standardized medical scoring scale utilized to quantify a patient's functional abilities, activity level, and general fitness.

Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation
A severe clotting disorder evaluated through coagulation panel testing in patients with leukemia.

Immunohistochemistry
A laboratory staining technique (IHC) utilizing chemical markers to visualize specific proteins in cancer or immune cells under a microscope.<SEP>A laboratory staining technique using chemical markers and microscopy to examine the immunophenotype of cells in tissue biopsies.<SEP>A laboratory staining technique using chemical markers to detect estrogen receptors, progesterone receptors, and HER2 protein levels under a microscope.<SEP>Immunohistochemistry (IHC) is a specialized microscopic staining technique that uses chemical markers to assess the immunophenotype of cells from tissue or biopsy samples.

Leukemia Predisposition Syndromes
Hereditary conditions passed down from biological parents that increase the risk of developing leukemia and influence clinical management.<SEP>Leukemia predisposition syndromes are hereditary cancer conditions passed down from parent to child that increase the risk of developing leukemia and can impact treatment.<SEP>Leukemia predisposition syndromes are hereditary cancer syndromes passed down biologically that increase leukemia risk and influence patient response to treatment.

AML Mutation Testing
AML mutation testing comprises laboratory methods used to identify genetic and chromosomal alterations unique to AML cancer cells in blood or bone marrow.<SEP>AML mutation testing comprises molecular and cytogenetic diagnostic tests—such as karyotype, FISH, NGS, and PCR—used to detect leukemia-specific chromosomal and gene abnormalities to guide therapy and prognosis.

Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization
Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a laboratory cytogenetic test used to identify missing or extra chromosomal material, including the 17p deletion.<SEP>Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a laboratory method using dye-labeled probes to identify specific, small genetic abnormalities in DNA without requiring cell growth.<SEP>Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a molecular cytogenetic testing technique that uses fluorescent dye probes bound to DNA to identify specific and sub-microscopic chromosomal abnormalities.

Karyotyping
Karyotyping is a cytogenetic testing method that visualizes an individual's 23 chromosome pairs from growing cells to identify structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities.

Next-Generation Sequencing
A detailed DNA sequencing diagnostic method used to identify gene mutations that affect gene function.<SEP>A high-throughput laboratory testing technique used to analyze multiple cancer biomarkers simultaneously.<SEP>A high-throughput molecular technique (NGS) used to identify DNA sequence variations and genetic mutations across cancer cells.<SEP>Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is an advanced molecular sequencing method used to analyze DNA sequences and identify specific genetic mutations that guide cancer treatment.<SEP>Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is an advanced molecular testing method that determines DNA sequences and identifies fine genetic mutations.

Polymerase Chain Reaction
A sensitive laboratory process (PCR) that creates millions to billions of copies of DNA, which can subsequently be used for next-generation sequencing.<SEP>A sensitive molecular testing technique that amplifies DNA or RNA to detect minimal residual abnormal cells and gene rearrangements.<SEP>Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a molecular testing technique used to examine DNA and identify specific genetic abnormalities and mutations in leukemia cells.<SEP>Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a sensitive laboratory technique that amplifies DNA or RNA to detect rare abnormal cells, evaluate treatment response, and monitor gene rearrangements.

FLT3
FLT3 is a specific gene and receptor tyrosine kinase protein referenced as an example of a biomarker that can undergo mutation in acute myeloid leukemia cells.

RUNX1::RUNX1T1
RUNX1::RUNX1T1 is a specific gene rearrangement and fusion product resulting from chromosome translocation t(8;21)(q22;q22) in acute myeloid leukemia.

Chromosome Translocation
Chromosome translocation is a structural genetic alteration involving the exchange or switching of material between two distinct chromosomes.

Gene Rearrangement
Gene rearrangement is a genetic alteration occurring at the molecular level where portions of genes are structurally rearranged or fused together.

Chromosomal Inversion
Chromosomal inversion is a structural genetic abnormality characterized by the switching or reversal of segments within a single chromosome, such as inv(16) and inv(3).

Chromosomal Deletion
Chromosomal deletion is a structural genetic abnormality where a segment or an entire chromosome or gene is lost or missing, exemplified by del(5q).

Gene Amplification
Gene amplification is a molecular abnormality where the copy number of a whole or partial chromosome or gene is increased or duplicated.

Point Mutation
Point mutation is a genetic alteration characterized by a change within a specific segment or nucleotide base of a gene.

Hematopoietic Cell Donor
Hematopoietic cell donors are biological family members evaluated for stem cell or bone marrow donation who may be screened for inherited leukemia predisposition syndromes.

Molecular Tumor Profiling
Molecular tumor profiling, also termed genomic testing or gene expression profiling, refers to diagnostic testing targeting somatic genetic mutations within leukemia cells to predict prognosis and guide therapy.

Cardiologist
A cardiologist is a heart specialist who evaluates cardiac health and monitors potential treatment-related side effects on heart function.<SEP>A medical specialist in heart health who evaluates cardiac function and monitors treatment side effects.

Karyotype
A diagnostic genetic test that visualizes chromosome pairs from blood or bone marrow samples to identify abnormalities, deletions, or rearrangements.<SEP>A karyotype is a cytogenetic test that evaluates a picture of chromosomes to detect missing, extra, rearranged, or abnormal chromosomal structures.<SEP>A karyotype is a laboratory evaluation that detects chromosomal abnormalities, including complex karyotypes involving three or more unrelated alterations.

Computed Tomography Scan
A diagnostic imaging test (CT scan) of the chest and abdomen used to determine whether rectal cancer has metastasized to distant organs such as the liver or lungs.<SEP>A type of imaging test using X-rays and computer processing to create detailed cross-sectional pictures of internal body structures.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging Scan
A non-radiation imaging modality utilizing radio waves and strong magnetic fields to visualize internal tissues.

Positron Emission Tomography Scan
A diagnostic imaging test that uses radioactive tracers to identify active cancer cells based on glucose uptake.

Electrocardiogram
A cardiac test that measures the electrical activity, rate, and rhythm of the heart, including the QTc interval.<SEP>A non-invasive cardiac test that measures electrical heart activity to assess rhythm, rate, and QT intervals.

Echocardiogram
An echocardiogram is an ultrasound-based cardiac diagnostic test used to evaluate heart structure, valve function, and ejection fraction.<SEP>An ultrasound procedure of the heart that records structural details and assesses heart function, such as ejection fraction.<SEP>An ultrasound-based heart test that uses sound waves to create moving images of the heart.

Patient
An individual diagnosed with cervical pre-cancer or cancer, receiving diagnostic staging, treatment, and ongoing surveillance.<SEP>An individual undergoing diagnostic evaluations, biopsies, and treatments, responsible for maintaining personal health records in a medical binder.<SEP>An individual undergoing diagnostic evaluations, imaging, and monitoring for leukemia.<SEP>The individual undergoing evaluation and imaging tests for suspected or diagnosed prostate cancer.

Reverse Transcriptase PCR
A specialized form of polymerase chain reaction used to detect specific genetic rearrangements such as PML::RARA.<SEP>Reverse transcriptase (RT) PCR is a specialized type of polymerase chain reaction used to detect specific gene rearrangements such as PML::RARA.

Brain CT Scan
A brain CT scan is a diagnostic imaging procedure using x-rays and computer technology to quickly identify bleeding inside the brain.<SEP>A computed tomography scan specifically focused on the brain to detect intracranial bleeding.

Brain MRI Scan
A brain MRI scan is an imaging test using magnets and radio waves to evaluate the brain and detect leukemic meningitis or swelling without radiation.<SEP>A magnetic resonance imaging scan of the brain used to detect complications such as leukemic meningitis.

Prolonged QTc Interval
A cardiac conduction anomaly detected on an ECG where ventricular repolarization is abnormally delayed, potentially caused by cancer therapies.

Multidisciplinary Team
A collaborative group of healthcare professionals, including specialists and care providers, responsible for diagnosing and treating the patient.<SEP>A collaborative team of diverse healthcare and psychosocial professionals who collectively plan, coordinate, and implement individualized breast cancer care.<SEP>A multidisciplinary team (MDT) consists of health care and psychosocial professionals from diverse backgrounds who collaborate to plan and implement cancer treatment.<SEP>A multidisciplinary team (MDT) is a collaborative group of healthcare and psychosocial care professionals from diverse specialties who coordinate, plan, and deliver treatment for cancer patients.<SEP>A specialized group of diverse healthcare providers and experts working together to diagnose, stage, and plan treatment for pancreatic cancer patients.

Hematologist
A hematologist or hematologic oncologist is a medical doctor and expert specializing in the diagnosis and treatment of blood diseases and blood cancers.<SEP>A hematologist or hematologic oncologist is a medical doctor and specialist who diagnoses and treats blood disorders and blood cancers like AML.

Prolonged QTc
Prolonged QTc is a cardiac condition in which the heart muscle takes longer than normal to recharge between beats, potentially leading to dangerous arrhythmias.

Ejection Fraction
Ejection fraction is a measurement of the percentage of blood pumped out of the heart's left side during each contraction, serving as an indicator of cardiac function.

Genetic And Biomarker Tests
Genetic and biomarker tests are diagnostic procedures used to detect specific gene mutations and chromosomal abnormalities to determine AML subtype and prognosis.

Insurance Provider
Healthcare insurers responsible for covering the costs of diagnostic tests, treatments, and procedures for cancer patients.

Catheter
A medical device consisting of a long, thin tube placed into a large vein, typically in the upper arm, to administer systemic therapy, fluids, and blood products.<SEP>A thin, long tube placed into a large vein, typically in the upper arm, used to administer systemic therapy, fluids, and blood products.

Port
A central venous catheter inserted into an upper chest vein beneath the collarbone to deliver continuous chemotherapy infusions.<SEP>A small, round medical device implanted in the chest to provide venous access for delivering systemic chemotherapy and other therapies.<SEP>A small, round vascular access disc surgically placed in the chest to deliver systemic therapies and medications.

Side Effects
Secondary adverse physiological reactions that occur as a result of cancer treatments such as chemotherapy and systemic therapies.

Antimetabolites
A class of chemotherapy drugs that includes capecitabine, fluorouracil, gemcitabine, and methotrexate.<SEP>A class of chemotherapy drugs that inhibit the utilization of DNA building blocks to prevent cancer cell replication.<SEP>A class of chemotherapy drugs, including cytarabine, cladribine, clofarabine, fludarabine, and methotrexate, that prevent the building blocks of DNA from being used.

Anthracyclines
A class of chemotherapy drugs that damage and disrupt DNA replication, leading to cell death in both cancerous and non-cancerous cells.<SEP>A class of chemotherapy drugs that includes doxorubicin, doxorubicin liposomal injection, and epirubicin.<SEP>A class of chemotherapy drugs, including daunorubicin, idarubicin, and mitoxantrone, that disrupt DNA production and may cause cardiac side effects.

Hypomethylating Agents
A category of therapeutic agents that prevent methyl groups from binding to DNA, helping silenced genes reactivate so leukemic blasts can mature normally.<SEP>A class of drugs that inhibit methyl groups from binding to DNA, allowing silenced genes to reactivate and leukemic blasts to mature.<SEP>A class of therapies, including azacitidine and decitabine, that block methyl groups from DNA to allow leukemic blasts to mature normally.

Ovarian Cancer
A cancer category associated with inherited germline mutations in genes including BRCA1 and BRCA2.<SEP>A cancer of the ovaries frequently tied to inherited mutations in BRCA1, BRCA2, and related genes.<SEP>A category of gynecologic cancer that commonly begins in the epithelial tissue surrounding the ovaries or in the fallopian tubes.<SEP>A form of cancer affecting the ovaries, characterized by symptoms like bloating, abdominal pain, and pelvic pressure, evaluated through physical exams and imaging to determine clinical stage and surgical eligibility.<SEP>A form of cancer that originates in the ovaries and may spread to the abdomen, lungs, or other parts of the body.<SEP>A group of malignancies affecting the ovaries and related reproductive structures, commonly diagnosed through biopsy, imaging, and surgical evaluation.<SEP>A gynecological cancer characterized by symptoms such as pelvic or abdominal pain, bloating, and difficulty eating, which can be diagnosed and managed through surgery, blood tests, and biomarker testing.<SEP>A gynecological malignancy linked through family medical history to a higher genetic risk of prostate cancer.<SEP>A malignancy affecting the ovaries and pelvic region, categorized into stages I through IV based on spread.<SEP>A malignancy whose risk is substantially increased in individuals carrying inherited BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations.<SEP>A medical diagnosis and category of malignancy originating in the ovaries, staged from Stage I to Stage IV.<SEP>A type of reproductive cancer associated with increased susceptibility among individuals affected by Lynch syndrome.<SEP>Ovarian cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of cells in the ovaries, commonly treated with surgery, chemotherapy, and maintenance therapies.<SEP>Ovarian cancer is a malignant condition affecting the ovaries, linked to an increased risk in people with Lynch syndrome.

Standard Of Care
A clinical classification referring to the best-known, evidence-based treatment regimen for a particular disease derived from past clinical trials.<SEP>The best-known and most widely accepted treatment protocols established through clinical trials.

Preferred Therapies
A classification of cancer treatments supported by the strongest clinical evidence regarding efficacy and safety.<SEP>A treatment categorization designating therapies supported by the strongest clinical evidence of efficacy and safety compared to alternatives.

Multi-Agent Chemotherapy
A chemotherapy regimen category that combines multiple distinct therapeutic agents working through different mechanisms to treat cancer.<SEP>A treatment regimen combining multiple chemotherapy drugs with different mechanisms of action to treat AML.

Intrathecal Chemotherapy
A chemotherapy administration method where drugs are injected directly into the cerebrospinal fluid within the spinal canal to treat cancer cells in the central nervous system.<SEP>A specialized chemotherapy administration category where medications are infused directly into the cerebrospinal fluid to treat cancer cells in the CSF or spine.<SEP>A specialized chemotherapy administration method where drugs such as cytarabine or methotrexate are injected directly into spinal fluid.<SEP>A specialized chemotherapy administration route where drugs are infused directly into the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).<SEP>A specialized chemotherapy category involving injection directly into the spinal fluid surrounding the spine and brain to treat central nervous system involvement.

CD33 Protein
A cell surface protein category commonly present on leukemic blasts in AML, targeted by conjugated therapies like gemtuzumab ozogamicin.

FLT3 Mutation
A category of genetic alterations in AML, including FLT3-ITD and FLT3-TKD, targeted by specific kinase inhibitor drugs.<SEP>A category of recurrent genetic mutations in AML, including FLT3-ITD and FLT3-TKD, targeted by specific small-molecule inhibitors.

Core Binding Factor AML
A genetic subtype category of AML characterized by CBF abnormalities causing a shortage of mature blood cells.

Female Reproductive System
An anatomical biological system comprising the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and vagina involved in reproduction.<SEP>The female reproductive system is a biological organ system comprising the cervix, uterus, vagina, ovaries, and fallopian tubes, functioning together for sexual reproduction.

Epithelial Ovarian Cancer
The most common classification of ovarian cancer, originating in the outer layer of tissue surrounding the ovaries.<SEP>The predominant category of ovarian cancer arising from the surface epithelial layer of the ovaries or nearby fallopian tubes.

Treatment Team
A multidisciplinary clinical team responsible for managing patient care, selecting biomarker tests, and designing oncology therapy plans.<SEP>A multidisciplinary group of healthcare professionals, including oncologists, nurses, and specialists, responsible for planning and delivering ovarian cancer care.<SEP>A multidisciplinary group of healthcare providers responsible for planning cancer treatment, performing procedures, and managing patient side effects.<SEP>A multidisciplinary medical group including endocrinologists, radiologists, nuclear medicine specialists, surgeons, and oncologists that designs and executes a thyroid cancer treatment plan.<SEP>A multidisciplinary medical group responsible for administering care, monitoring adverse side effects, providing supportive medications, and advising cancer patients.<SEP>A multidisciplinary medical group that utilizes biopsy, pathology, and molecular diagnostic findings to formulate patient care plans.<SEP>A treatment team is a multidisciplinary group of medical professionals providing care, counseling, and surgical management for bladder cancer patients.<SEP>The medical and healthcare providers responsible for monitoring patient symptoms, weighing treatment risks, and determining therapy eligibility.<SEP>The medical care team responsible for delivering standard or systemic therapy, managing side effects, and evaluating eligibility for clinical trials.<SEP>The multidisciplinary group of healthcare professionals managing chemotherapy administration, side effects, and follow-up care.<SEP>The multidisciplinary healthcare team responsible for managing patient care, providing preoperative instructions, and guiding therapy decisions.

Gynecologic Oncologist
A specialized doctor and surgeon who specializes in surgery and chemotherapy for gynecologic cancers, typically performing initial surgeries.<SEP>A specialized medical practitioner with expertise in performing surgery and administering chemotherapy for female reproductive cancers.<SEP>A surgical specialist with expert training in treating cancers that originate in female reproductive organs.

High-Grade Serous Carcinoma
One of the most common and aggressive subtypes of ovarian cancer, typically treated with a combination of surgery and chemotherapy.<SEP>The most common and fast-growing type of epithelial ovarian cancer.

High-Grade Endometrioid Carcinoma
One of the most common subtypes of epithelial ovarian cancer.<SEP>One of the most common subtypes of ovarian cancer, commonly managed with surgical intervention and chemotherapy.

Less Common Ovarian Cancers
Rare forms of ovarian cancer that can originate in the epithelium, supporting tissues, or reproductive cells.

Primary Peritoneal Cancer
A cancer that forms in the lining of the abdominal wall and organs, treated similarly to ovarian cancer.

Fallopian Tube Cancer
A type of cancer that begins in the fallopian tube, treated under similar protocols as ovarian cancer.

Cancer Grade
A classification metric estimating the speed of tumor growth and spreading potential, divided into low grade (LG) and high grade (HG).<SEP>A classification rating indicating how abnormal cancer cells appear under a microscope and how rapidly they may grow and spread.<SEP>A classification scale ranging from GX to G4 assessing cellular differentiation and the likelihood of tumor growth and spread.<SEP>A histologic staging factor that assesses the abnormality of tumor cells under a microscope to predict growth and spread rates.<SEP>A histological measurement describing the degree of abnormality of tumor cells under a microscope, categorized into GX, G1, G2, and G3.

Cancer Stage
A classification scale from stage 0 to stage 4 describing how deeply a tumor has invaded the bladder wall layers and spread to distant sites.<SEP>A diagnostic categorization describing the extent to which cancer has spread from the ovary throughout the body.

Low-Grade Serous Carcinoma
A less common subtype of epithelial ovarian cancer characterized by slower growth compared to high-grade forms.

Low-Grade Endometrioid Carcinoma
A less common type of epithelial ovarian cancer.

Carcinosarcoma
A rare and aggressive type of epithelial ovarian cancer, also known as malignant mixed Mullerian tumors.

Clear Cell Carcinoma
A less common histology of epithelial ovarian cancer.

Mucinous Carcinoma
A less common subtype of epithelial ovarian cancer.

Borderline Epithelial Tumor
An ovarian tumor with low malignant potential classified under less common epithelial ovarian neoplasms.

Malignant Sex-Cord Stromal Tumors
A rare category of non-epithelial ovarian cancer arising from the supportive structural tissues of the ovary.

Malignant Germ Cell Tumors
A less common type of non-epithelial ovarian cancer that originates in the reproductive egg cells.

Abdominal And Pelvic Exam
A physical clinical evaluation utilized in the assessment and diagnostic workup of suspected ovarian cancer.

Genetic Counselors
Healthcare professionals on the multidisciplinary care team who specialize in assessing hereditary risk factors and genetic testing for cancer.

Social Workers
Healthcare professionals who assist cancer patients in coping with daily problems, emotional distress, and financial or insurance stresses.<SEP>Supportive care professionals within the treatment team who assist cancer patients with psychosocial, logistical, and emotional needs.

Cervical Cancer
A cancer affecting the cervix, diagnosed and evaluated through various biopsies, blood tests, and imaging procedures to guide treatment planning.<SEP>A cancer of the cervix staged using tumor size, lymph node involvement, and distant spread to guide treatment planning.<SEP>A gynecological malignancy that develops in the cervix, commonly diagnosed via cervical biopsy and managed with surgery, radiation, or systemic therapies.<SEP>A malignancy caused by HPV; a medical history of cervical cancer or precancer is a risk factor for anal cancer.<SEP>A malignancy of the cervix caused by HPV, for which screening via Pap or HPV/Pap co-testing is recommended.<SEP>A malignancy of the cervix encompassing types such as squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and adenosquamous carcinoma, staged based on the spread of the tumor.<SEP>A malignancy of the cervix evaluated and staged through diagnostic imaging and physical examinations.<SEP>A malignancy of the cervix known to be caused by persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus.<SEP>A malignancy of the cervix requiring structured post-treatment surveillance, monitoring for recurrence, and biomarker profiling for advanced cases.<SEP>A malignancy of the cervix that can spread to pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes, as well as distant organs such as the liver, lungs, or bones.<SEP>A type of cancer affecting the cervix, specifically screened and detected via a Pap test.<SEP>A type of cancer that develops in the cervix, commonly treated with chemoradiation, brachytherapy, and systemic therapies.<SEP>Cervical cancer is a common malignancy of the female reproductive system that arises from abnormal cellular changes in the cervix, predominantly linked to human papillomavirus (HPV).<SEP>Cervical cancer is a malignancy originating in the cervix, commonly caused by persistent HPV infection and categorized into various histological types including squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma.<SEP>Cervical cancer is a type of cancer addressed in the text, categorized into specific subtypes and treated using modalities such as surgery, chemoradiation, and systemic therapy.

Uterine Cancer
A cancer of the uterus linked to hereditary mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes including MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, and PMS2.<SEP>A cancer of the uterus linked to hereditary mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes such as MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, and PMS2.<SEP>A form of cancer involving the uterus that can be ruled out using an endometrial biopsy.<SEP>Uterine cancer refers to malignancies originating in the uterus, such as endometrial cancer and uterine sarcomas, which are diagnosed and treated differently from cervical cancer.

Abdominal Exam
A physical examination where a provider feels areas of the abdomen to check organ size, tenderness, and signs of ascites or fluid buildup.

Pelvic Exam
