A clinical physical exam assessing abnormal changes in the ovaries, cervix, and uterus, often utilizing a speculum.

Pap Test
A cervical screening procedure involving the collection and testing of cervical cells for abnormalities and cancer.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure where cervical cells are sampled during a pelvic exam to detect cervical cancer or pre-cancer.

Endometrial Biopsy
A procedure sampling the uterine lining during an initial pelvic evaluation to rule out uterine cancer.

Rectovaginal Exam
A physical examination evaluating the rectum and vagina simultaneously to check for cancer spread in the intervening space.

Transabdominal Ultrasound
An ultrasound procedure involving gel and an external probe moved over the abdomen and pelvis to create images of internal organs.

Transvaginal Ultrasound
An internal imaging procedure where an ultrasound probe is placed into the vagina to provide a clearer view of the ovaries.<SEP>An ultrasound procedure involving an internal probe to examine the cervix and pelvis using sound waves.

Clinical Staging
A pre-treatment assessment process used to estimate how far ovarian cancer has spread before surgical confirmation.

Ascites
A condition involving abnormal fluid buildup in the abdomen or around the ovaries, assessed during physical examinations for ovarian cancer.

Healthcare Provider
A medical professional or doctor who examines the patient, evaluates symptoms, performs pelvic exams, and orders diagnostic testing.

Genetic Counselor
A genetic counselor is a healthcare specialist who discusses family risk and coordinates testing for inherited cancer syndromes related to rectal cancer.<SEP>A healthcare professional specializing in genetics who evaluates familial risk, advises patients, and coordinates hereditary syndrome testing.<SEP>A healthcare specialist with expertise in genetic diseases who assists patients in deciding on germline testing and interpreting test results.<SEP>A medical specialist trained in genetic diseases who guides patients in choosing and interpreting germline tests for inherited cancer risks.<SEP>A specialized healthcare expert trained to assist patients in understanding gene mutations and hereditary disease risks.<SEP>A specialized healthcare professional with expertise in genetic diseases who guides patients through germline testing decisions and results interpretation.<SEP>A specialized healthcare provider who counsels patients on family history, hereditary risk, and genetic testing for inherited cancer conditions.<SEP>A trained healthcare professional who explains genetic testing results and counsels patients regarding hereditary cancer risk.<SEP>An expert who evaluates familial medical history and genetic risk factors to assess their potential implications for a patient's cancer care.

Hereditary Ovarian Cancer
A subtype of ovarian cancer caused by inherited genetic mutations passed down from parent to child.

BRCA Mutation
A BRCA mutation is a genetic alteration that impairs DNA repair and enhances tumor sensitivity to PARP inhibitor maintenance therapies.<SEP>A critical genetic mutation biomarker in DNA repair genes that influences ovarian cancer treatment planning and signifies homologous recombination deficiency.<SEP>Genetic alterations in BRCA1 or BRCA2 that guide maintenance therapy choices, particularly PARP inhibitor eligibility.<SEP>Genetic alterations in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes that significantly increase the risk of developing hereditary ovarian and breast cancers.

Chest X-ray
A fast, painless imaging test using low amounts of radiation to check whether cancer has spread to the lungs.

Diagnostic Laparoscopy
A minimally invasive surgical procedure used to visually evaluate the extent of cancer within the abdomen and collect tissue samples.

Sedative
A class of medication administered to patients to relieve anxiety and promote relaxation during medical procedures in enclosed spaces.

Fine-Needle Aspiration Biopsy
A minimally invasive biopsy technique that utilizes a thin needle to extract a small sample of tumor tissue for pathological testing.

Core Biopsy
A biopsy procedure utilizing a hollow needle to remove cylindrical tissue samples from suspicious lesions.

Paracentesis
A procedural aspiration where a thin needle is inserted through the belly wall to draw peritoneal fluid for diagnostic evaluation.

Maintenance Therapy
A course of medical treatment administered following primary therapy to prevent cancer progression, relapse, or recurrence.<SEP>A phase of extended cancer treatment designed to prevent recurrence, frequently guided by BRCA mutation status.<SEP>A post-treatment regimen administered for advanced ovarian cancers after effective initial surgery and chemotherapy.<SEP>An extended phase of cancer treatment prescribed after successful primary chemotherapy to sustain disease remission.<SEP>Maintenance therapy consists of periodic scheduled cancer treatments given over months or years to prevent tumor recurrence.<SEP>Maintenance therapy is a systemic treatment category administered after successful initial response to chemotherapy and surgery to prevent recurrence or prolong disease-free survival.<SEP>Ongoing therapeutic regimens administered following initial cancer treatments, often selected based on tumor biomarker characteristics such as BRCA or HRD.

Hereditary Cancer
A group of cancers caused by inherited genetic mutations, including mutations in the BRCA genes.

Homologous Recombination Deficiency (HRD)
A DNA repair deficiency condition in tumors, occurring with or without BRCA mutations, used to determine eligibility for maintenance therapies.

Tumor Markers
Proteins such as CEA and CA 15-3 found in blood or biopsy tissue that may indicate cancer progression or growth.<SEP>Substances found in blood or body tissues, such as CA-125, inhibin, and AFP, used to assist in diagnosing ovarian cancer and monitoring therapeutic response.

Gastrointestinal Tract Examination
Endoscopic procedures, including colonoscopy and upper endoscopy, utilized to evaluate the digestive system using illuminated camera scopes.

Initial Surgery
The primary surgical procedure during which tumor resection and diagnostic biopsies for ovarian cancer are typically conducted.

Registered Dietitian Or Nutritionist
A healthcare professional specializing in diet and nutritional planning to optimize patient recovery and treatment outcomes.

Colonoscopy
A colonoscopy is a medical examination procedure during which polyps in the colon and rectum can be identified and removed via polypectomy.<SEP>A colonoscopy is an endoscopic medical examination of the colon during which polyps can be detected and removed.<SEP>A colonoscopy is an endoscopic procedure used to examine the colon and rectum, perform polypectomies, and monitor for cancer recurrence during surveillance.<SEP>A diagnostic endoscopic examination where a scope is inserted into the anus to evaluate the rectum and colon.<SEP>A medical examination procedure used to detect, diagnose, and remove polyps or tumors in the colon.<SEP>An endoscopic examination recommended one year following surgical resection for stage 1 colon cancer to monitor for recurrence.<SEP>An endoscopic medical examination of the colon recommended at set intervals for post-treatment surveillance in colon cancer patients.<SEP>An endoscopic screening and surveillance procedure recommended at intervals of 3 to 5 years following rectal cancer treatments.<SEP>An examination procedure used to inspect the colon and rectum and safely remove polyps.

Upper Endoscopy
An endoscopic imaging procedure where a scope is guided down the throat to inspect the esophagus, stomach, and small bowel.

Complete Blood Count (CBC)
A diagnostic blood test measuring red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets to evaluate general physiological status, infection fighting, and bleeding control.<SEP>A standard blood screening test that measures white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets, often paired with a differential to assess blood cell balance.<SEP>A standard blood test analyzing red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets as part of baseline medical evaluation.

Blood Chemistry Profile
A blood evaluation testing chemical concentrations related to organ function, bone health, and nutritional intake like protein levels.<SEP>A diagnostic blood test measuring levels of various chemicals to evaluate organ function and identify potential cancer spread.

CA-125 Test
The primary tumor marker test for ovarian cancer, measuring cancer antigen-125 protein levels in the bloodstream.

Less Common Ovarian Cancers (LCOCs)
A subclass of rare ovarian malignant tumors frequently monitored by specialized tumor markers like inhibin, β-hCG, and AFP.

Recurrent Ovarian Cancer
A clinical presentation where ovarian malignancy returns following initial therapy, warranting expanded biomarker and molecular testing.<SEP>The return or relapse of ovarian cancer after initial treatment, requiring biomarker profiling and tailored therapeutic approaches.

Endometriosis
A non-malignant gynecological disorder capable of elevating CA-125 levels, complicating ovarian cancer differential diagnosis.

Diverticulitis
An inflammatory gastrointestinal condition that can benignly elevate serum CA-125 concentrations.

Hysterectomy and Bilateral Salpingo-Oophorectomy (BSO)
The most common surgical procedure for ovarian cancer, involving the removal of the uterus, cervix, both ovaries, and both fallopian tubes.

Fertility-Sparing Surgery
A surgical approach, such as unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, that preserves the uterus and allows potential future pregnancy in early-stage disease.

Cytoreductive Surgery
Also referred to as debulking surgery, this procedure aims to remove as much metastatic tumor tissue as possible when cancer has spread beyond the ovaries.

Surgical Staging
A comprehensive surgical procedure to sample tissues and organs across the abdomen and pelvis to accurately determine the extent of cancer spread.<SEP>A diagnostic staging system (Stage I, II, or III) based on pathologic analysis of tumor depth and lymph node involvement following surgery.<SEP>A minimally invasive surgical procedure used to remove and examine pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes to guide radiation and systemic therapy.<SEP>An operative assessment involving tissue and fluid sampling to determine the accurate post-surgery pathologic stage of ovarian cancer.

Laparotomy
A surgical approach involving an extensive vertical abdominal incision, commonly utilized for comprehensive staging and debulking procedures.<SEP>A surgical procedure involving a traditional large abdominal incision to access pelvic organs.

Laparoscopy
A minimally invasive surgical technique performed through small abdominal incisions, utilized in select, localized ovarian cancer cases.

BRCA Genes
Genes involved in DNA repair whose inherited mutations represent the most common cause of hereditary ovarian cancer.

Microsatellite Instability (MSI)
A condition of genetic hypermutability identified through molecular biomarker testing.<SEP>A molecular marker reflecting defective DNA mismatch repair, evaluated via tumor tissue testing to guide targeted therapy.

Mismatch Repair (MMR)
A biological mechanism responsible for repairing DNA replication errors; tested on tumor tissue to inform treatment options.<SEP>A cellular DNA repair mechanism evaluated as a biomarker in recurrent cervical cancer.

HER2 Expression
A molecular biomarker tested on tumor tissue to evaluate cancer characteristics and targeted treatment eligibility.

Tumor Mutational Burden (TMB)
A genomic biomarker measuring the total number of mutations present in tumor tissue to help determine therapy options.<SEP>A genomic biomarker measuring the total number of mutations present in tumor tissue.

BRAF V600E Mutation
A specific genetic mutation tested in removed tumor tissue to guide personalized cancer treatment.

Folate Receptor Alpha (FRα) Expression
A tumor tissue biomarker evaluated in ovarian cancer to identify eligibility for targeted therapies.

RET Mutations
Genetic alterations evaluated via tumor biomarker testing to inform targeted therapeutic strategies.

NTRK Gene Fusion
A genetic alteration evaluated in cervical sarcoma to guide targeted therapeutic options.<SEP>A genomic alteration evaluated through tumor tissue testing that can guide targeted oncologic treatment.

Unilateral Salpingo-Oophorectomy (USO)
A fertility-sparing surgical procedure removing one ovary and fallopian tube in appropriate early-stage ovarian cancer cases.

In Vitro Fertilization (IVF)
An assisted reproductive technology using patient or donor eggs to achieve pregnancy following fertility-sparing procedures or BSO.

American Joint Committee on Cancer
An organization that developed a standardized staging system to describe the extent of cancer in the body, including ovarian cancer.<SEP>The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) is an organization that developed a standardized cancer staging system to determine cancer extent, location, and subtype.<SEP>The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) is an organization that developed the TNM staging system used for staging anal cancer, including anal canal and perianal tumors.<SEP>The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) is an organization that developed the tumor, node, metastasis (TNM) staging system used to classify colon cancer.<SEP>The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) is an organization that formulated a standardized staging system to evaluate the extent, location, and subtype of cancer.

data.entity_name: International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics
data.content:
International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics
An international medical organization that established the widely used FIGO staging system for ovarian cancer.<SEP>An international organization that created and maintains the FIGO staging system used globally to stage cervical cancer.

FIGO Staging System
A clinical staging classification system developed by FIGO with four primary stages (I to IV) used to determine the extent of cervical cancer.<SEP>A standard cancer classification system established by FIGO that defines ovarian cancer stage according to primary tumor extent, lymph node spread, and distant metastases.

AJCC Staging System
A standardized cancer classification system developed by the American Joint Committee on Cancer for evaluating cancer extent.

Surgical Menopause
A condition of premature menopause induced by the surgical removal of both ovaries, causing a rapid decrease in estrogen levels.<SEP>A sudden, severe menopausal state induced when both ovaries are surgically removed during treatment, leading to an immediate decline in estrogen.

Deep Vein Thrombosis
A medical condition involving blood clots, identified as a significant risk after major abdominal cancer surgery.

Ovarian Cancer Surgery
A surgical operation aimed at resecting cancerous tissue, ovaries, uterus, fallopian tubes, omentum, and lymph nodes, as well as providing pathologic staging.

Interval Cytoreductive Surgery
A surgical procedure conducted after preliminary chemotherapy cycles to debulk remaining ovarian cancer.

Peritoneal Washing
A procedure during surgery where the abdominal cavity is rinsed with fluid to collect and evaluate microscopic cancer cells.

Menopausal Symptom Team
A specialized group of healthcare providers recommended to consult with patients regarding surgical menopause and hormone replacement therapy options.

Microscopic Metastases
Cancer cells that have spread beyond the primary pelvic or ovarian site and can only be detected under a microscope.

Cardiovascular Disease
A category of diseases affecting the heart and blood vessels, noted as a long-term risk associated with insufficient estrogen.<SEP>Heart and blood vessel conditions representing long-term health risks resulting from estrogen deficiency following surgical menopause.

Osteoporosis
A bone-thinning condition representing a long-term risk of estrogen deprivation caused by surgical removal of both ovaries.<SEP>A condition characterized by bone loss, identified as a long-term risk of estrogen deficiency.

Vaginal Atrophy
A condition characterized by thinning, drying, and inflammation of vaginal tissues caused by estrogen deficiency following bilateral oophorectomy.<SEP>A medical condition where the vaginal lining becomes thin, dry, and inflamed, commonly linked to low estrogen levels.<SEP>Thinning, drying, and inflammation of the vaginal lining caused by sudden estrogen reduction following surgical menopause.

Hormone Replacement Therapy
A medical treatment providing exogenous hormones to manage severe symptoms and risks associated with surgical menopause.<SEP>A therapeutic category distinct from cancer endocrine therapy, specifically used to manage symptoms associated with menopause.

Hyperthermic Intraperitoneal Chemotherapy
An intraoperative procedure where heated chemotherapy is circulated within the abdominal cavity during interval cytoreductive surgery for stage 3 ovarian cancer.

FIGO
The International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) provides the classification system used worldwide to stage cervical cancer.<SEP>The International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO), an organization that establishes the standard staging system used to classify ovarian cancer.

Stage 1 Ovarian Cancer
An early-stage category of ovarian cancer where the disease is confined to one or both ovaries, subdivided into substages 1A, 1B, and 1C.

Stage 2 Ovarian Cancer
A specific stage of ovarian cancer with limited existing research regarding post-initial treatment maintenance therapy using PARP inhibitors.<SEP>A staging category where ovarian cancer involves one or both ovaries and has extended or spread into pelvic organs such as the uterus, fallopian tubes, bladder, or rectum.

Stage 3 Ovarian Cancer
An advanced staging category where ovarian cancer has spread to the retroperitoneal lymph nodes, abdominal lining, or surface of the liver or spleen.

Stage 4 Ovarian Cancer
The most advanced staging category of ovarian cancer characterized by distant metastases, such as malignant pleural effusion or parenchymal liver and spleen metastases.

Taxanes
A class of chemotherapy drugs that includes docetaxel, paclitaxel, and albumin-bound paclitaxel.<SEP>A class of chemotherapy medications, including paclitaxel and docetaxel, commonly combined with platinum agents to treat ovarian cancer.

Oxaliplatin
A platinum-containing chemotherapy medication used in cancer treatment regimens.

Paclitaxel
A taxane chemotherapy drug commonly administered with carboplatin for ovarian cancer, known for causing peripheral neuropathy.

Docetaxel
A taxane class chemotherapy drug used in systemic cancer treatment regimens.

Bevacizumab
A targeted therapy medication that may be added to chemotherapy and continued alone as maintenance therapy.<SEP>A targeted therapy medication, also known as Avastin, that inhibits the formation of new blood vessels supplying tumor cells and can be added to chemotherapy regimens.<SEP>Bevacizumab (Avastin) is a targeted therapy drug that inhibits the growth of new blood vessels feeding tumors, used alongside chemotherapy or as maintenance therapy.

Peripheral Neuropathy
A neurological condition and common adverse effect of paclitaxel characterized by nerve damage, tingling, numbness, and pain in the hands and feet.

Neoadjuvant Therapy
Preoperative systemic treatment administered before surgical intervention to shrink the tumor and reduce cancer burden.<SEP>Systemic cancer treatment such as chemotherapy administered before surgical intervention to reduce tumor volume.

Adjuvant Chemotherapy
Systemic chemotherapy administered following surgical resection to destroy remaining cancer cells and reduce recurrence risk.

High-Grade Serous Tumors
An aggressive histological subtype of ovarian tumors that typically requires six cycles of chemotherapy even when diagnosed at stage 1.

Surgical Spill
An intraoperative event occurring when the tumor capsule of an ovary ruptures or breaks open during surgical excision, designating stage 1C1.

Stage 1C Ovarian Cancer
A substage of stage 1 ovarian cancer defined by capsule rupture, external surface involvement, or positive peritoneal washings.

Stage 4A Ovarian Cancer
A substage of stage 4 ovarian cancer characterized by the presence of malignant cells in pleural effusion fluid around the lungs.

Stage 4B Ovarian Cancer
A substage of stage 4 ovarian cancer involving metastasis to distant lymph nodes, inside the liver or spleen, or organs outside the peritoneal cavity.

Intravenous Chemotherapy
Intravenous chemotherapy is a route of chemotherapy administration where medication is delivered directly into the bloodstream through a vein or port.

Intraperitoneal Chemotherapy
Intraperitoneal chemotherapy is a specialized drug administration method where high doses of chemotherapy are delivered directly into the abdomen via a catheter.

PARP Inhibitors
A class of targeted cancer therapies that block the PARP repair protein, causing cancer cells with BRCA mutations to die.<SEP>A class of targeted pharmacological therapies used against cancers harboring specific molecular markers and DNA repair defects.<SEP>PARP inhibitors are a class of oral targeted maintenance medications, including olaparib, niraparib, and rucaparib, particularly effective in HRD-positive and BRCA-mutated cancers.

Myelodysplastic Syndrome
Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) is a rare bone marrow cancer characterized by inadequate production of healthy blood cells, which can progress to acute myeloid leukemia.

Olaparib
A PARP inhibitor medication used as maintenance therapy for up to two years, either alone or combined with other therapies.<SEP>Olaparib (Lynparza) is an oral PARP inhibitor targeted therapy approved for maintenance treatment in ovarian cancer patients.

Niraparib
A PARP inhibitor medication that may be administered alone for up to three years as maintenance therapy.<SEP>Niraparib (Zejula) is an oral PARP inhibitor prescribed for maintenance therapy following initial chemotherapy.

Rucaparib
A PARP inhibitor medication administered alone as maintenance therapy for up to two years.<SEP>Rucaparib (Rubraca) is an oral PARP inhibitor utilized as maintenance therapy after initial cancer treatment.

Homologous Recombination Deficiency
Homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) is a cellular characteristic of impaired DNA repair in cancers that predicts positive response to PARP inhibitors.

CA-125 Testing
CA-125 testing is a tumor marker blood evaluation conducted prior to each chemotherapy cycle to assess treatment response.

Observation
Observation is a surveillance management strategy without active drug intervention, considered for specific patients showing complete response.

Platinum-Resistant Cancer
A classification of ovarian cancer that does not improve or worsens during platinum-based chemotherapy, or recurs within six months following treatment.

Platinum-Sensitive Cancer
A classification of ovarian cancer where complete remission is achieved and cancer returns more than six months following platinum-based chemotherapy.

PARP Inhibitor
A class of targeted maintenance therapies, including olaparib, niraparib, and rucaparib, used in the treatment and maintenance of ovarian cancer.

Secondary Cytoreductive Surgery
A surgical procedure performed in select cases of recurrent platinum-sensitive cancer to remove all visible tumor prior to systemic recurrence treatment.

Throat Cancer
A form of cancer that forms in the throat or oropharynx, located in the back of the mouth and neck.<SEP>A malignancy developing in the head and neck, staged via clinical and pathologic metrics and influenced by HPV/p16 status.<SEP>A malignancy of the throat for which diagnostic endoscopy, biopsies, and p16 HPV testing are recommended.<SEP>A specific malignancy that originates in the oropharynx, primarily presenting as squamous cell carcinoma and affecting structures such as the soft palate, tonsils, throat walls, and tongue base.<SEP>A type of malignancy, specifically squamous cell carcinoma of the oropharynx, often linked to HPV infection and staged using p16 biomarker testing.<SEP>Throat (oropharyngeal) cancer is a malignancy affecting the pharynx and throat area, frequently staged using TNM classification and evaluated with p16 (HPV) testing.<SEP>Throat cancer is a head and neck malignancy frequently associated with Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection.

Ovarian Cancer Survivor
An individual who experienced ovarian cancer and provided reflection on life-affirming personal growth following a life-altering cancer diagnosis.

Non-Platinum Chemotherapy
Alternative chemotherapy regimens administered when ovarian cancer fails to respond to or recurs rapidly following platinum drugs.<SEP>Chemotherapy alternatives prescribed for individuals with kidney conditions or health issues that preclude platinum-based drugs.

Mirvetuximab Soravtansine-Gynx
An antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) targeted therapy preferred for recurrent ovarian tumors expressing the folate receptor alpha biomarker.

Antibody Drug Conjugate
A class of targeted therapeutic agents combining monoclonal antibodies with cytotoxic drugs, exemplified by mirvetuximab soravtansine-gynx.

Hypersensitivity Reaction
A potentially life-threatening allergic reaction triggered by repeat exposure to platinum chemotherapy agents.

Surveillance
A post-treatment clinical category involving monitoring and routine follow-up care to check for cancer recurrence.<SEP>A post-treatment clinical follow-up protocol consisting of scheduled tests and procedures to monitor patients for potential cancer recurrence.<SEP>Routine clinical follow-up consisting of periodic physical exams, pelvic exams, and tumor marker monitoring to detect cancer relapse.<SEP>Surveillance refers to the structured follow-up monitoring protocol after recurrence treatment, including imaging, physical exams, and anoscopy.<SEP>The structured clinical follow-up phase following cancer therapy, aimed at detecting potential disease recurrence early.

CA-125
A tumor marker checked via blood testing to monitor treatment response and detect recurrence in ovarian cancer.

Folate Receptor Alpha
A biomarker whose presence on tumor cells indicates suitability for targeted therapy with mirvetuximab soravtansine-gynx.

Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors
A class of cancer immunotherapy treatments that may cause side effects covered in patient guidelines.<SEP>A class of immunotherapy drugs that target PD-1 and PD-L1 proteins to restore the immune system's anti-tumor response.<SEP>A class of immunotherapy drugs used in biomarker-guided cancer treatment, associated with distinct immune-related side effects.<SEP>A specific category of immunotherapy drugs, including nivolumab and pembrolizumab, used to treat metastatic anal cancer.

Oropharynx
The anatomical region in the throat comprising the soft palate, tonsils, side and back walls of the throat, and the base of the tongue.<SEP>The anatomical region in the throat including the back of the mouth and soft palate, in which throat cancer can form.

Head and Neck Cancers
A group of cancers originating in the head or neck area, including the oral cavity, oropharynx, nasal cavity, nasopharynx, larynx, and hypopharynx.

data.entity_name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head and Neck
data.content:
Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head and Neck
Also referred to as SCCHN or HNSCC, this is the most common histological type of head and neck cancer, arising in the thin, flat squamous cells of the mucus membranes.

Testing for Throat Cancer
The clinical diagnostic evaluation process used prior to treatment planning, which includes general health evaluations, p16 (HPV) testing, imaging, scoping procedures, biopsies, and biomarker testing.

p16 (HPV) Testing
A diagnostic procedure performed to test for human papillomavirus association in throat cancer.

Scoping Procedures
Endoscopic diagnostic examinations utilized to visualize the throat and head and neck structures.

Human Papillomavirus Testing
A diagnostic biomarker test (often using p16) performed on tumor tissue to detect the presence of HPV in throat cancer.

Screening For Depression
A mental health assessment recommended as part of the initial evaluation to detect psychological distress or depression.

Fertility Counseling
A clinical guidance session addressing fertility preservation and pregnancy prevention during cancer treatment across all genders.

Screening For Hepatitis B
An infectious disease laboratory screening recommended before initiating specific cancer treatments.

Pre-Anesthesia Exam
A medical evaluation conducted prior to administering anesthesia to ensure patient safety during procedures.<SEP>A pre-anesthesia exam is a clinical consultation and airway assessment performed by an anesthesiologist prior to surgery to evaluate perioperative risks.

Speech And Swallowing Evaluation
A functional assessment evaluating swallowing, speech, and nutrition capacity prior to or during treatment.

Help To Quit Smoking
A supportive intervention designed to help patients cease tobacco use to enhance treatment efficacy and survival.

data.entity_name: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
data.content:
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
A public health agency offering smoking cessation resources and guidance via CDC.gov/tobacco.<SEP>The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is a national public health agency referenced for its tobacco cessation support resources.

ECOG Performance Status
A functional rating scale from 0 to 5 that evaluates a patient's overall fitness and ability to perform daily self-care and activities.<SEP>ECOG Performance Status is a clinical assessment metric ranging from 0 to 5 that measures a patient's level of physical functioning and ability to perform activities of daily living.

Smoking and Vaping
Smoking and vaping refer to tobacco and nicotine consumption behaviors that significantly elevate cancer risk and negatively impact surgical recovery and treatment efficacy.<SEP>Tobacco and nicotine use behaviors that hinder cancer treatment efficacy and increase complications during chemotherapy.

Head and Neck Cancer Surgery
Head and neck cancer surgery is a complex surgical procedure performed to resect tumors in the head and neck, requiring careful perioperative planning.

Mind and Body Therapists
Healthcare professionals integrated into cancer care teams who assist patients in managing emotional and physical distress.

Nutritionist or Dietician
Specialized nutrition professionals who provide dietary recommendations, monitor weight loss, and ensure adequate nutrition prior to and during cancer treatment.

Anesthesiologist
A medical specialist who administers anesthesia to manage pain and consciousness during surgical operations and clinical procedures.<SEP>Medical physician who performs pre-anesthesia airway and health assessments and administers anesthesia during surgical procedures.

data.entity_name: Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C Screening
data.content:
Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C Screening
A pre-treatment blood testing procedure conducted to identify previous or active viral hepatitis infection before initiating cancer therapy.

Lung Function Tests
Pulmonary function tests (PFTs) conducted to measure lung volumes, ventilation speed, and gas exchange capacity prior to medical interventions.

Hepatitis B
A viral infection spread by contact with blood and bodily fluids that causes chronic liver inflammation, cirrhosis, and liver cancer.<SEP>A viral liver disease that can potentially be reactivated by cancer treatments, causing severe liver injury.

Hepatitis C
A viral infection affecting the liver that is evaluated prior to cancer therapy to prevent hepatic complications.<SEP>A viral infection transmitted via bodily fluids that leads to chronic hepatitis, liver scarring, liver failure, and liver cancer.

Anesthesia
A drug-induced loss of feeling or awareness administered to prevent pain and allow surgical or invasive interventions to proceed safely.

Human Papillomavirus
A common viral infection that affects skin and mucous membranes and is the primary cause of anal cancer.<SEP>A family of viruses that infect epithelial tissues and mucous membranes, recognized as the primary cause of squamous cell carcinomas of the throat, especially type HPV16.<SEP>A group of over 100 virus strains, including high-risk types such as HPV16, responsible for causing anal, cervical, vaginal, and other cancers, as well as genital warts.<SEP>A virus associated with certain forms of throat and oropharyngeal cancer, distinct from p16-negative cancers.<SEP>Commonly known as HPV, a sexually transmitted virus strongly linked as a major risk factor for developing anal cancer.<SEP>Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a common viral infection recognized as the leading sexually transmitted cause of cervical cancer.

p16 Testing
A diagnostic biomarker test that detects overexpression of the p16 protein as a surrogate marker for HPV infection in throat cancer specimens.

Hormonal Birth Control
A category of contraception methods that may or may not be advised for oncology patients during active cancer therapy.<SEP>Prescription contraceptive options relying on hormones that may or may not be clinically advised for individuals receiving cancer therapy.

Intrauterine Devices
A form of long-acting reversible contraception (IUDs) considered as an alternative method for pregnancy prevention during therapy.<SEP>Long-acting reversible contraceptive devices inserted into the uterus, noted as an option to evaluate with a healthcare provider during treatment.<SEP>Non-hormonal or hormonal medical contraceptive devices (IUDs) placed in the uterus to prevent pregnancy.

p16 Protein
A cellular protein encoded on chromosome 9 that regulates and slows cell division, acting as an overexpressed surrogate marker in HPV-driven cancers.

HPV Type 16
A specific viral genotype of human papillomavirus responsible for approximately 90% of HPV-related throat cancers.

data.entity_name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Throat
data.content:
Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Throat
A specific histological type of cancer arising in the oropharynx, particularly the tonsils and base of the tongue, frequently linked to HPV.

Claustrophobia
A clinical fear or dread of enclosed spaces that can complicate imaging procedures conducted in closed MRI scanners.<SEP>A psychological condition marked by a fear of enclosed spaces, influencing the choice between open and closed MRI scanners.

Fine-Needle Biopsy
A diagnostic procedure guided by ultrasound or CT imaging used to collect tissue or cell samples from abnormal areas.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure, also known as fine-needle aspiration (FNA/FNB), that uses thin needles to extract cells from suspicious lesions or lymph nodes.

Endoscopy
A scoping procedure that uses an endoscope inserted through the mouth or nose to examine internal passages, assess tumors, and guide biopsies.

Fiberoptic Nasopharyngolaryngoscopy
A diagnostic procedure performed on an awake patient using a topical numbing spray to examine the larynx and surrounding structures.

Laryngoscopy
A category of throat examinations using mirrors or specialized scopes to inspect the voice box, vocal cords, and hypopharynx.

Indirect Laryngoscopy
A simple throat examination technique using a light and a small mirror positioned at the back of the throat.

Fiberoptic Laryngoscopy
A fast examination performed by inserting a flexible scope through the nose to view the throat and voice box.<SEP>A quick examination using a small flexible scope passed through the nose into the throat to examine the airway under local numbing spray.

Direct Laryngoscopy
A detailed examination performed under general anesthesia in an operating room using a laryngoscope to examine the throat, determine tumor resectability, and collect biopsies.<SEP>An in-depth endoscopic procedure performed under general anesthesia in an operating room to view the deep throat and obtain tissue biopsies.

Operating Room
A sterile hospital surgical suite where direct laryngoscopy is conducted under general anesthesia.

Esophagoscopy
A procedure performed under anesthesia in an operating room where an endoscope is guided down the throat into the esophagus to look for abnormal growths.

Bronchoscopy
A procedure under anesthesia where a scope is inserted through the nose or mouth to examine the trachea and bronchi, detect cancer, or perform treatments.

Panendoscopy
A comprehensive examination performed under anesthesia that combines laryngoscopy, pharyngoscopy, esophagoscopy, and bronchoscopy to assess the upper aerodigestive tract and obtain tissue biopsies.

HPV Testing
A diagnostic test using p16 biomarker analysis recommended for patients diagnosed with throat cancer.

Tumor Histology
The specific cancer subtype classification determined by microscopic cellular analysis.

MSI-H/dMMR
A classification of tumors characterized by high microsatellite instability or deficient mismatch repair.<SEP>A genetic alteration status signifying microsatellite instability-high or deficient mismatch repair within cancer cells.<SEP>A genetic biomarker classification characterized by microsatellite instability-high or deficient mismatch repair in cancer cells.<SEP>A genetic condition characterized by microsatellite instability-high or deficient mismatch repair, leading to uncorrected DNA replication errors in cancer cells.

Pharyngoscopy
An endoscopic procedure used to examine the pharynx and oropharynx, often performed as part of a panendoscopy.

Primary Tumor
A localized initial mass of cancer cells that forms before disease spreads to adjacent tissues or distant organs.<SEP>The initial mass formed by cancer cells at the original anatomical site within the breast tissue before any metastatic spread.<SEP>The initial, localized mass of cancer cells that forms within the breast tissue before invading adjacent structures or spreading.<SEP>The original or main cancerous growth identified during endoscopic evaluations such as direct laryngoscopy.

Cytology
The microscopic evaluation of individual cells performed by a pathologist to identify cancer.

Tumor P16 (HPV) Testing
Tumor p16 testing is a biomarker diagnostic test recommended for all patients diagnosed with oropharyngeal throat cancer to guide staging and treatment decisions.

Tumor Mutation Testing
A class of diagnostic testing that analyzes tumor or blood samples to identify non-inherited genetic aberrations that may be treated with targeted therapies.<SEP>A diagnostic category of molecular tests performed on tumor or blood samples to identify specific somatic DNA mutations and genomic aberrations.<SEP>A diagnostic evaluation identifying genetic alterations within a bone tumor to inform tailored cancer treatment strategies.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure testing tumor tissue or blood for somatic DNA mutations, such as PIK3CA, to identify targeted therapy options.<SEP>Tumor mutation testing, or tumor genomic aberration testing, examines tumor tissue or blood for specific acquired DNA alterations that can be targeted by specialized therapies.

Cell-Free DNA Testing
Cell-free or circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) testing uses a blood sample to detect tumor cells or tumor DNA fragments to monitor treatment response and cancer recurrence.

P16- Throat Cancer
A specific category of squamous cell carcinoma of the throat that tests negative for the p16 protein and is not mediated by human papillomavirus (HPV).

Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
A rapidly progressing blood cancer originating in lymphocytes and lymphoblasts, most frequently diagnosed in pediatric populations.<SEP>A type of cancer of the blood and bone marrow characterized by the overproduction of lymphoblasts, commonly treated with chemotherapy and systemic therapies.<SEP>Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a blood cancer characterized by an overproduction of abnormal lymphoid progenitor cells and lymphoblasts in the bone marrow and blood.<SEP>Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a fast-growing blood cancer in which the bone marrow produces too many immature lymphocytes known as lymphoblasts.<SEP>Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a fast-growing blood cancer that originates in lymphoid progenitor cells and disease-fighting white blood cells known as lymphocytes.<SEP>Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a fast-growing cancer of the blood and bone marrow starting in lymphocytes, commonly diagnosed in infants, children, and young adults.<SEP>Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a rapid-growing type of blood cancer that originates in lymphoid progenitor cells, resulting in an overproduction of immature lymphocytes known as lymphoblasts.

B-ALL
A primary subtype of acute lymphoblastic leukemia that originates in B-cell lineage lymphocytes.<SEP>B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) is a classification of ALL that originates in B-cell precursors and encompasses multiple genetic subtypes.<SEP>B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) is a leukemia subtype originating in B-cell lineage lymphoblasts, distinguished in clinical management from mature B-cell ALL.<SEP>B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) is a subtype of ALL that originates in B-cell lymphocytes and is more common than T-ALL.<SEP>B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) is the most common form of ALL, originating in B-cell lymphocytes.<SEP>B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, the most common type of ALL, encompassing subtypes such as BCR::ABL1-negative, BCR::ABL1-like, and BCR::ABL1-positive.

T-ALL
A primary subtype of acute lymphoblastic leukemia that originates in T-cell lineage lymphocytes.<SEP>T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is a less common form of ALL that originates in T-cell lymphocytes.<SEP>T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is a subtype of ALL originating in T-cell lymphocytes that can lead to an enlarged thymus and breathing issues.<SEP>T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is a subtype of ALL that originates in T-cell lymphocytes and can cause an enlarged thymus and respiratory issues.<SEP>T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is one of the two primary classifications of acute lymphoblastic leukemia.<SEP>T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, a less common subgroup of ALL that originates in T-cell lymphocytes.

Locoregionally Advanced Cancer
A disease state where tumor growth has extended to tissues, organs, or lymph nodes within the head and neck.

Lymphoblasts
Immature lymphocytes that proliferate excessively in acute lymphoblastic leukemia, crowding out healthy bone marrow.<SEP>Immature lymphoid cells produced in bone marrow that overproliferate in acute lymphoblastic leukemia, crowding out normal blood cells.<SEP>Immature white blood cells produced excessively in the bone marrow during acute lymphoblastic leukemia, displacing normal blood-forming cells.<SEP>Lymphoblasts are immature precursor cells that develop into lymphocytes; in acute lymphoblastic leukemia, abnormal lymphoblasts proliferate excessively.<SEP>Lymphoblasts, or blasts, are immature lymphoid cells that multiply abnormally in acute lymphoblastic leukemia, crowding out normal bone marrow and inhibiting healthy blood cell production.

B-Cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) is the most common form of ALL, originating in B-cell lymphocytes.

T-Cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is a subtype of ALL originating in T-cell lymphocytes, often causing an enlarged thymus and breathing complications.

Burkitt Leukemia
Also called mature B-cell ALL, Burkitt leukemia is a rare subtype of ALL that is essentially the same as Burkitt lymphoma but managed with different treatments.<SEP>Burkitt leukemia is a rare and mature subtype of B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia.<SEP>Burkitt leukemia, also known as mature B-cell ALL, is a rare subtype of ALL that is biologically similar to Burkitt lymphoma but managed with distinct treatment protocols.<SEP>Mature B-cell ALL, also known as Burkitt leukemia, is a rare subtype of B-ALL that closely aligns biologically with Burkitt lymphoma but follows distinct treatment approaches.

B-Cell Lymphoblastic Lymphoma
Also referred to as B-LL or B-LBL, a condition where B-cell lymphoblasts proliferate predominantly in lymph nodes rather than bone marrow.<SEP>B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma (B-LL or B-LBL) is a disease manifestation where B-cell lymphoblasts grow primarily in the lymph nodes instead of bone marrow.

T-Cell Lymphoblastic Lymphoma
Also known as T-LL or T-LBL, a condition in which T-cell lymphoblasts grow primarily in the thymus instead of bone marrow.<SEP>T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma (T-LL or T-LBL) is a condition where T-cell lymphoblasts grow mainly in the thymus rather than in the bone marrow.

Adolescents and Young Adults
Adolescents and young adults (AYAs) is a cancer patient demographic comprising individuals aged 15 to 39 years at diagnosis who may be treated in pediatric or adult care centers.<SEP>Adolescents and young adults (AYAs) is a patient category defined as individuals aged 15 to 39 years at the time of initial cancer diagnosis who may receive treatment at pediatric or adult cancer centers.

B Cells
A subtype of white blood cells produced in the bone marrow and located in the lymphatic system that fight infections; in CLL, abnormal B cells proliferate uncontrollably.<SEP>B cells, or B lymphocytes, are specialized white blood cells responsible for producing antibodies to protect against infection.<SEP>B cells, or B lymphocytes, are specialized white blood cells that produce antibodies to protect the body against infection.<SEP>Immune cells primarily located in the lymphatic system that undergo malignant transformation in CLL.

T Cells
T cells, or T lymphocytes, are white blood cells that fight infections, destroy tumor cells, and modulate immune responses.<SEP>T cells, or T lymphocytes, are white blood cells that fight infections, kill tumor cells, and regulate immune system responses.

Pediatric Patients
Pediatric patients refers to a clinical demographic consisting of infants, children, and individuals aged 18 years or younger receiving specialized pediatric care.

ALL
Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a cancer that affects lymphoid progenitor blood cells, leading to an overproduction of lymphoblasts in bone marrow, blood, and other organs.

BCR::ABL1-Negative B-ALL
BCR::ABL1-negative or BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL is the most common form of B-ALL, typically treated with clinical trials and multiagent chemotherapy.

BCR::ABL1-Positive B-ALL
A subtype of B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia driven by the BCR::ABL protein produced by the BCR::ABL1 gene, treated with intensive systemic therapies.<SEP>BCR::ABL1-positive B-ALL is an aggressive subtype of B-ALL driven by the BCR::ABL1 gene fusion, requiring targeted and intensive systemic therapies.

Infant ALL
A specific classification of acute lymphoblastic leukemia occurring in infants under 12 months of age, requiring specialized treatment approaches.<SEP>Infant ALL is a distinct category of acute lymphoblastic leukemia occurring in children under 12 months of age, requiring specialized treatment protocols.

Rectal Cancer
A disease category involving malignant tumors situated within the rectum, managed through local excision, transabdominal resection, and adjuvant therapies.<SEP>A form of cancer originating in the rectum; although related to colon cancer under colorectal cancer, it follows distinct treatment guidelines.<SEP>A form of colorectal cancer that develops in the rectum, requiring staging via imaging and treatment involving surgery, radiation therapy, and biomarker testing.<SEP>A malignancy of the rectum that can also be treated with abdominoperineal resection (APR).<SEP>A malignancy of the rectum that may also be treated using abdominoperineal resection (APR).<SEP>Rectal cancer is a category of cancer that originates in the rectum, most commonly arising from non-cancerous polyps called adenomas.<SEP>Rectal cancer is a form of cancer that originates on the inner lining of the rectum, commonly developing from polyps or lesions.<SEP>Rectal cancer is a malignancy that begins in the inner lining of the rectum, which can invade pelvic tissue or metastasize if left untreated.

Colorectal Cancer
A broad classification of gastrointestinal malignancy that includes rectal cancer, noted for increasing incidence rates in younger adult populations.<SEP>A broader disease category encompassing cancers that form in either the colon or rectum.<SEP>A digestive system cancer that predominantly begins in glandular cells as adenocarcinoma, contrasted with anal cancer.<SEP>A major category of cancer that affects the colon or rectum, often beginning as polyps in the lining of the colon.<SEP>A malignant disease of the colon or rectum linked to hereditary mutations in mismatch repair genes including MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, and PMS2.<SEP>Cancer affecting the colon or rectum, associated with germline mutations in MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, and PMS2.<SEP>Colorectal cancer is a malignancy evaluated in personal or family history to identify inherited conditions associated with thyroid cancer.<SEP>Colorectal cancer is an overarching classification encompassing cancers of both the colon and rectum.

Colon Cancer
A common and treatable cancer that begins in the large intestine (colon), usually arising from non-cancerous polyps.<SEP>A major type of cancer that begins in the large intestine, typically developing from polyps and categorized by stages and genetic biomarkers.<SEP>A malignancy of the large intestine discussed in the context of post-treatment surveillance protocols across stages 1, 2, and 3.<SEP>A malignancy of the large intestine noted in family health histories linked to elevated cancer risks.<SEP>Colon cancer is a cancer that develops in the colon; while related to rectal cancer under colorectal cancer, it requires distinct treatment protocols.

Hyperplastic Polyps
Hyperplastic polyps are non-cancerous growths on the inner lining of the colon and rectum that rarely transform into malignant tumors.<SEP>Non-cancerous growths on the colon lining that rarely develop into colorectal cancer.

Inflammatory Polyps
Benign growths occurring in the colon and rectum that have minimal risk of progressing to cancer.<SEP>Inflammatory polyps are benign colorectal mucosal growths that rarely progress to cancer.

Multiagent Chemotherapy
Multiagent chemotherapy is a core cancer treatment protocol combining multiple chemotherapeutic agents used in the treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia.<SEP>Multiagent chemotherapy is a standard systemic cancer therapy protocol combining multiple chemotherapeutic agents to treat all patients with ALL.

Steroids
Steroids are a drug class routinely administered alongside systemic multiagent chemotherapy in the treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia.<SEP>Steroids are a primary class of therapeutic medications administered to patients undergoing treatment for ALL.

Pediatric Leukemia Center
A pediatric leukemia center is a specialized medical institution experienced in treating children with leukemia.<SEP>A specialized medical facility experienced in treating children diagnosed with leukemia, recommended for expert care and consultations.

Patient Advocacy Groups
Organizations providing external support, resources, and guidance for cancer patients and their families.<SEP>Patient advocacy groups are non-profit support entities that provide resources, guidance, and assistance for patients and families navigating cancer care.<SEP>Patient advocacy groups are support organizations that offer guidance, resources, and assistance to cancer patients navigating their care.<SEP>Support organizations that offer guidance, resources, and assistance for patients undergoing bone cancer diagnosis and care.

ALL Specialist
An ALL specialist is a medical expert focused on diagnosing and managing patients diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

Oncologist
A cancer physician who receives diagnostic imaging and biomarker results to determine and direct cancer therapies.<SEP>A cancer specialist physician who reviews blood smears and oversees treatment planning for cancer patients.<SEP>A medical doctor specializing in cancer care who conducts physical examinations, oversees surveillance, and guides treatment strategies.<SEP>A medical specialist responsible for performing physical exams, monitoring recovery, and evaluating symptoms and recurrence during cancer surveillance.<SEP>A physician specializing in cancer care who receives imaging test results and directs cancer treatment plans.<SEP>A physician specializing in cancer treatment who receives imaging interpretation from the radiologist to plan cancer management.<SEP>An oncologist is a physician specializing in cancer care who receives imaging interpretations to help stage the disease and plan patient treatment.

Polypectomy
A minor surgical procedure performed during a colonoscopy to remove polyps and prevent colon cancer.<SEP>A minor surgical procedure performed during a colonoscopy to remove polyps before they can transition into cancer.<SEP>A polypectomy is a minor surgical procedure performed during a colonoscopy to excise polyps from the lining of the colon and rectum.<SEP>A polypectomy is a minor surgical procedure performed during a colonoscopy to remove polyps from the bowel lining.<SEP>A polypectomy is a minor surgical procedure performed during a colonoscopy to remove polyps from the bowel wall.

Mismatch Repair Testing
A diagnostic biomarker test analyzing tumor samples for mismatch repair deficiency (dMMR) or microsatellite instability (MSI-H) to guide treatment.<SEP>Mismatch repair testing is a diagnostic laboratory procedure that analyzes rectal tumor tissue for mutations in genes responsible for fixing damaged DNA.

Liquid Biopsy
A category of blood-based diagnostic testing that analyzes circulating tumor DNA to detect remnants of cancer cells.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure where a blood sample is taken to detect circulating cancer cells or tumor DNA.<SEP>A liquid biopsy, or circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) test, is a blood-based diagnostic procedure under clinical study to identify microscopic rectal cancer cells and recurrence risk.<SEP>A minimally invasive diagnostic test that analyzes a blood sample to detect circulating cancer cells.

CEA Test
A CEA blood test measures the level of carcinoembryonic antigen to monitor colorectal cancer spread and response.

Biomarker
A biological characteristic or molecule measured to evaluate cancer type, behavior, and potential treatment responses.<SEP>A biomarker is a measurable biological indicator or targetable genetic alteration in cancer cells used to guide treatment plans.

Endometrial Cancer
Cancer of the inner lining of the uterus, for which individuals with Lynch syndrome carry an elevated risk of developing.<SEP>Endometrial cancer is a distinct subtype of uterine cancer that develops within the lining of the uterus.<SEP>Endometrial cancer is a malignancy affecting the uterus lining, known to have elevated incidence in individuals carrying Lynch syndrome mutations.<SEP>Endometrial cancer is a malignancy of the uterine lining evaluated during risk assessments for inherited cancer syndromes linked to thyroid cancer.

Hyperplastic Polyp
A hyperplastic polyp is a benign growth in the colon and rectum that rarely transforms into cancer.

Inflammatory Polyp
An inflammatory polyp is a non-cancerous growth on the colorectal inner lining that rarely progresses to malignancy.

Pelvic MRI
A magnetic resonance imaging test of the pelvis preferred for staging rectal cancer by assessing tumor depth in the rectal wall and lymph node spread.<SEP>Magnetic resonance imaging with contrast centered on the pelvis, recommended after surgery or chemoradiation.<SEP>Pelvic MRI is an advanced diagnostic imaging technique used for staging rectal cancer and monitoring recurrence after surgical procedures.

Endorectal Ultrasound
An ultrasound procedure using an inserted probe and sound waves to evaluate rectal cancer extent in the pelvis or guide biopsies, particularly when MRI is not feasible.

Ovarian Transposition
A surgical procedure (oophoropexy) that moves one or both ovaries out of the path of radiation beams to protect hormone production and future pregnancy.<SEP>A surgical procedure (oophoropexy) that repositions the ovaries and fallopian tubes away from the radiation field to preserve fertility.<SEP>A surgical procedure that moves one or both ovaries outside the radiation field to preserve ovarian function and avoid premature menopause.<SEP>A surgical procedure, also known as oophoropexy, that shifts ovaries out of the radiation field to preserve ovarian function.

Contrast Agent
A chemical substance or dye injected into the bloodstream to make tissues, organs, and blood vessels stand out sharply during an MRI scan.<SEP>A diagnostic substance injected intravenously or consumed orally to enhance the clarity and definition of medical imaging scans.<SEP>A substance administered orally or intravenously prior to CT scans to enhance picture clarity, which can occasionally cause allergic reactions.

Premature Ovarian Insufficiency
A clinical condition also known as radiation-induced premature menopause, caused by radiation damage to the hormone-producing and reproductive function of the ovaries.

Sperm Banking
A fertility preservation method, medically known as semen cryopreservation, where semen is frozen in liquid nitrogen for future reproductive use.<SEP>A fertility preservation technique (semen cryopreservation) involving freezing semen in liquid nitrogen prior to cancer treatment.<SEP>A method of fertility preservation that involves collecting and freezing semen in liquid nitrogen for future use.

Egg Freezing
A fertility preservation technique (oocyte cryopreservation) involving harvesting and freezing unfertilized eggs before cancer treatment.<SEP>A reproductive preservation procedure, scientifically termed oocyte cryopreservation, in which unfertilized eggs are harvested and frozen for later pregnancy attempts.<SEP>Also called oocyte preservation, a medical procedure in which unfertilized eggs are removed, frozen, and stored for potential future pregnancy.<SEP>Also known as oocyte cryopreservation, a procedure where unfertilized eggs are removed, frozen, and stored for future reproductive use.

Ovarian Tissue Banking
A fertility preservation procedure involving surgical removal and cryopreservation of ovarian tissue containing eggs for future re-implantation.<SEP>A fertility preservation procedure where ovarian tissue containing eggs is removed, cryopreserved, and can later be re-implanted into the body.<SEP>A fertility preservation technique in which ovarian tissue containing eggs is removed, frozen, and preserved for potential reimplantation.

Mismatch Repair Deficiency
A biomarker category (dMMR/MSI-H) evaluated in colon cancer tumors to determine molecular characteristics and guide management.<SEP>A tumor biomarker characteristic (dMMR or MSI-H) resulting in defective DNA mismatch repair, triggering clinical evaluation for hereditary Lynch syndrome.

Google
A technology and search engine company referenced regarding patients seeking online diagnostic information.<SEP>A technology company providing online search services, referenced in relation to patients looking up medical diagnoses and statistics on the internet.<SEP>Google is a multinational technology company whose search engine is cautioned against as an unverified source of medical advice ('Dr. Google') for patients seeking health information.

Pedunculated Polyp
A pedunculated polyp is a mushroom-shaped growth with a distinct stalk and rounded top that protrudes from the colon wall.<SEP>A pedunculated polyp is a mushroom-shaped growth with a round top and a stalk protruding from the colon wall.

Sessile Polyp
A sessile polyp is a flat growth lacking a stalk on the rectal wall, which has a higher likelihood of recurrence following treatment.<SEP>A sessile polyp is a flat growth on the colon wall that lacks a stalk.

Malignant Polyp
A malignant polyp is a colon growth in which cancerous cells have begun to develop.<SEP>A malignant polyp is an abnormal growth on the rectal wall in which cancer cells have begun to develop.

T1 Tumor
A T1 tumor is an early-stage rectal cancer that has not extended beyond the second (muscle) layer of the rectal wall.<SEP>A cancer staging category for smaller rectal tumors that can be treated with abdominal surgery.

T2 Tumor
A T2 tumor is a rectal cancer classification where the tumor has invaded into the muscle layer of the rectum.<SEP>A staging category defining rectal tumors that have invaded into the muscular layer of the rectal wall.

Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection
Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection (ESD), also referred to as endoscopic mucosal resection, is a minimally invasive procedure designed to excise T1 rectal tumors in one piece.

Transanal Local Excision
Transanal local excision is a surgical technique for excising low-risk T1 tumors located near the end of the rectum through the anus without removing lymph nodes.

Transanal Endoscopic Microsurgery
Transanal Endoscopic Microsurgery (TEM) is an advanced minimally invasive surgical technique used to remove tumors located higher in the rectum.

Transanal Minimally Invasive Surgery
Transanal Minimally Invasive Surgery (TAMIS) is an advanced technique utilized to excise tumors located higher up in the rectum.

Microsatellite Stable (MSS)
Microsatellite stable (MSS) is a molecular status classification often evaluated in patients diagnosed with rectal cancer.

Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS)
Endoscopic ultrasound (or endorectal ultrasound) is an imaging modality used to assess tumor depth in polyps and monitor patients during post-treatment surveillance.

Flexible Sigmoidoscopy
Flexible sigmoidoscopy is an endoscopic examination used in post-procedure surveillance following endoscopic submucosal dissection to check for cancer recurrence.

Proctoscopy
A medical procedure using an endoscope to evaluate the anus and rectum for cancer involvement.<SEP>An endoscopic examination of the rectum and bowel under anesthesia to detect cervical cancer extension.<SEP>Proctoscopy is an endoscopic examination of the rectum recommended as a surveillance tool following transanal local excision.

Transabdominal Surgery
A surgical procedure involving cutting into the abdomen to remove rectal tumors, surrounding tissue, and at least 12 nearby lymph nodes.<SEP>Transabdominal surgery is a major surgical procedure indicated when rectal tumors present high-risk features or invade the muscle layer as T2 tumors.

Early Rectal Cancer
Early rectal cancer refers to localized cancerous growths in the rectum that are potentially curable via minimally invasive techniques if detected early.

Locally Advanced Cancer
A cancer stage classification describing tumors that have extended locally, most commonly treated using chemoradiation.<SEP>A category of advanced rectal cancer that typically warrants treatment using chemoradiation.<SEP>A stage of cervical cancer that has extended beyond early margins and is most commonly managed with chemoradiation.<SEP>Locally advanced cancer describes rectal cancer that has progressed into deeper rectal tissues or nearby nodes without distant metastasis.

Low Anterior Resection
A specialized type of transabdominal surgery used to remove tumors located in the mid to upper rectum, often allowing colorectal or coloanal anastomosis.

Abdominoperineal Resection
A surgical procedure for tumors in the lower rectum that removes the anus, rectum, and surrounding sphincter or pelvic floor muscle, requiring a permanent colostomy.<SEP>A surgical procedure removing the anus, rectum, and nearby tissues, often requiring a colostomy, used for persistent or recurrent anal cancer.<SEP>Abdominoperineal resection (APR) is a major surgical procedure involving the removal of the anus, rectum, and part of the colon, typically followed by a permanent colostomy.<SEP>Abdominoperineal resection (APR) is a radical surgical procedure that removes the anus, rectum, and surrounding tissue, requiring a permanent colostomy.

Local Excision
A conservative surgical procedure that removes the tumor along with a margin of surrounding normal tissue, indicated for certain low-risk perianal cancers.<SEP>A minor surgical procedure to remove localized rectal tumors, after which further treatments may be necessary if high-risk features or muscle invasion are detected.<SEP>A surgical procedure considered for low-grade (G1) and intermediate-grade (G2) perianal cancers to remove the lesion with clear surgical margins.<SEP>A surgical procedure that serves as an alternative to chemoradiation for certain slow-growing stage I and II perianal cancers.

Colostomy Creation
A surgical procedure in which part of the colon is routed through the abdominal wall to create a stoma, either temporarily to allow healing or permanently.

Colorectal Anastomosis
A surgical reconnection of the colon to the remaining rectum following a low anterior resection to restore near-normal bowel movements.

Coloanal Anastomosis
A surgical reconnection attaching the colon directly to the anus when the remaining rectum cannot be reconnected.

Watch And Wait
A clinical management strategy and monitoring period during which CLL is closely tracked without immediate therapy.<SEP>A clinical management strategy for CLL where immediate treatment is deferred until symptoms develop or the disease progresses.<SEP>A clinical observation strategy agreed upon by doctor and patient after effective chemoradiation before pursuing further surgery.

T3 Cancer
A cancer staging category denoting larger rectal cancers that have not spread to lymph nodes and are eligible for abdominal surgery.

Stage 1 Cancer
A pathologic cancer stage where the rectal tumor has grown into the second or muscle layer without needing further treatment.

Stage 2 Cancer
A pathologic cancer stage where the tumor penetrates through the rectal wall, usually requiring chemotherapy or chemoradiation.

Stage 3 Cancer
A pathologic cancer stage indicating that cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes, almost always necessitating post-operative chemoradiation or chemotherapy.

OX Regimen
A chemotherapy regimen containing oxaliplatin, known to potentially cause peripheral neuropathy in fingers and toes.

IRI Regimen
A chemotherapy regimen containing irinotecan, frequently associated with abdominal cramping, nausea, diarrhea, and hair loss.

RCC Subtypes
Subtypes of renal cell carcinoma, which represent variants of kidney cancer.

Renal Cell Carcinoma
Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC) is the most common form of kidney cancer, originating in the cells that line the renal tubules in the kidney.<SEP>The most common type of kidney cancer, accounting for approximately 90% of cases, arising from cells that line the renal tubules.

Clear Cell RCC
Clear Cell RCC (ccRCC) is the most common subtype of Renal Cell Carcinoma, occurring in roughly 7 out of 10 patients, characterized by pale or clear-appearing cells under microscopic histology.<SEP>The most common histological subtype of renal cell carcinoma, accounting for about 70% of RCC cases, characterized by pale or clear-looking cells under microscopy.

Non-Clear Cell RCC
A grouping of subtypes of renal cell carcinoma that do not exhibit the clear cell histological pattern under microscopy.<SEP>Non-Clear Cell RCC (nccRCC) is a classification encompassing several subtypes of RCC other than clear cell carcinoma, including papillary, chromophobe, and collecting duct variants.

Urothelial Carcinoma
A type of cancer that begins in the cells lining the renal pelvis and ureter, sharing characteristics with bladder cancer.

Wilms Tumor
A type of kidney cancer, also called nephroblastoma, that typically develops in young children.

Renal Sarcoma
A rare form of cancer that originates in the blood vessels or connective tissue of the kidney.

Irinotecan
A chemotherapy drug whose presence is indicated by 'IRI' in regimen names, commonly causing side effects such as abdominal cramping, nausea, diarrhea, and hair loss.

Bladder Cancer
A cancer of the bladder that shares many pathological features with urothelial carcinoma.<SEP>A disease category where malignant cells form in the tissues of the bladder, most commonly beginning in the urothelial cells.<SEP>A disease characterized by abnormal cell growth in the inner layer of the bladder, presenting with symptoms such as blood in the urine and categorized across several stages.<SEP>A disease characterized by malignant cell growth in the bladder wall, classified by grade, histological subtype, and stage of muscle invasion.<SEP>A malignancy affecting the urinary bladder and urinary tract that requires specialized diagnostic testing, staging, and treatment.<SEP>A malignancy of the urinary bladder whose treatment depends on cancer stage, grade, and overall health.<SEP>A malignant disease of the urinary bladder and urinary tract investigated and monitored via cystoscopy and imaging scans.<SEP>Bladder cancer is a common cancer in adults that begins when cells in the inner lining (urothelium) of the bladder grow uncontrollably, potentially invading muscle layers and other parts of the body.<SEP>Bladder cancer is a form of cancer requiring treatments such as bladder removal surgery, intravesical therapy, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy.<SEP>Bladder cancer is a malignancy of the urinary bladder, including forms such as muscle-invasive bladder cancer, that requires surgical and therapeutic interventions.<SEP>Bladder cancer is a malignancy originating in the tissues of the urinary bladder, requiring treatments such as surgery, intravesical instillation, or systemic therapies.<SEP>Bladder cancer is a type of cancer affecting the urinary bladder and urinary tract that requires multidisciplinary care, diagnostic testing, and surveillance.<SEP>Bladder cancer is a type of cancer that primarily begins in the urothelial cells lining the bladder wall and is evaluated based on stage and grade.

Soft Tissue Sarcoma
A category of malignant tumors of the connective tissues, referenced in patient guidelines alongside renal sarcoma.<SEP>A major class of sarcomas that develop in supportive body tissues like muscles, fat, nerves, tendons, and blood vessels.

Transitional Cell Cancer
The historical medical designation for urothelial carcinoma, arising in the lining of the urinary tract.

Advanced Kidney Cancer
A severe stage of renal cancer characterized by tumor growth into and beyond the fibrous tissue of Gerota's fascia.

Urinary System
An organ system consisting of the kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra responsible for filtering blood, balancing fluids, and removing waste in the form of urine.

Papillary RCC
Papillary RCC (PRCC) is the most common subtype of non-clear cell RCC, found in about 1 out of 10 RCC patients, characterized by long, thin finger-like microscopic structures.

Chromophobe RCC
Chromophobe RCC is a subtype of non-clear cell RCC characterized by pale cells that are larger and structurally distinct from clear cells.

Translocation RCC
Translocation RCC is an RCC subtype characterized by specific gene fusions that promote cancer, frequently diagnosed in children and younger adults.

Collecting Duct RCC
Collecting Duct RCC (cdRCC) is a rare subtype of non-clear cell RCC that develops in the cells lining the kidney's collecting ducts or tubules.

Renal Medullary Carcinoma
Renal Medullary Carcinoma (RMC) is a rare subtype of non-clear cell RCC frequently diagnosed in young individuals of African descent who carry the sickle cell trait or sickle cell disease.

Unclassified RCC
Unclassified RCC is a diagnostic category for kidney cancer cells that do not conform to any established subtype or show characteristics of more than one subtype.

Sarcomatoid RCC
Sarcomatoid RCC (sRCC) refers to kidney cancers where cells take on the appearance of sarcoma; it can arise from nearly any RCC subtype and tends to be more aggressive and prone to metastasis.

Kidney Cancer Diagnosis
Kidney Cancer Diagnosis is the clinical evaluation process utilizing imaging, blood tests, urine tests, biopsy, and biomarker assessments to detect, classify, and stage RCC.

data.entity_name: Clear Cell Papillary Renal Cell Tumor
data.content:
Clear Cell Papillary Renal Cell Tumor
Clear Cell Papillary Renal Cell Tumor is a recently defined histological subtype of renal neoplasm.

Fumarate Hydratase-Deficient RCC
Fumarate hydratase-deficient RCC is a recently recognized, rare subtype of renal cell carcinoma characterized by deficient FH enzyme activity.

ELOC-Mutated RCC
ELOC (formerly TCEB1)-mutated RCC is a recently classified molecular subtype of renal cell carcinoma defined by specific ELOC gene alterations.

Sarcoma
A rare classification of cancers that include soft tissue sarcomas and bone sarcomas, making up most primary bone cancers.<SEP>A rare form of malignant tumor that can arise in the cervix, distinguished from common epithelial cervical carcinomas.<SEP>Sarcoma is a broad category of cancer that originates in connective tissues, including muscles, fat, blood vessels, fibrous tissue, and nerves.

Sickle Cell Disease
Sickle cell disease and sickle cell trait are genetic red blood cell disorders strongly associated with increased risk of developing renal medullary carcinoma.

Histology
A diagnostic classification method based on the microscopic examination of the structure of tumor cells and tissues.<SEP>Histology refers to the microscopic study and characterization of tumor tissue architecture and cell type, essential for determining RCC subtypes and treatment strategies.<SEP>The anatomical study and microscopic classification of cells, tissues, and organs used to determine tumor characteristics and inform treatment planning.<SEP>The microscopic examination and study of tissue and tumor cell morphology used to assign cancer grade.

B-Cell ALL
B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) is the most common classification of ALL that originates in B-cell lymphocytes.

T-Cell ALL
T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is a major classification of ALL that originates in T-cell lymphocytes.

Adult Cancer Center
A medical facility specialized in treating cancer in adult patients, providing diagnostic, staging, and therapeutic interventions.<SEP>A specialized medical healthcare facility providing adult cancer treatment and related patient care services.

Monocytes
A specific type of white blood cell involved in fighting infections as part of the leukocyte family.

AYA
Adolescents and young adults (AYAs) are patients aged 15 to 39 at the time of cancer diagnosis, representing a distinct oncology demographic.

Pediatric Cancer Center
A specialized medical institution focusing on the diagnosis, management, and treatment of childhood and adolescent cancers.

Pediatric Oncologist
A specialized medical doctor who diagnoses and treats cancer in infants, children, adolescents, and young adults.

Adult Oncologist
A physician specializing in the diagnosis and treatment of cancer in adult patients.

B Cell
A type of lymphocyte white blood cell in which B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and related lymphomas originate.

T Cell
A type of lymphocyte white blood cell involved in immune response and the origin of T-ALL and T-LBL malignancies.

Lymphoblast
An immature lymphocyte cell produced in abnormally high amounts in the bone marrow during acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

Stem Cells
Progenitor cells located in the bone marrow from which blood cells and acute myeloid leukemia originate.

Blood Cancer
Blood cancer is a broader category of malignancies that disrupt normal blood cell development and function in the bone marrow and bloodstream.

Lactate Dehydrogenase Test
A blood test measuring LDH levels, utilized in general health evaluations and leukemia workups to assess cellular damage and turnover.<SEP>A blood test measuring the level of the LDH enzyme, which can indicate tissue and cellular damage caused by cancer.<SEP>A diagnostic blood test that measures LDH enzyme released by damaged or rapidly proliferating tumor cells.

Brain CT
A non-contrast computed tomography scan of the head indicated when a central nervous system bleed is suspected in an AML patient.

Brain MRI
A contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging scan of the brain performed when leukemic meningitis is suspected.

CNS Bleed
A central nervous system hemorrhage, an acute complication screened for using brain CT imaging in symptomatic AML patients.

Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplant
A medical donor cell transplant procedure requiring human leukocyte antigen compatibility to avoid graft rejection or immune reaction.

Bone Marrow Test
A clinical procedure in which bone marrow samples are extracted and analyzed to establish a definitive diagnosis of leukemia.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure comprising bone marrow aspirate and biopsy to extract liquid and core cellular samples from the bone marrow.

Fertility And Reproductive Specialists
Specialized medical professionals who guide cancer patients through fertility preservation options prior to treatment.

Blood Relatives
Genetically related family members whose tissue or blood samples are tested first to identify a match for an allogeneic stem cell donor.

White Blood Cell Differential
A hematologic laboratory test that counts each specific subtype of white blood cell and detects abnormal blasts.

Hemoglobin
A standard complete blood count metric evaluating oxygen-carrying capacity, used to indicate the need for a red blood cell transfusion.

Absolute Neutrophil Count
A laboratory metric measuring neutrophil levels to evaluate a patient's immune defense against bacterial infections.

Lactate Dehydrogenase
A cellular enzyme biomarker released into the bloodstream by dying cells or rapidly multiplying tumor cells.

Red Blood Cell Transfusion
A therapeutic medical procedure administered when a patient's hemoglobin levels fall below safe clinical thresholds.

Performance Status Scales
Measurement systems, such as the ECOG score and Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS), used to assess a patient's functional health and help determine appropriate cancer treatment plans.

AML Genetic Changes
Acquired chromosomal and molecular abnormalities—including deletions, insertions, inversions, point mutations, and translocations—used to classify AML and guide targeted therapies.

Hematopathology Review
A diagnostic microscopic review of bone marrow biopsy and aspirate samples to analyze cell size, shape, and overall appearance for AML diagnosis.

Molecular Testing
A diagnostic classification comprising genomic testing, tumor profiling, gene expression analysis, and tumor sequencing to evaluate DNA mutations and molecular features.<SEP>A specialized laboratory procedure conducted to identify genetic mutations and biomarkers within tumor biopsy tissue.<SEP>Comprehensive diagnostic evaluations—also known as genomic profiling, tumor profiling, or gene expression profiling—used to identify somatic genetic changes and mutations in leukemia cells.

FLT
A specific mutated gene and protein marker evaluated in AML cells to guide prognostic determination and targeted treatment strategies.

Chromosome Translocation And Gene Rearrangement
