Structural alterations where genetic material switches between chromosomes or genes, exemplified by t(8;21)(q22;q1) and RUNX1::RUNX1T.

RUNX1::RUNX1T
A specific gene rearrangement fusion resulting from a chromosome translocation found in acute myeloid leukemia cells.<SEP>RUNX1::RUNX1T is a genetic mutation and fusion marker associated with acute myeloid leukemia and leukemia predisposition assessment.

PML::RARA
PML::RARA is a specific gene rearrangement evaluated in leukemia diagnosis and monitored for targeted therapy response.

Hereditary Cancer Syndromes
Hereditary cancer syndromes are inherited genetic conditions passed from parent to child that predispose individuals to cancer development.

Hematopoietic Cell Donors
Biological family members evaluated as potential hematopoietic stem cell donors who may be tested for leukemia predisposition syndromes.

Fluorodeoxyglucose
A radiopharmaceutical tracer composed of fluoride and glucose used in FDG-PET/CT imaging to trace cancer metabolism.<SEP>A radiotracer (FDG) utilized in PET/CT imaging to measure sugar uptake by cells in the body.<SEP>A radiotracer made of fluoride and glucose used in FDG-PET/CT scans to highlight cells taking up high amounts of sugar.

Genetic and Biomarker Tests
Laboratory evaluations analyzing gene mutations and chromosomal abnormalities in leukemia cells to determine subtype and prognosis.

Cladribine
An antimetabolite chemotherapy medication (also known as Mavenclad) used in the treatment of leukemia by preventing DNA synthesis.

Clofarabine
An antimetabolite drug (also known as Clolar) used in chemotherapy regimens for leukemia to disrupt cancer cell DNA replication.

Cytarabine
A chemotherapy drug administered in high doses as an alternative treatment strategy for primary CNS lymphoma.<SEP>A core antimetabolite chemotherapy agent (also called Ara-C) administered at varying doses or via intrathecal injection to treat acute myeloid leukemia.<SEP>An antimetabolite chemotherapy medication commonly administered in combination regimens for acute myeloid leukemia.

Fludarabine
An antimetabolite chemotherapy drug that interferes with DNA synthesis in leukemia cells.

Methotrexate
A chemotherapy drug that blocks folate metabolism to inhibit cancer cell growth, frequently used in high doses for primary CNS lymphoma.<SEP>An antimetabolite chemotherapy agent that can be injected into spinal fluid (intrathecally) or given systemically to treat cancer.<SEP>The principal chemotherapy medication utilized in the treatment of primary CNS lymphoma.

Daunorubicin
A traditional chemotherapy drug used in combination with cytarabine and targeted agents to treat acute myeloid leukemia.<SEP>An anthracycline chemotherapy agent that damages DNA to cause leukemic cell death, which carries lifetime dose limits due to cardiac risks.

Idarubicin
An anthracycline medication (Idamycin PFS) used in acute myeloid leukemia treatment regimens.

Mitoxantrone
An anthracycline-class drug (Novantrone) employed to disrupt DNA synthesis in cancer cells.

CPX-351
A dual-drug liposomal formulation (also known as Vyxeos) combining cytarabine and daunorubicin to deliver antimetabolite and anthracycline therapy together.

Azacitidine
A hypomethylating agent (marketed as Vidaza) used to reverse gene silencing in leukemic cells, allowing them to differentiate into mature normal blood cells.<SEP>A hypomethylating agent that prevents methyl groups from binding to DNA, helping restore normal gene regulation in leukemic blasts.

Blood Cells
Blood cells are specialized cells formed from hematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow, encompassing red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.<SEP>Formed elements circulating in blood plasma, categorized primarily into red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.

Decitabine
A hypomethylating agent (marketed as Dacogen) that blocks DNA methyl groups to restore normal gene expression and cell maturation in leukemia.

Gemtuzumab Ozogamicin
A targeted therapy conjugate linked to chemotherapy that binds the CD33 surface protein on leukemic blast cells to induce targeted cytotoxic destruction.

Gilteritinib
A targeted kinase inhibitor used to treat acute myeloid leukemia characterized by specific FLT3 mutations.

Quizartinib
A targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor indicated for acute myeloid leukemia harboring FLT3-ITD mutations.

Midostaurin
A targeted small-molecule inhibitor used to treat AML carrying FLT3 gene alterations.

Sorafenib
A targeted kinase inhibitor employed in the treatment of acute myeloid leukemia with FLT3-ITD mutations.<SEP>A targeted multikinase inhibitor (marketed as Nexavar) recommended for progressive thyroid cancer that cannot be surgically removed and does not take up iodine.

Core Binding Factor
A genetic transcription factor complex whose abnormalities in acute myeloid leukemia cause a deficit in mature blood cell production.

CD33
A cell surface receptor protein prominently expressed on leukemic blasts, serving as a specific target for gemtuzumab ozogamicin.

CML
Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) is a blood cancer linked to the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene and the Philadelphia chromosome, characterized by uncontrolled growth of myeloid progenitor cells.

Specialized Cancer Centers
Medical centers with specific clinical expertise and experience in managing and treating Chronic Myeloid Leukemia.

Caregivers
Family members, friends, or peers who provide emotional support, meals, transportation, and advocacy during doctor visits for cancer patients.<SEP>Individuals providing personal and emotional care to patients with advanced or metastatic disease.<SEP>Loved ones and supporters providing physical, mental, emotional, and practical care to individuals diagnosed with brain tumors.

BCR::ABL1 Gene
A fused abnormal oncogene created by the exchange between chromosomes 9 and 22 that produces an unregulated protein driving CML.

Mature B-cell ALL
Mature B-cell ALL, also known as Burkitt leukemia, is a rare subtype of ALL that is biologically essentially the same as Burkitt lymphoma but managed with distinct treatment strategies.

B-cell Lymphoblastic Lymphoma
B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma (B-LL or B-LBL) is a disease where B-cell lymphoblasts primarily proliferate in the lymph nodes rather than in the bone marrow.

T-cell Lymphoblastic Lymphoma
T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma (T-LL or T-LBL) is a condition in which T-cell lymphoblasts grow primarily in the thymus rather than in the bone marrow.

Pediatric ALL
Pediatric ALL refers to acute lymphoblastic leukemia occurring in infants, children, and young adults up to 18 years of age, as well as select adolescents and young adults treated in pediatric oncology settings.

B-Cell Lymphocytes
B lymphocytes or B cells are white blood cells that produce antibody proteins to protect against infection.

T-Cell Lymphocytes
T lymphocytes or T cells are specialized immune cells that fight infections, kill tumor cells, and regulate immune responses.

Pediatric Cancer Centers
Pediatric cancer centers are specialized healthcare facilities providing oncology treatment tailored for infants, children, and eligible adolescent and young adult patients.

Adult Cancer Centers
Adult cancer centers are specialized medical institutions providing oncology diagnosis and care for adult patients, including some adolescent and young adult populations.

Pancreatic Cancer
A cancer that begins in the pancreas, an organ in the digestive system that regulates enzymes and blood sugar levels.<SEP>A complex form of cancer affecting the pancreas, requiring comprehensive diagnostic testing, multidisciplinary staging, and specialized treatment planning.<SEP>A malignancy of the pancreas that is genetically correlated with germline mutations in genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2.<SEP>A malignant disease that originates in the pancreas, with risk factors including lifestyle habits, chemical exposure, underlying health conditions, and hereditary genetic syndromes.<SEP>A serious abdominal cancer associated with familial cancer syndromes involving BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations.

Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
The most common form of pancreatic cancer, arising from the exocrine cells that line the ducts of the pancreas.

Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumor
A less common form of pancreatic cancer that originates from the hormone-producing endocrine cells of the pancreas.

BCR::ABL1-Negative Or BCR::ABL1-Like B-ALL
A common subtype of B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia where a clinical trial is often the preferred treatment.

Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma
A specific form of pancreatic cancer that develops from exocrine cells lining the ducts of the pancreas.

Hereditary Breast-Ovarian Cancer Syndrome
A hereditary genetic condition recognized as increasing the risk of developing pancreatic cancer.

Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome
A genetic condition identified as a hereditary risk factor for developing pancreatic cancer.

Familial Malignant Melanoma Syndrome
Also known as melanoma-pancreatic cancer syndrome or FAMMM, a hereditary condition that elevates the risk of pancreatic cancer.

Hereditary Pancreatitis
A genetic inflammatory condition of the pancreas known to heighten the risk of pancreatic cancer.

Pancreatic Cancer Stages
A disease classification system ranging from stage 0 to stage 4 based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, artery invasion, and distant metastasis.

Drug Treatment
A nonsurgical therapeutic approach that utilizes cancer medications and regimens based on tumor markers to manage cancer progression and alleviate symptoms.

Stage 0 Pancreatic Cancer
A stage where cancer cells are found only in the innermost layer of the duct wall and have not invaded deeper tissue.

Stage 1 Pancreatic Cancer
A cancer stage where the tumor is four centimeters or smaller and remains localized completely within the pancreas.

Stage 2 Pancreatic Cancer
A stage where the tumor exceeds four centimeters or has spread to between one and three nearby lymph nodes.

Stage 3 Pancreatic Cancer
An advanced local stage where the tumor has invaded nearby major arteries or spread to four or more lymph nodes.

Stage 4 Pancreatic Cancer
A stage characterized by widespread metastatic dissemination, commonly affecting organs such as the liver, lungs, or abdominal lining.

Metastatic Pancreatic Cancer
Pancreatic cancer that has spread to distant organs and tissues far from the pancreas.

Biomarker Tests
A category of specialized blood and urine diagnostic tests—such as 4Kscore, PHI, IsoPSA, ExoDx, and PCA3—used alongside PSA testing to determine the need for further diagnostic intervention.<SEP>A group of diagnostic laboratory evaluations, including FISH, DNA sequencing, and karyotyping, used to identify specific genetic characteristics and mutations to guide cancer treatment.<SEP>Profiling tests performed on cancer tissues to identify specific molecular markers that guide drug regimens and tailored treatments.

Imaging
Diagnostic procedures used to visualize brain structures, detect tumors, and determine tumor characteristics.<SEP>Diagnostic scanning techniques critical for visualizing tumor size, locating disease, and staging pancreatic cancer.<SEP>Diagnostic scanning techniques, including FDG-PET/CT, CT, and MRI, used to evaluate cancer stage, recurrence, or therapeutic response.<SEP>Medical diagnostic imaging modalities paired with screening tests like PSA or physical exams to assess the prostate.<SEP>Radiological and diagnostic scan procedures utilized to stage bladder cancer and determine whether it has spread.

Endoscopic Tests
Diagnostic procedures using an endoscope to evaluate the pancreas and surrounding structures.<SEP>Internal diagnostic examinations utilized to visualize the gastrointestinal and pancreatic areas to detect abnormalities.

Multidisciplinary Consult
A collaborative evaluation and consultation session involving diverse medical specialists to evaluate test results and plan treatment.

Chronic Inflammation Of The Pancreas
A persistent inflammatory condition of the pancreas that increases the risk of pancreatic cancer development.

Pesticides
Cancer-causing chemicals whose significant exposure represents a major environmental risk factor for developing pancreatic cancer.

Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
A non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate gland (BPH) that shares common urinary symptoms with prostate cancer by compressing the urethra.<SEP>Also called an enlarged prostate, a common non-cancerous condition that causes urinary symptoms similar to prostate cancer by pressing against the bladder and urethra.

Multidisciplinary Care Team
A collaborative group of diverse physicians, specialists, and allied health providers who work and communicate together to coordinate and deliver comprehensive cancer patient care.<SEP>A collaborative group of healthcare providers and specialists responsible for assessing, planning, and administering comprehensive treatment for a bladder cancer patient.<SEP>A multidisciplinary care team is a collaborative group of various medical specialists and care providers working together to diagnose, treat, and manage bladder cancer.<SEP>A specialized group of medical providers from various fields (such as oncologists, radiologists, surgeons, and counselors) collaborating at high-volume centers to evaluate and treat cancer patients.

Consult Meeting
A collaborative clinical session where the multidisciplinary care team reviews medical records, evaluates test results, and determines personalized care and treatment plans for a patient.

Jaundice
A clinical condition and medical symptom characterized by the yellowing of the skin and eyes, frequently serving as an early indicator of pancreatic cancer.

Erectile Dysfunction
A condition characterized by difficulty achieving an erection, identified as one of the potential symptoms associated with prostate issues.<SEP>A condition characterized by difficulty achieving or maintaining an erection, noted as a potential symptom of prostate conditions.<SEP>A male reproductive health condition characterized by difficulty achieving or maintaining an erection, noted as a potential symptom of prostate disorders.

Early-Stage Prostate Cancer
A clinical classification of prostate cancer that has not spread beyond the prostate gland, often referred to as localized prostate cancer.<SEP>A localized presentation of prostate cancer with low risk of metastasis, often not requiring extensive diagnostic imaging tests.<SEP>Also referred to as localized prostate cancer, this stage remains confined within the prostate gland, has high survival rates, and is often curable.<SEP>Early-stage prostate cancer, also known as localized prostate cancer, refers to cancer that has not spread beyond the prostate gland and is typically highly treatable.

Advanced-Stage Prostate Cancer
A clinical classification of prostate cancer that has spread outside the prostate to surrounding areas or distant body parts such as bones, liver, lungs, and distant lymph nodes.<SEP>A severe progression of prostate cancer where malignant cells spread beyond the prostate gland to other parts of the body through metastasis.<SEP>A severe stage of prostate cancer where cancer cells may spread outside the prostate gland to other areas of the body.<SEP>A stage of prostate cancer that has spread outside the prostate to regional areas, lymph nodes, bones, or other organs such as the liver or lungs; also known as metastatic prostate cancer.<SEP>Advanced-stage prostate cancer refers to cancer that has spread outside the prostate to regional lymph nodes or metastasized to distant organs and bones.

Risk Factors For Prostate Cancer
A group of conditions and attributes, including age over 65, family history, genetic mutations like BRCA2, race, obesity, and diet, that increase the likelihood of developing prostate cancer.<SEP>Factors associated with an increased likelihood of developing prostate cancer, notably advancing age (especially 65 and older) and family medical history.

Prostate
The prostate is an organ and gland in the male reproductive system located beneath the bladder that produces semen and prostate-specific antigen (PSA).

BRCA2 Gene
The BRCA2 gene is a specific gene whose inherited mutations or abnormalities are linked to an increased risk of prostate cancer and other cancers.

Prostate-Specific Antigen
A protein produced by the prostate gland whose elevated presence in blood can serve as an indicator of prostate issues or cancer.<SEP>Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is a protein produced by the prostate gland that nourishes and assists in the transmission of semen.

Semen
Semen is a reproductive fluid composed of secretions from the prostate and seminal vesicles along with sperm from the testicles.

Urethra
A tube carrying urine and semen from the bladder and reproductive structures out of the body, surrounded by the prostate gland.<SEP>The urethra is a tube that transports urine from the bladder out of the body and carries semen during ejaculation, surrounded by the prostate.

Bladder
An organ in the pelvis that stores urine, situated directly above the prostate gland.<SEP>The bladder is an organ in the urinary system that stores urine, situated directly above the prostate.

Seminal Vesicles
Glands located above the prostate and behind the bladder that make and store fluid that contributes to semen.<SEP>The seminal vesicles are two glands located above the prostate and behind the bladder that produce fluid contributing to semen.

Regional Prostate Cancer
A form of advanced-stage prostate cancer that has spread beyond the prostate into other regions of the pelvis.<SEP>A subcategory of prostate cancer where the disease has extended from the prostate gland to nearby areas like adjacent lymph nodes, but no farther.<SEP>Regional prostate cancer, also known as locally advanced prostate cancer, is cancer that has grown from the prostate gland to nearby lymph nodes but not further.

Metastatic Prostate Cancer
A clinical category of prostate cancer describing cancer cells that have traveled through the bloodstream or lymphatic system to distant organs or tissues.<SEP>An advanced stage of prostate cancer where malignant cells have spread beyond the primary tumor to regional lymph nodes or bones.<SEP>Metastatic prostate cancer is an advanced stage where cancer cells spread from the prostate to bones, lymph nodes, liver, lungs, and other distant body parts.<SEP>Metastatic prostate cancer refers to advanced prostate cancer that has spread outside the prostate to bones, pelvic lymph nodes, or other organs.

Early Detection Screening
Diagnostic tests designed to detect prostate cancer at an early stage, which are advised earlier and more frequently for high-risk demographics such as Black males.<SEP>Early detection screening involves clinical diagnostic tests to detect prostate cancer early, especially vital for higher-risk groups.

Black Males
A demographic group in the United States disproportionately affected by higher incidence, more aggressive onset, and double the mortality rate from prostate cancer compared to white males.<SEP>A demographic group in the United States noted to have a higher incidence of prostate cancer, earlier onset, more aggressive disease, and double the mortality rate compared to white males.

White Males
A demographic group compared in epidemiological studies against Black, Hispanic, and Asian males regarding prostate cancer rates and mortality.<SEP>A demographic group used as a comparative baseline in the United States regarding prostate cancer risk, age of onset, and mortality rates.

Diet And Lifestyle
Health habits and lifestyle factors, such as dietary fat intake, exercise, smoking, and obesity, that influence the risk, progression, and aggressiveness of prostate cancer.<SEP>Modifiable personal habits and health factors—such as dietary fat intake, consumption of fruits and vegetables, smoking, obesity, and physical exercise—that affect prostate cancer incidence and progression.

Health Care Providers
A professional category encompassing specialists, radiologists, gynecologists, pathologists, and primary care clinicians who evaluate, diagnose, and treat diseases such as breast cancer.<SEP>Medical professionals and clinical teams responsible for conducting screening tests, evaluating cancer aggressiveness, and designing personalized cancer therapies.<SEP>Medical professionals and doctors who evaluate symptoms, conduct screening tests, and manage prostate cancer diagnosis and care.<SEP>Medical professionals responsible for administering tests, diagnosing disease stages, planning treatment options, and monitoring patient recovery.<SEP>Medical professionals responsible for diagnosing, evaluating symptoms, and recommending specialized testing or treatments for prostate disorders.

Cancer Researchers
Scientists and medical investigators working to understand the underlying causes and cellular mechanisms of prostate cancer.<SEP>Scientists and specialists investigating the causes, biological factors, and treatment therapies of prostate cancer.

Active Surveillance
A clinical monitoring strategy for managing prostate cancer that involves periodic confirmatory biopsies without immediate treatment.<SEP>A disease management approach that closely monitors cancer growth through tests and imaging rather than immediately initiating aggressive treatment.<SEP>A management strategy for early-stage prostate cancer involving regular monitoring and testing without immediate treatment, aiming to avoid treatment side effects.<SEP>A non-surgical management method involving regular ultrasound monitoring for small, low-risk papillary thyroid tumors.<SEP>A non-surgical management strategy involving regular monitoring of very-low-risk thyroid cancers instead of immediate surgical intervention.

Prostate-Specific Antigen Test
A diagnostic blood test measuring the level of PSA protein to detect or monitor prostate cancer and evaluate treatment response.

Digital Rectal Exam
A clinical physical examination (DRE) of the lower rectum and anus recommended every 3 to 6 months for surveillance after recurrence treatment in patients who did not undergo APR.<SEP>A clinical physical examination of the rectum used as a screening tool to detect abnormal signs of prostate cancer.<SEP>A physical clinical examination used to feel for irregular or hardened areas on the prostate indicative of a tumor.<SEP>A physical diagnostic examination in which a physician inserts a gloved, lubricated finger into the anus and rectum to check for growths or abnormalities.<SEP>A physical examination in which a doctor inserts a gloved finger into the rectum to check the size, texture, and abnormalities of the prostate gland.<SEP>A physical examination of the lower rectum performed repeatedly after diagnosis to evaluate anal cancer.<SEP>A physical examination procedure in which a doctor manually palpates the prostate gland through the rectum to detect hardening, irregularities, or tumors.<SEP>A physical examination procedure utilized to evaluate the size and texture of the prostate gland.<SEP>A standard physical examination method used to detect prostate abnormalities, frequently paired with the PSA test.

Hormone Therapy

A biomarker evaluation determining whether cancer cells overexpress the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 protein.<SEP>A molecular diagnostic marker indicating the level of human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 in breast cancer cells.

Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)
A routine blood panel assessing organ function, including liver function tests (LFTs) and alkaline phosphatase.

Breast MRI
A specialized magnetic resonance imaging study of the breast used to evaluate tissue changes and tumor extent.<SEP>An MRI test of the breast performed with contrast while lying face down, typically used in addition to mammography.

PET-CT
An advanced imaging modality combining positron emission tomography and computed tomography used for cancer staging.

Nurse
A healthcare professional who assists in patient care, clinical communication, and managing portal messages within the healthcare setting.<SEP>A healthcare worker who assists providers and attends clinical procedures, such as physical breast examinations.

Breast Exam
A physical diagnostic examination in which a medical provider palpates the entire breast and armpit to assess for abnormalities.

Alkaline Phosphatase Test
A diagnostic blood evaluation measuring ALP enzyme levels to detect bone tumors, liver disorders, or pregnancy.<SEP>A diagnostic blood test measuring ALP enzyme levels; elevated levels can signal cancer metastasis to the bone or liver.

Bone X-ray
A low-dose radiation imaging test used to detect tumors and bone issues, often ordered if pain is present or after an abnormal bone scan.

Spine And Brain MRI
An MRI scan conducted to identify potential breast cancer metastasis to the spine or brain.

PET-CT Scan
A medical imaging technique combining Positron Emission Tomography (PET) and Computed Tomography (CT) to detect cancer and abnormal bodily activity.<SEP>An advanced imaging modality combining positron emission tomography and computed tomography into a single evaluation.

Sodium Fluoride PET-CT
A specialized PET-CT scan utilizing a sodium fluoride radiotracer, often used as an alternative to a bone scan to detect cancer in bones.<SEP>A specific PET-CT imaging technique that may be utilized as an alternative to a standard bone scan.

Radiotracer
A radioactive substance injected into a vein that releases small amounts of radiation, utilized in bone scans and PET scans to highlight damage or cancer.

Bilateral Mammogram
A type of mammogram that involves capturing x-ray images of both breasts for treatment planning.

2D Digital Mammography
Standard two-dimensional digital x-ray imaging used for screening and diagnostic breast examinations.

FDG PET-CT
A diagnostic scan using F-18 fluorodeoxyglucose radiotracer to identify cancer cells in lymph nodes and distant body sites.

FES PET-CT
A PET-CT imaging procedure using radioactive estrogen, employed when breast cancer is estrogen receptor-positive.

Vacuum-Assisted Core Biopsy
A minimally invasive biopsy technique that employs suction with a vacuum device to obtain tissue samples.

Excisional Biopsy
A surgical procedure in which all or part of a lymph node is removed by cutting into the skin for diagnostic examination.<SEP>A surgical procedure in which an entire abnormal area or tumor is removed for examination.<SEP>A surgical procedure in which an entire lymph node is removed by a surgeon for examination and diagnostic testing.

Incisional Biopsy
A biopsy method that involves making an incision to remove a portion of an abnormal area for diagnostic testing.<SEP>A surgical biopsy procedure in which only part of a lymph node is removed for diagnostic evaluation.

Axillary Lymph Node Needle Biopsy
A diagnostic needle biopsy targeting lymph nodes near the armpit to evaluate whether cancer cells have spread.

Mastectomy
A surgical operation or procedure to remove all or part of the breast to eliminate cancerous tissue.<SEP>A surgical operation performed to remove the breast, during which a sentinel lymph node biopsy may also be conducted.<SEP>A surgical procedure performed by surgical oncologists to remove breast tissue affected by cancer, often followed by breast reconstruction.<SEP>A surgical procedure that involves the surgical removal of one or both breasts, often used in cancer treatment.

Lumpectomy
A breast-conserving surgical procedure to excise a tumor and an optimal margin of surrounding normal tissue.<SEP>A surgical operation to remove a breast tumor while conserving breast tissue, often accompanied by a sentinel lymph node biopsy.

Stereotactic Needle Biopsy
A biopsy technique where mammography is used to guide the needle into the tumor.

Open Biopsy
A surgical diagnostic procedure involving a craniotomy to open the skull and excise tissue samples from a brain tumor.<SEP>A surgical procedure to excise a tumor in order to evaluate tissue structure and confirm histological diagnosis.<SEP>One of the standard types of surgical biopsy procedures for gliomas, used when tumor resection is not viable.

Hormone Receptor-Positive Breast Cancer
A classification of breast cancer where cancer cells express estrogen and/or progesterone receptors that stimulate growth and can be targeted by endocrine therapy.<SEP>A subtype of breast cancer where cancer cells express estrogen or progesterone receptors, making them susceptible to endocrine therapies.

Hormone Receptor-Negative Breast Cancer
A breast cancer classification where cells lack both estrogen and progesterone receptors, often growing faster than hormone receptor-positive cancers.

Estrogen Receptor-Positive Breast Cancer
A subset of breast cancer in which cancer cells express estrogen receptors that receive growth signals stimulated by estrogen.

HER2-Positive Breast Cancer
A breast cancer classification marked by elevated levels of the HER2 protein, making it eligible for HER2-targeted therapy.<SEP>A subtype of breast cancer characterized by high amounts of the HER2 protein or amplification of the HER2 gene, leading to increased cell growth and division.

Endocrine Therapy
A cancer treatment category, also known as hormone therapy, that blocks estrogen or progesterone to treat hormone receptor-positive breast cancer.<SEP>A category of medical cancer treatment involving the modulation or suppression of hormones.<SEP>A medical treatment approach that blocks estrogen receptor signaling or deprives cancer cells of hormones to halt growth in hormone receptor-positive cancers.<SEP>A systemic treatment class utilized in breast cancer therapy based on hormone receptor status such as estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor.<SEP>A targeted treatment for hormone receptor-positive breast cancers that slows or stops cancer cell growth by interfering with hormones.<SEP>Hormonal systemic therapy used in hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, often combined with targeted inhibitors like CDK4/6 or mTOR inhibitors.

In Situ Hybridization
A specialized molecular test that counts the number of copies of the HER2 gene, typically used when immunohistochemistry results are unclear.

Hormone Receptor Testing
A laboratory diagnostic procedure performed on biopsy samples from newly identified tumors to assess estrogen and progesterone receptor status.

Tumor Marker Testing
A diagnostic evaluation conducted on blood or biopsy tissue samples to identify specific proteins associated with cancer.

ER-Low-Positive Invasive Breast Cancer
A subcategory of invasive breast cancer in which estrogen receptors are identified in only 1 to 10 out of every 100 cancer cells, and for which endocrine therapy might not be recommended.

Tumor Mutational Burden
A genomic metric (TMB-H) measuring the number of mutations per million base pairs in tumor DNA, used to predict response to immune checkpoint inhibitors.

PD-1 And PD-L1 Testing
Evaluation of the immune proteins PD-1 and PD-L1 on cancer cells to determine candidate eligibility for checkpoint inhibitor therapy.

FISH
Fluorescence in situ hybridization, a molecular cytogenetic testing method using fluorescent dye probes that bind to specific pieces of DNA.<SEP>Fluorescence in situ hybridization, a specialized genetic testing method used to analyze CLL cells for treatment planning.

BRCA Tests
Genetic assessments evaluating mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, which are associated with increased risks of breast, ovarian, and other cancers.

Family Cancer Health History
A recorded collection of health information and cancer diagnoses among biological relatives used to identify hereditary health patterns.

Targeted Therapies
Cancer treatments targeted at specific molecular changes in tumor cells, selected based on biomarker testing results.<SEP>Medical cancer therapies specifically designed to target distinct gene alterations, such as PIK3CA mutations.

HER2
A cellular protein and established biomarker tested in breast cancer to inform therapeutic strategies.<SEP>A protein biomarker tested in recurrent cervical cancer to assess eligibility for targeted agents.

PIK3CA
A specific tumor gene mutation that can be detected through tumor mutation testing and treated with targeted therapies.

PD-1
Programmed death protein 1, an immune protein on cell surfaces that suppresses anti-tumor immune responses and serves as a drug target.

PD-L1
A biomarker protein evaluated in recurrent, progressive, or metastatic cervical cancer to assess suitability for immunotherapy.<SEP>Programmed death-ligand 1, an immune protein expressed on cancer cells targeted by checkpoint inhibitors.

Carcinoembryonic Antigen
A protein tumor marker (CEA) tested in blood or tissue to monitor cancer growth or spread.

CA 15-3
A protein biomarker monitored in breast cancer patients that may reflect disease progression.

Mismatch Repair Proteins
Cellular repair proteins (MMR) that fix short DNA replication errors; deficiency leads to microsatellite instability.<SEP>Proteins responsible for recognizing and repairing errors in short, repeated DNA sequences called microsatellites.

Breast Cancer Staging
A system used to classify the extent of breast cancer based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, metastasis (TNM), and biomarker status to determine prognosis and treatment.

Hereditary Genetic Testing
Diagnostic genetic testing recommended based on family medical history to identify inherited mutations linked to breast cancer risk.

Biomarker Status
The classification of tumor receptors and biological markers including estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and HER2 that guide treatment.

Stage 3 Breast Cancer
An advanced breast cancer classification characterized by tumors involving skin, chest wall, or fixed lymph nodes.

Stage 4 Breast Cancer
An advanced cancer classification denoting metastatic breast cancer that has spread to distant organs and other parts of the body.

Hereditary Breast Cancer
A form of breast cancer attributed to inherited gene mutations, representing approximately one in ten breast cancer cases.

Prognostic Stage
A breast cancer classification framework that incorporates anatomic TNM measures, tumor grade, and biomarker status (such as ER, PR, and HER2) under standard-of-care assumptions.

Tumor Size (T)
A staging metric within the TNM system measuring the size, depth, and local invasion of the primary tumor in centimeters or millimeters.

Lymph Node Status (N)
A staging metric assessing the spread of cancer to nearby regional lymph nodes, such as axillary, internal mammary, infraclavicular, and supraclavicular nodes.

Distant Metastasis (M)
A staging metric identifying whether breast cancer cells have spread to distant body organs such as the bones or lungs.

Progesterone Receptor Status
A biomarker category evaluating the presence of progesterone receptors (PR) on cancer cells, used in prognostic staging.

Drug Therapy
Pharmacological treatment administered before or after surgery, altering staging notation (such as ypT) when given preoperatively.

Axillary Lymph Nodes
Regional lymph nodes located under the arm, typically the initial site of regional breast cancer spread.

Internal Mammary Lymph Nodes
Regional lymph nodes situated near the breastbone that are assessed during clinical staging.

Infraclavicular Lymph Nodes
Regional lymph nodes situated beneath the collarbone evaluated for cancer involvement.

Supraclavicular Lymph Nodes
Regional lymph nodes located above the collarbone monitored during clinical staging of breast cancer.

Isolated Tumor Cells (ITCs)
Very small clusters of malignant cells detected in lymph nodes that fall within the N0 regional node category.

Lymph Node Micrometastasis
A cluster of approximately 200 cancerous cells within regional lymph nodes, designated as N1mi.

Tumor Micrometastasis
A minute collection of cancer cells smaller than 1 mm within primary tumor assessment, designated as T1mi.

Doctors
Medical professionals who evaluate diagnostic findings, assign cancer stages, and communicate treatment plans.

HER2-Targeted Therapy
A specialized class of systemic therapies targeted specifically at HER2 receptors on cancer cells to inhibit breast tumor growth.<SEP>A systemic therapy class designed to target HER2 expression in cancer cells using antibodies, inhibitors, and antibody-drug conjugates.<SEP>A targeted cancer therapy category comprising antibodies, inhibitors, and antibody-drug conjugates that target HER2 proteins.

Bone-Strengthening Therapy
A supportive therapeutic category utilized in breast cancer care to protect and strengthen bones, particularly during advanced or metastatic disease.

Diagnostic Radiologist
A medical specialist who interprets imaging studies such as mammograms and ultrasounds to detect and evaluate breast abnormalities.<SEP>A physician specializing in interpreting diagnostic medical imaging, such as x-rays, to detect and monitor disease.

Surgical Oncologist
A surgeon specialized in performing oncologic operations, such as lumpectomies or mastectomies, to remove cancerous tissue.

Oncology Nurse
A specialized healthcare provider who administers systemic treatments, coordinates patient care, and assists with managing adverse side effects.<SEP>An oncology nurse provides direct, hands-on care for cancer patients, administering systemic therapy, managing clinical care, addressing inquiries, and helping manage treatment side effects.

Oncology Pharmacist
A clinical expert who specializes in selecting, dosing, and managing antineoplastic drugs and symptom-relief medications.

Clinical Social Worker
A mental health and supportive care provider who diagnoses and treats emotional concerns, addresses anxiety, and assists patients with financial and logistical challenges.

Local Therapy
A treatment approach focused on the breast, chest wall, and lymph node area, including procedures such as mastectomy and radiation therapy.<SEP>Site-specific medical interventions used to manage localized tumor lesions in organs such as the liver, lungs, or bones prior to systemic therapy.

Modified Radical Mastectomy
A surgical procedure frequently used for inflammatory breast cancer in which the entire breast and axillary lymph nodes, and sometimes part of the chest wall muscle, are removed.<SEP>A surgical procedure in which the entire breast, some lymph nodes, and potentially part of the chest wall muscle are removed.

Clinical Social Workers
Mental health professionals who diagnose and treat behavioral, mental, and emotional issues in patients facing cancer.

Inhibitor Therapy
A systemic treatment category that includes CDK4/6, mTOR, and PARP inhibitors such as palbociclib, everolimus, and olaparib.

Breast Reconstruction
A surgical procedure, often performed in stages as delayed reconstruction, to rebuild the breast following a mastectomy.

Plastic Surgeon
A specialized surgeon consulted to perform breast reconstruction surgery following cancer treatment.

Cancer Centers and Hospitals
Healthcare facilities with specialized experience and high procedure volumes for treating complex diseases like inflammatory breast cancer.

Myeloid Growth Factors
A therapeutic class of treatments used to boost white blood cell counts and prevent infections during chemotherapy.

CDK4/6 Inhibitors
A category of targeted inhibitor drugs that block cyclin-dependent kinase proteins to impede cancer cell division, often combined with endocrine therapy.

mTOR Inhibitors
A category of targeted drugs that inhibit mTOR cell proteins to restore the efficacy of endocrine therapy.

Regional Nodal Irradiation
A radiation therapy approach targeting lymph nodes in areas such as the infraclavicular, supraclavicular, or axillary bed.

Whole Breast Radiation Therapy
Radiation therapy directed at the entire breast tissue, commonly administered using a linear accelerator.

Herbal Supplements
Botanical and dietary products, including turmeric, gingko biloba, green tea extract, and St. John's wort, that can cause adverse drug interactions during systemic therapy.

Antibody Drug Conjugates
A class of targeted therapeutic agents (ADCs) that deliver cell-specific chemotherapy directly into HER2-positive cancer cells.

HER2 Antibodies
Targeted agents that block external HER2 growth signals and stimulate the immune system to target cancer cells.

HER2 Inhibitors
Targeted therapeutic agents that block intracellular growth signals generated by HER2 proteins.

Ovarian Suppression
A medical intervention involving ovarian suppression or ablation required for premenopausal individuals receiving CDK4/6 inhibitor regimens.<SEP>A therapeutic medical process using pharmacological agents, such as LHRH agonists, to temporarily stop the ovaries from producing hormones.

Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction Test
A diagnostic monitoring procedure measuring the heart's pumping efficiency before and during trastuzumab treatment.

Drug Interaction
An adverse pharmacological event where herbal supplements, vitamins, or concurrent medications alter the efficacy or safety of systemic cancer therapy.

MTOR Inhibitors
A class of targeted drugs that inhibit the mTOR cell protein to help restore the effectiveness of endocrine therapy in cancer treatment.

PIK3CA Inhibitors
A class of targeted therapies that inhibit mutated PIK3CA gene activity to counteract cancer cell growth and drug resistance.

Aromatase Inhibitors
A class of endocrine therapy drugs that prevent the enzyme aromatase from converting androgen into estrogen.

Estrogen Receptor Modulators
A category of anti-estrogen therapies that prevent hormones from binding to receptors, including SERMs and SERDs.

Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulators
A subclass of estrogen receptor modulators, known as SERMs, that prevent estrogen from attaching to hormone receptors.

Selective Estrogen Receptor Degraders
A subclass of estrogen receptor modulators, known as SERDs, that block and degrade estrogen receptors.

Primary CNS Lymphoma
A distinct category of lymphoma affecting the central nervous system.<SEP>A form of cancer affecting the central nervous system for which various treatment options including chemotherapy, radiation, and stem cell rescue are utilized.<SEP>A rare and aggressive cancer category that originates in the lymphocytes of the central nervous system, including the brain, spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, or eyes.<SEP>A rare and aggressive cancer of lymphocytes that primarily develops in the central nervous system, including the brain, spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and eyes.<SEP>A rare cancer affecting the central nervous system, including the brain and eyes, treatable with radiation, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and stem cell rescue.<SEP>A rare cancer category affecting the central nervous system, including the brain, cerebrospinal fluid, spine, and eyes.<SEP>A rare type of cancer affecting the central nervous system, treated typically through a multi-step process including induction and consolidation phases.<SEP>A rare type of cancer that develops deep within brain tissue, typically treated with chemotherapy, steroids, or clinical trials rather than surgery.<SEP>A rare type of cancer that develops deep within the central nervous system, requiring specialized diagnostic tests, staging, and treatment regimens.<SEP>Primary CNS lymphoma is a type of cancer that originates in the central nervous system, affecting the brain, spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, or eyes.<SEP>Primary central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma is a type of cancer that develops in the brain, spine, or central nervous system with symptoms resembling other neurological conditions.

Bilateral Oophorectomy
A surgical procedure to remove both ovaries, functioning as a form of surgical endocrine therapy.

Ovarian Ablation
A medical radiation procedure used to permanently stop the ovaries from producing hormones.

Premenopause
A biological reproductive state characterized by regular menstrual cycles, where the ovaries serve as the primary source of estrogen and progesterone.<SEP>A reproductive biological state in which the ovaries function as the primary source of estrogen and progesterone.

Menopause
A biological life stage and hormonal transition in which menstrual cycles cease, often addressed with hormone replacement therapy.

Amenorrhea
A medical condition characterized by the cessation of menstrual periods, which can occur during and after medical treatment.<SEP>A medical condition involving the temporary or permanent cessation of menstrual periods, which can occur as a side effect of cancer treatment.

Steroidal Aromatase Inhibitors
A subclass of aromatase inhibitor medications, exemplified by exemestane (Aromasin), that irreversibly inactivate aromatase enzymes.

Non-Steroidal Aromatase Inhibitors
A subclass of aromatase inhibitor medications, including anastrozole and letrozole, that competitively inhibit aromatase enzymes.

Testosterone-Suppressing Therapy
A category of endocrine therapy used to reduce androgen levels in patients assigned male at birth who continue to produce testosterone.

HER2-Negative Breast Cancer
A subtype of breast cancer that does not overexpress the HER2 protein, specified as a requirement for PARP inhibitor treatment.

Secondary CNS Lymphoma
A category of lymphoma that starts in another part of the body and subsequently spreads to the brain or spinal cord.

Immunodeficiency Disorder
A classification of illnesses that weaken the immune system's capacity to fight infections and diseases, acting as a risk factor for primary CNS lymphoma.

HIV
A viral pathogen category that causes AIDS and weakens the immune system, frequently linked to primary CNS lymphoma.<SEP>Human immunodeficiency virus, an infection that significantly elevates an individual's risk of developing anal cancer.<SEP>Human immunodeficiency virus, identified as a risk factor contributing to the development of anal cancer.

Epstein-Barr Virus
A common human virus category that causes mononucleosis and remains dormant in the body, recognized as a risk factor for primary CNS lymphoma.<SEP>A viral pathogen whose DNA testing is utilized as needed during evaluation and treatment planning for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.<SEP>Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a biological marker whose presence in the blood or lymph nodes is factored into prognostic staging for nasopharyngeal cancer.<SEP>Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a viral pathogen whose presence in neck lymph nodes is used to identify early-stage T0 nasopharyngeal tumors.

Autoimmune Disease
A category of diseases in which the immune system overreacts and attacks healthy tissues and organs.

Organ Transplant
A major medical and surgical procedure that necessitates immunosuppressive medications, resulting in increased risk of infections and cancers such as primary CNS lymphoma.

Older Adults
A demographic age category, primarily individuals in their 60s and 70s, representing the age group most frequently diagnosed with primary CNS lymphoma.

Brain Tumor
A broad classification of abnormal cell growths occurring in the brain or central nervous system, which can be benign or malignant.<SEP>A broad clinical classification of abnormal growths located in the brain, which can include primary CNS lymphoma.<SEP>A broad disease category referring to intracranial neoplasms, of which gliomas are a specific type.<SEP>An abnormal growth of cells within the brain that can cause intracranial pressure, physical weakness, cognitive issues, and mood changes.

Central Nervous System
The anatomical system comprising the brain and spinal cord, identified in pathology reports as the origin of primary gliomas.<SEP>The anatomical system comprising the brain and spinal cord, which is the primary site of origin and spread for primary CNS lymphoma.<SEP>The biological body system consisting of the brain and spinal cord that receives sensory input, processes information, and controls bodily actions.

Immune System
The biological defense network that protects the human body from infection, disease, and abnormal cellular growths.

AIDS
Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome is an advanced disease state that severely compromises the immune system, raising the risk of HPV persistence and cervical cancer.<SEP>Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, an advanced immune deficiency state caused by the HIV virus.

Mononucleosis
An infectious illness caused by infection with the Epstein-Barr virus, commonly referred to as mono.

Stem Cell Transplant
An intensive medical procedure utilized as a treatment option for patients diagnosed with primary CNS lymphoma.

Neurological Exam
A clinical diagnostic examination used to evaluate brain function, nerve responses, and sensory or motor coordination in suspected primary CNS lymphoma.<SEP>A clinical examination involving tests of alertness, thinking, balance, coordination, reflexes, strength, hearing, touch, and smell to evaluate brain function.<SEP>A neurological exam is a clinical evaluation of a patient's alertness, balance, reflexes, coordination, senses, and nerve health during the diagnosis of CNS conditions.

Eye Exam
A diagnostic procedure performed alongside a neurological examination to check the health and condition of the nerves at the back of the eyes.<SEP>A diagnostic test conducted to evaluate the health of the nerves at the back of the eye during a neurological assessment.<SEP>A specialized diagnostic examination performed by an eye specialist using a slit lamp to inspect the retina, optic nerve, and vitreous for lymphoma involvement.<SEP>A specialized ophthalmologic examination used to detect lymphoma involvement or vision changes within ocular structures.<SEP>An ophthalmic assessment recommended prior to starting treatment for specific conditions like nasopharyngeal cancer.

Impaired Immune System
A medical condition characterized by a compromised or weakened immune response, serving as a primary risk factor for developing primary CNS lymphoma.

Remission
A clinical disease state in which symptoms and signs of cancer disappear following successful therapeutic intervention.

Relapse
The recurrence of primary CNS lymphoma following initial rounds of treatment, representing a key scenario where stem cell rescue is evaluated.<SEP>The recurrence of primary CNS lymphoma in the brain, spinal cord, or eye after a period of remission.

Specialized Treatment Center
Medical centers and hospitals with specialized expertise and clinical experience in diagnosing and treating lymphomas of the brain.

Stephanie E. Weiss
Stephanie E. Weiss, MD, FASTRO, is a medical doctor and radiation oncology specialist associated with imaging documentation of primary CNS lymphoma.<SEP>Stephanie E. Weiss, MD, FASTRO, is a medical specialist who contributed diagnostic imaging for the clinical publication.

Brain Cancer
Brain cancer refers to malignancies affecting brain tissue, which can present clinical signs and symptoms similar to primary CNS lymphoma.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
A diagnostic imaging technique that can be combined with PET scans to assess the extent of cancer.<SEP>An imaging technique utilizing magnetic fields and radio waves, without radiation, to produce detailed images of soft tissue and pelvic structures.<SEP>Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a diagnostic imaging category used in specific colon cancer scenarios, such as examining the liver or rectum, or clarifying CT findings.<SEP>Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the primary non-invasive diagnostic imaging method using magnetic fields and radio waves to visualize soft tissues and tumors in the brain and spine.

Computed Tomography
An imaging procedure using x-rays and computer processing, often administered with contrast agents, to examine the pelvis, chest, and abdomen for cancer spread.<SEP>An imaging scan using x-rays and computer processing to create detailed 3-D images of the chest, abdomen, or pelvis.<SEP>An x-ray imaging modality (CT) combined with a contrast agent to produce detailed cross-sectional views of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis to detect cancer spread.<SEP>Computed tomography (CT) is a primary category of diagnostic medical imaging used to evaluate the presence and extent of colon cancer in the body.<SEP>Computed tomography (CT) is an X-ray imaging procedure that generates cross-sectional 3D images of the body, utilized as an alternative when MRI is unavailable.

Stereotactic Biopsy
A highly precise surgical procedure using a frame or markers and a hollow needle to extract tissue from hard-to-reach or vital brain areas.<SEP>A stereotactic biopsy is a specialized diagnostic surgical procedure in which a needle is guided into the brain to extract tumor tissue for pathological testing.<SEP>A stereotactic biopsy is an image-guided surgical procedure performed by a neurosurgeon to extract tumor tissue from vital brain areas for definitive histological diagnosis.<SEP>A surgical diagnostic procedure performed by a neurosurgeon using imaging navigation and a thin hollow needle to obtain a small brain tumor sample.<SEP>The standard diagnostic biopsy procedure for primary CNS lymphoma, utilizing precision targeting to extract tumor samples from deep or vital brain regions.

Gadolinium
Gadolinium is an intravenous contrast agent used in MRI scans to highlight blood vessels, organs, and tumor tissues in primary CNS lymphoma.

Neurological Illnesses
Medical conditions of the nervous system that share overlapping symptoms and clinical signs with primary CNS lymphoma.

Physical Examination
A clinical evaluation assessing vital signs, body organs, lymph nodes, and head and neck structures to inform diagnosis and treatment planning.<SEP>An initial general medical evaluation conducted by clinicians before specialized diagnostic imaging and biopsy procedures.

Neurosurgeon
A medical specialist who performs surgical procedures on the brain, including stereotactic biopsies, open biopsies, and tumor resections.<SEP>A surgical specialist who performs brain surgeries, including resections and stereotactic biopsies.<SEP>A surgical specialist who performs stereotactic brain biopsies using image-guided navigation systems.

Vitreoretinal Lymphoma
Vitreoretinal lymphoma is a manifestation of primary CNS lymphoma that affects the vitreous and retina within the eyes.

Vitrectomy
A vitrectomy is a procedure where a needle removes a small sample of the eye's vitreous gel for diagnostic testing and cancer confirmation.

Ophthalmologist
A medical eye doctor who performs comprehensive eye examinations and vitrectomies to assess and detect ocular lymphoma involvement.

Positron Emission Tomography
An advanced imaging modality (PET) that uses an injected radioactive drug to detect metabolically active cancer cells throughout the body.<SEP>An imaging procedure involving radioactive glucose injection to detect metabolically active cancer cells, often combined with CT or MRI.<SEP>An imaging test utilizing a radioactive sugar tracer to detect actively metabolizing cancer cells in the body.

Testicular Ultrasound
An ultrasound imaging procedure used to evaluate whether lymphoma has spread to the testicles.

NCCN Guidelines For Patients
Educational and clinical practice materials published by NCCN to guide cancer patients through disease management.<SEP>Patient-oriented clinical practice guidelines developed by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network to provide educational guidance regarding cancer diagnosis and treatment.

HIV Blood Test
A recommended diagnostic test for individuals diagnosed with primary CNS lymphoma to determine the need for concurrent antiretroviral therapy.

Hepatitis B Testing
A blood screening required prior to immunotherapy to prevent the potential reactivation of the hepatitis B virus.

Stem Cell Rescue
A medical intervention often requiring high-dose chemotherapy as an essential preparatory component for treating certain cancers.<SEP>A medical procedure involving the harvesting, freezing, and reinfusion of a patient's stem cells following high-dose chemotherapy to restore healthy blood-forming cells in bone marrow.<SEP>An intensive medical procedure, also known as hematopoietic stem cell transplant, consisting of stem cell harvesting, high-dose chemotherapy, and stem cell reinfusion to restore bone marrow.<SEP>An intensive medical treatment category often paired with chemotherapy to restore blood-forming cells in lymphoma treatment.

Psychological Distress
A mental health condition encompassing depression and anxiety commonly experienced by individuals diagnosed with brain tumors.

Ultrasound Of The Testicles
A post-diagnosis imaging examination used to detect potential lymphoma spread to the testicles if whole-body PET/CT findings warrant it.

Eye Examination
A thorough diagnostic evaluation recommended for all individuals diagnosed with primary CNS lymphoma to check for ocular lymphoma involvement.

Antiretroviral Therapy
Specialized pharmacological therapy required for individuals diagnosed with both primary CNS lymphoma and HIV alongside cancer treatment.

Clinical Depression
A psychiatric mood disorder affecting approximately one in three patients diagnosed with primary brain tumors.

Informed Consent
A formal process and signed agreement wherein clinical trial participants are detailed on study objectives, risks, benefits, and rights prior to enrolling.<SEP>A formal process and voluntary agreement in which trial participants are fully informed about study procedures, risks, and benefits before enrolling.

Placebo
An inactive substance used in clinical trials, almost never administered alone in cancer trials but sometimes paired with standard therapies.<SEP>An inactive substance used in clinical trials, rarely administered alone in cancer trials, often coupled with standard therapies.

Intraocular Chemotherapy
A chemotherapy treatment category delivered directly into the eye or via a vein to address primary CNS lymphoma affecting the eyes.

High-Dose Methotrexate
The primary chemotherapy drug category used to treat primary CNS lymphoma, requiring hospitalization and supportive care due to potential organ toxicity.

Whole-Brain Radiation Therapy
A radiation therapy technique that targets the entire brain to treat multiple lesions and microscopic tumors associated with primary CNS lymphoma.<SEP>The most frequently employed radiation treatment technique for patients with primary CNS lymphoma.

Eye Surgeon
A medical specialist who performs surgical procedures to treat eye complications, such as cataracts resulting from intraocular chemotherapy.<SEP>A medical surgical specialist who performs routine operations to repair vision problems such as radiation-induced cataracts.

Induction Phase
The initial phase of cancer treatment aimed at destroying the main tumor burden, often utilizing chemotherapy or radiation therapy.<SEP>The initial phase of cancer treatment for primary CNS lymphoma designed to wipe out lymphoma cells, often lasting several months and utilizing high-dose chemotherapy.

Consolidation Phase
The second phase of cancer treatment for primary CNS lymphoma designed to eliminate any remaining cancer cells and prevent recurrence.<SEP>The secondary phase of cancer therapy administered to eliminate leftover cancer cells following initial induction treatment.

Ocular Radiation Therapy
A targeted radiation treatment modality focused specifically on the eyes or expanded via WBRT to treat primary CNS lymphoma affecting ocular structures.

Cataracts
An ocular medical condition and potential adverse side effect of intraocular chemotherapy, characterized by clouding of the eye lens that can be treated surgically.<SEP>An ocular medical condition that impairs vision, which can be caused as a complication of radiation therapy to the eyes.

A structured treatment schedule—commonly lasting 14, 21, or 28 days—alternating medication administration with rest periods to allow bodily recovery.

WBRT
Whole brain radiation therapy, a form of radiation treatment that can be expanded to include the eyes to treat primary CNS lymphoma.

Rituximab
A monoclonal antibody immunotherapy medication administered via IV infusion that targets CD20 proteins on cancerous blood cells in primary CNS lymphoma.<SEP>An immunotherapy drug commonly paired with high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy to treat primary central nervous system lymphoma.<SEP>The main immunotherapy agent used in the treatment of primary CNS lymphoma.

Monoclonal Antibody
A type of immunotherapy engineered to hunt and bind to specific surface proteins on cancer cells.

CD20
A specific surface protein found on cancerous blood cells and certain healthy blood cells, targeted by rituximab.

High-Dose Chemotherapy
An aggressive chemotherapy treatment administered during stem cell rescue to eradicate remaining lymphoma cells and existing bone marrow cells.

Stem Cell Removal
The initial procedural stage of a stem cell rescue involving the collection and cryopreservation of healthy stem cells from blood or bone marrow.

The final procedural phase of stem cell rescue where cryopreserved stem cells are thawed and transfused into the patient to restore depleted bone marrow.

Induction
The initial phase of cancer treatment aimed at destroying lymphoma cells and inducing disease remission.

Consolidation
A subsequent phase of cancer treatment administered after initial induction to eliminate residual disease and maintain long-term remission.

Integrative Medicine
A complementary healthcare approach provided by hospital facilities to support conventional cancer treatments and enhance patient well-being.

Multidisciplinary Care
A collaborative approach to healthcare involving a team of doctors, medical specialists, and allied health providers working together for patient care.

Treatment For The Spine
A specialized component or phase of central nervous system lymphoma treatment targeted at cancer found in the spine or spinal fluid.

Treatment For The Eyes
A specific therapeutic phase or consideration in managing central nervous system lymphoma involving ocular manifestations.

Blood-Brain Barrier
A protective biological layer surrounding the brain that prevents toxins, pathogens, and certain chemotherapy drugs from entering brain tissue.

Temozolomide
A chemotherapy medication used in combination therapy or as an alternative agent for treating primary CNS lymphoma.

Vincristine
A chemotherapy medication that may be included alongside methotrexate and rituximab in induction protocols.

Procarbazine
An oral chemotherapy medication utilized as part of multi-agent induction therapy for primary CNS lymphoma.

Ibrutinib
A targeted therapy medication considered an alternative induction option for primary CNS lymphoma patients unable to receive methotrexate.

Lenalidomide
An immunomodulatory medication utilized with or without rituximab as an alternative induction therapy for primary CNS lymphoma.

Pemetrexed
An antifolate chemotherapy drug used as an alternative induction agent in primary central nervous system lymphoma.

Pomalidomide
An immunomodulatory therapy medication listed as an alternative induction agent for primary CNS lymphoma.

The Colon
The primary section of the large intestine where water is absorbed from digested food before stool moves into the rectum.

The Rectum
The terminal six inches of the large bowel where stool is held before exiting the body.

The Cecum
The anatomical pouch situated at the beginning of the colon, from which the appendix extends.

The Appendix
A small, closed, finger-sized tube extending from the cecum.

Non-Metastatic Colon Cancer
A classification of colon cancer that has not spread to distant organs, typically treated with colectomy and potentially chemotherapy.

Metastatic Colon Cancer
A secondary cancer that originates in the large intestine (colon) and spreads to the liver.<SEP>An advanced classification of colon cancer where the cancer has spread to other organs such as the liver or lungs, requiring systemic and local therapies.

Colectomy
A colectomy is a major surgical procedure that removes the cancerous part of the colon along with nearby lymph nodes.<SEP>A surgical procedure involving the resection of all or part of the colon, after which residual microscopic disease may be evaluated.<SEP>A surgical procedure involving the resection of part or all of the colon, commonly used to treat non-metastatic colon cancer.<SEP>A surgical procedure to resect part or all of the colon, which carries potential side effects such as anastomotic leak, bowel obstruction, and hernia.

CEA Blood Test
A blood test measuring carcinoembryonic antigen levels, utilized to monitor colon cancer presence and recurrence.

Circulating Tumor DNA
A biomarker test category involving tumor-derived DNA fragments circulating in the blood.

Polyps
Growths in the colon lining, such as hyperplastic and inflammatory polyps, from which almost all colon cancers originate if left untreated.

Local Therapies
Targeted medical treatments directed specifically at localized secondary tumors in the liver and lungs in metastatic colon cancer.

Inherited Cancer Syndromes
Genetic disorders passed through families, such as Lynch syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis, which significantly heighten cancer risks.

Diagnostic Colonoscopy
A specialized follow-up colon examination performed to thoroughly check the colon and identify other potential areas of cancer.

Colorectal Cancer Survivor
An individual diagnosed with colorectal cancer at age 44 whose patient perspective emphasizes advocating for timely care, family history awareness, and self-care.

ctDNA Testing
Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) testing, also known as a liquid biopsy, is a category of diagnostic test that identifies tumor DNA fragments released into the bloodstream.

Carcinoembryonic Antigen Test
A tumor marker blood test (CEA) used in the baseline diagnostic and evaluative testing of colon cancer patients.

Pedunculated Polyps
A structural classification of colon polyps characterized by a mushroom-like stalk attaching them to the colon wall.

Sessile Polyps
A flat, broad-based classification of colon polyps that grow directly against the colon lining.

Non-Metastatic Cancer
A category of localized colon cancer that has not spread beyond the primary colon region to distant sites.

The American Joint Committee
The American Joint Committee is a medical organization referenced in the context of colon cancer staging guidelines and classification.

Colostomy
A colostomy is a surgical procedure that creates an abdominal stoma to divert the flow of stool when reconnecting the colon is unsafe.<SEP>A surgical procedure attaching the bowel to an opening on the abdomen, redirecting stool into an external pouch, often required after anal removal.<SEP>A surgical procedure connecting the colon to an external abdominal stoma to route stool into an ostomy bag, used if the rectum or anus is removed.<SEP>A surgical procedure that creates an opening in the abdominal wall for waste excretion, often required following an abdominoperineal resection.

Invasive Colon Cancer
Invasive colon cancer is a malignancy that grows through the colon wall layers and may spread to lymph nodes or other organs.

Bowel Blockage
A bowel blockage is an obstruction caused when a colon tumor grows large enough to impede the passage of stool and gas.

Anastomotic Leak
A surgical complication characterized by leakage at the anatomical site where the colon is reconnected after a colectomy.<SEP>An anastomotic leak is a complication of colon resection surgery where fluid leaks from the site where the colon was reconnected.

One-Stage Colectomy
A one-stage colectomy is a surgical intervention that removes the tumor and resolves a bowel blockage in a single operation.

Stent Placement
Stent placement is a procedure in which a mesh metal tube is inserted to open a blocked colon, permitting stool passage prior to cancer surgery.

Open Colectomy
An open colectomy is a surgical method for removing colon tumor tissue through a large abdominal incision.

Minimally Invasive Colectomy
A minimally invasive colectomy is a surgical method that uses several small abdominal incisions and specialized tools to excise cancerous colon tissue.

Stage 0 Colon Cancer
A stage of colon cancer characterized by abnormal cells located solely on the innermost layer of the colon wall, also known as carcinoma in situ.

Stage 1 Colon Cancer
A stage where colon cancer has grown into the second or third layer of the colon wall without spreading to lymph nodes or distant organs.

Stage 2 Colon Cancer
A stage where colon cancer has grown into or through the fourth layer of the colon wall without lymph node involvement or distant spread.

Stage 3 Colon Cancer
A stage where colon cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes or produced tumor deposits in fat around the colon.

Stage 4 Colon Cancer
An advanced stage where colon cancer has metastasized to distant organs outside the colon, such as the liver or lungs.

dMMR/MSI-H Cancers
A molecular subtype of colon cancer with deficient mismatch repair or high microsatellite instability that is responsive to immune checkpoint inhibitors.

pMMR/MSS Cancers
A molecular subtype of colon cancer characterized by proficient mismatch repair and microsatellite stability, typically managed with chemotherapy.

Checkpoint Inhibitors
A class of immunotherapy drugs that enhance the immune system's response to identify and eradicate cancer cells, particularly in dMMR/MSI-H colon cancers.<SEP>A subcategory of immunotherapy drugs that block inhibitory immune mechanisms to empower the immune system to fight cancer.

Pembrolizumab (Keytruda)
An immune checkpoint inhibitor drug recommended for use before colectomy in patients with dMMR/MSI-H colon cancer.

Nivolumab (Opdivo)
An immune checkpoint inhibitor medication utilized before surgery for dMMR/MSI-H colon cancer, administered with or without ipilimumab.

Ipilimumab (Yervoy)
An immunotherapy checkpoint inhibitor drug used in combination with nivolumab for treating dMMR/MSI-H colon cancer prior to surgery.

FOLFOX
A combination chemotherapy regimen consisting of 5-FU, leucovorin, and oxaliplatin recommended as a first-line treatment option for metastatic anal cancer.<SEP>A multi-drug chemotherapy regimen administered over six months, recommended for high-risk stage 2 and all stage 3 colon cancers.

CAPEOX
A chemotherapy regimen administered over three months, recommended as an adjuvant treatment option for high-risk stage 2 and stage 3 colon cancers.

Capecitabine
An oral chemotherapy medication prescribed as a single agent or part of combination regimens for treating stage 2 and stage 3 colon cancers.<SEP>An oral chemotherapy medicine taken twice daily on radiation days, which can cause adverse effects like hand-foot syndrome.<SEP>An oral chemotherapy medicine used in combination with mitomycin and radiation to treat anal cancer.

5-Fluorouracil (5-FU)
A chemotherapy drug often given with leucovorin as an adjuvant treatment regimen for stage 2 and stage 3 colon cancers.

North Africa
A geographic region identified as having an elevated incidence of nasopharyngeal carcinoma.<SEP>A geographical region in Africa where nasopharyngeal cancer is noted to commonly occur.

Native America
A geographic and demographic designation noted for a higher occurrence of nasopharyngeal cancer.<SEP>A region/population group identified with higher occurrences of nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
A rare type of head and neck cancer that begins in the nasopharynx, frequently presenting as squamous cell carcinoma.<SEP>A type of cancer affecting the nasopharynx, which connects the nasal cavity to the back of the mouth, categorized under head and neck cancers.<SEP>Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (NPC) is a type of cancer that originates in the nasopharynx, often evaluated and categorized using the TNM staging system.<SEP>Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a type of cancer arising in the nasopharynx that is staged based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, and distant spread.

Surveillance Follow-Up Testing
A post-treatment monitoring regimen consisting of periodic physical exams, imaging, and lab tests to detect cancer recurrence early.

Cancer Survivors
Individuals who have completed cancer treatment and require ongoing survivorship care and monitoring.

Comprehensive Cancer Center
A specialized medical facility staffed by experts in evaluating and treating nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

Nasopharyngeal Fiberoptic Exam
An endoscopic procedure using a lighted fiberoptic scope to directly inspect the nasopharynx and oropharynx for tumors.

MRI With Contrast
A magnetic resonance imaging scan from collarbone to skull base performed to evaluate tumor extent in nasopharyngeal cancer.

Distant Metastases
The spread of cancer cells from the primary nasopharyngeal site to distant organs such as the chest or other body areas.

Mind and Body Therapist
A supportive care provider on the treatment team who assists cancer patients with managing emotional distress, anxiety, and depression.

Nutritionist
A healthcare specialist who provides targeted dietary and nutritional counseling suited to a patient's medical condition.<SEP>A nutritional professional or dietician who consults with cancer patients to formulate optimal dietary and hydration plans prior to therapy.

Speech and Swallowing Therapist
A specialized therapist who evaluates and monitors a patient's capacity to speak and swallow before and after cancer treatment.

Birth Control
Contraceptive options, including barrier methods and intrauterine devices (IUDs), advised during and after cancer treatment to prevent pregnancy.

Biopsy of Metastasis
A targeted biopsy procedure performed on suspected areas of cancer spread, such as lymph nodes or the lung, to confirm metastasis.

Cannabis
A psychoactive substance whose consumption may alter the required dosage of anesthesia during surgical procedures.

EBV-Related Cancer
EBV-related cancer is a disease classification caused by the Epstein-Barr virus, which accounts for the majority of nasopharyngeal cancers.

TMB-H
Tumor mutational burden-high is a genomic biomarker classification defined by 10 or more mutations per million base pairs of tumor DNA.

HPV-Related Cancer
A category of malignant neoplasms caused by human papillomavirus infection, which includes most throat cancers.

Tumor HPV Testing
A diagnostic procedure performed on tumor tissue to detect human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, commonly used in throat and certain nasopharyngeal cancers.

TNM Scores
A cancer staging metric that scores primary tumor size and extent, regional lymph node involvement, and distant metastasis.

Infectious Mononucleosis
A common viral disease caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), which is also linked to EBV-related cancers.

data.entity_name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma Of The Nasopharynx
data.content:
Squamous Cell Carcinoma Of The Nasopharynx
A specific histological subtype of nasopharyngeal carcinoma evaluated using standard TNM staging criteria.

Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia
Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) refers to abnormal cervical cellular changes or dysplasia categorized into grades 1, 2, or 3, which can progress to invasive cancer if untreated.

Low-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion
A form of mild anal dysplasia (LSIL) representing abnormal cell growth that may precede anal cancer.<SEP>Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) is a classification of mild cervical dysplasia corresponding to CIN 1.

High-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion
High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) is a clinical classification representing moderate to severe cervical dysplasia (CIN 2 and 3) considered a pre-cancerous condition.<SEP>Moderate to severe anal dysplasia (HSIL) featuring abnormal cellular changes with higher risk of malignant progression.

Head and Neck Tumors
Head and neck tumors are a broad category of neoplasms measured in centimeters, of which nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a specific type.

data.entity_name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Nasopharynx
data.content:
Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Nasopharynx
Squamous cell carcinoma of the nasopharynx is a specific histologic subtype of nasopharyngeal cancer evaluated by TNM staging.

Sexually Transmitted Infection
Infections transmitted through sexual contact; a history of STIs serves as a risk factor for anal cancer.<SEP>Sexually transmitted infections are communicable diseases spread through sexual activity, with HPV being the most prevalent.

Pap Smear
The Pap smear is a preventive diagnostic screening test that detects cervical changes, substantially reducing cervical cancer incidence.

Uterine Sarcomas
Uterine sarcomas are rare malignancies forming in the muscle or supportive tissues of the uterus, treated differently from cervical cancer.

Cervical Dysplasia
Cervical dysplasia refers to the presence of abnormal cells on the cervical lining, categorized into mild, moderate, or severe cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN).<SEP>Cervical dysplasia represents premalignant cellular abnormalities on the surface of the cervix, categorized into grades 1, 2, or 3.

Childbirth
Childbirth is the physiological event during which the cervix dilates and effaces to allow a baby to move from the uterus through the vagina.

Menstruation
Menstruation is the periodic physiological shedding of uterine tissue and blood that passes through the external os of the cervix into the vagina.

Human Papillomavirus (HPV)
Human papillomavirus is a common sexually transmitted virus with over 100 strains, responsible for causing almost all cervical cancers as well as several other malignancies and genital warts.

High-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (HSIL)
High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion refers to moderate or severe dysplasia (CIN 2 and 3) on the cervix and is considered a pre-cancerous condition.

Low-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (LSIL)
Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion denotes mild cervical dysplasia (CIN 1) characterized by abnormal surface cells.

Neuroendocrine Carcinoma of the Cervix (NECC)
Neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix is the rarest and most aggressive histological subtype of cervical cancer.

HPV Vaccine
A preventive vaccine covering nine strains of HPV, recommended for individuals up to age 45 to protect against new infections and HPV-related cancers.<SEP>The HPV vaccine is an immunization that protects against multiple strains of human papillomavirus, preventing new infections and HPV-associated cancers.

Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)
Human immunodeficiency virus is a pathogen that causes immune system deficiency, increasing vulnerability to persistent HPV infection and cervical cancer.

HPV-16
HPV-16 is one of the highest-risk strains of human papillomavirus linked to the development of cervical cancer and other malignancies.

HPV-18
HPV-18 is a high-risk strain of human papillomavirus known to cause cervical cancer and is targeted by specific HPV vaccines.

Sexually Transmitted Infection (STI)
A broad class of infections passed through sexual contact, of which HPV is noted as an extremely common example.

Anal Cancer
