A form of malignancy located in the anus that is caused by long-term infection with human papillomavirus.<SEP>A malignancy developing in the tissues of the anus, frequently linked to HPV infection and characterized by symptoms such as rectal bleeding, itching, and pain.<SEP>A malignancy of the anal canal, commonly treated with concurrent chemotherapy regimens and radiation therapy.<SEP>A malignancy of the anus discussed in the text, requiring diagnostic testing, staging, and individualized treatment planning.<SEP>A malignancy originating in either the anal canal or the perianal region, most commonly manifesting as squamous cell carcinoma.<SEP>A type of cancer occurring in the anus and anal canal, predominantly caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) infection.<SEP>An uncommon cancer of the digestive system that most frequently originates in the squamous cells of the anal canal or perianal region.<SEP>Anal cancer is a malignancy affecting the anal canal, whose treatments can lead to bowel changes, sexual side effects, and pelvic health complications.<SEP>Anal cancer is a malignancy arising in the anal canal or perianal region, staged from stage 0 (precancer) to stage IV based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, and distant metastasis.<SEP>Anal cancer is a rare type of malignancy affecting the anal canal or perianal area, requiring specialized treatment regimens and follow-up care.<SEP>Anal cancer is a type of cancer arising in the tissues of the anus, forming the central subject of the patient inquiry guide.

Penile Cancer
A malignancy affecting the male genital organs associated with human papillomavirus infection.<SEP>A rare malignancy affecting the penis, identified as one of the cancer types caused by human papillomavirus.<SEP>A type of malignancy occurring on the penis that can be caused by infection with HPV strains.

Vaginal Cancer
A form of gynecologic cancer occurring in the vagina, listed among malignancies associated with HPV.<SEP>A gynecological cancer of the vaginal canal etiologically linked to human papillomavirus infection.<SEP>A malignancy linked to HPV infection; a personal history of vaginal cancer elevates the risk of anal cancer.

Vulvar Cancer
A gynecologic cancer developing on the external female genitalia, induced by persistent HPV infection.<SEP>A gynecological cancer affecting the external female genitalia that can be caused by human papillomavirus infection.<SEP>An HPV-associated cancer of the external female genitalia; a prior history increases the risk of anal cancer.

Genital Warts
Abnormal benign skin growths that form on the anus or genitals as a result of HPV infection.<SEP>Abnormal skin growths that develop on the anus, genitals, or other areas of the body as a result of infection with certain HPV types.

Cervical Biopsy
A diagnostic medical procedure that involves removing tissue samples from the ectocervix or endocervical canal to diagnose cervical cancer and pre-cancer.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure wherein tissue samples are removed from the cervix to test for dysplasia and cervical cancer.<SEP>A medical procedure that involves removing small samples of tissue from the cervix to diagnose cervical cancer.

Glassy-Cell Carcinoma
A distinct and uncommon histological subtype of cervical cancer noted in diagnostic considerations.

Transformation Zone
The specific anatomical area on the cervix where the ectocervix meets the endocervix, where most pre-cancers and cervical cancers originate.

HIV Specialist
A healthcare professional specializing in managing human immunodeficiency virus, to whom HIV-positive cancer patients may be referred.

Cone Biopsy
A diagnostic and therapeutic surgical procedure that removes a cone-shaped section of tissue from the cervix to treat or assess early-stage cancer.<SEP>A surgical diagnostic procedure used to excise a cone-shaped wedge of cervical tissue to assess tumor margins and confirm stage 1A cancer.<SEP>A surgical procedure used for diagnosing and excising early-stage cervical cancer tissue, preserving the uterus.<SEP>Also known as cervical conization, a surgical procedure that removes a cone-shaped section of the cervix including the transformation zone for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.

Cold Knife Conization
A surgical technique for cone biopsy that utilizes a scalpel to excise cervical tissue.

Loop Electrosurgical Excision Procedure
A cone biopsy technique that uses a thin loop of heated, electrified wire to remove cervical tissue.

Endocervical Curettage
A procedure using a curette to scrape a tissue sample from the cervical canal following a cone biopsy.

Pelvic Examination
A physical examination to evaluate the size, position, and appearance of the cervix and uterus.

Technician
A medical staff member who operates the imaging equipment and communicates with the patient during a CT scan.

HIV Test
A laboratory test recommended to check for human immunodeficiency virus infection before proceeding with cancer care.

Pre-Cancer
Abnormal cell changes identified by a pathologist in cervical tissue that have not yet progressed into invasive malignancy.

Early-Stage Cervical Cancer
A localized phase of cervical cancer for which cone biopsy may serve as an effective definitive treatment.<SEP>A stage category of cervical cancer (such as stages 1A and small 1B) typically managed with surgical interventions like hysterectomy or cone biopsy.

Symptoms Of Cervical Cancer
Clinical indicators such as watery vaginal discharge that prompt medical investigation and history taking.

data.entity_name: Small Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma of the Cervix
data.content:
Small Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma of the Cervix
A rare, specific type of cervical cancer that follows dedicated surveillance protocols post-treatment.<SEP>A specific subtype of cervical cancer (NECC) for which an MRI of the brain is recommended as part of initial testing.

Fertility-Sparing Treatment
A category of treatment strategies designed to preserve reproductive potential, typically indicated for small, early-stage cancers.<SEP>A therapeutic approach designed to preserve reproductive potential in patients with early-stage cervical cancer limited to the cervix.<SEP>A treatment approach for stage 1 cervical cancers that preserves the uterus and ovaries to allow for natural pregnancy.<SEP>A treatment classification designed to preserve reproductive capability, such as trachelectomy for early-stage cervical cancer.<SEP>Conservative oncologic treatment that preserves reproductive organs, necessitating specialized MRI surveillance post-surgery.

Reproductive Endocrinologist
A doctor specializing in fertility preservation procedures such as ovarian transposition, egg freezing, and surrogacy.<SEP>A medical doctor who specializes in fertility and provides expert consultation when fertility-sparing treatments are considered.

Surrogate
A gestational carrier who volunteers to have embryos transferred into their uterus to carry a pregnancy to term.

Examination Under Anesthesia
Diagnostic evaluation procedures (EUAs) performed under general anesthesia to inspect surrounding organs for cancer involvement.

Cystoscopy
A diagnostic procedure using a lighted lens to inspect the bladder and urinary tract under anesthesia.<SEP>A diagnostic procedure using a viewing instrument inserted through the urethra to inspect the bladder lining for cancer.<SEP>An endoscopic diagnostic procedure used to examine the interior of the bladder.<SEP>An endoscopic examination of the bladder under anesthesia to assess potential local cancer invasion.<SEP>An examination procedure using a cystoscope to inspect the inside of the urethra and bladder for signs of cancer and obtain tissue biopsies.<SEP>Cystoscopy is an endoscopic procedure using a lighted tube with a camera to examine the urethra and bladder for signs of cancer and to obtain biopsies.

Embryo Freezing
A fertility preservation procedure where fertilized embryos are frozen and stored for future use in assisted reproduction.

X-Ray
A conventional medical diagnostic imaging test that utilizes radiation, contrasted with non-radiation techniques like MRI.<SEP>A foundational radiation-based imaging modality whose multi-angle pictures are compiled to generate CT scans.<SEP>An x-ray is a diagnostic radiography procedure that uses low doses of radiation to produce images of internal body structures.

Stage 1 Cervical Cancer
A stage where cancer is confined strictly to the cervix, ranging from microscopic lesions (1A) up to larger tumors (1B).<SEP>Early-stage cervical cancer where imaging such as FDG-PET/CT or pelvic MRI is utilized depending on whether fertility-sparing or non-fertility-sparing treatment was performed.

Stage 2 Cervical Cancer
A stage where cervical cancer has extended beyond the cervix into the upper vagina or the surrounding parametrium.

Stage 3 Cervical Cancer
A stage where cervical cancer has reached the lower third of the vagina, pelvic wall, or regional lymph nodes.

Stage 4 Cervical Cancer
An advanced stage where cervical cancer has invaded nearby organs like the bladder or rectum, or metastasized to distant organs.

Stage 1A Cervical Cancer
A subcategory of cervical cancer where the tumor is 5 millimeters or smaller and confined to the cervix.

Stage 1B Cervical Cancer
A subcategory of stage 1 cervical cancer divided into sub-stages 1B1, 1B2, and 1B3 based on tumor sizes extending beyond 5 mm.

Stage 2A Cervical Cancer
A subcategory of stage 2 cervical cancer where the tumor has grown into the upper vagina, divided into 2A1 and 2A2 based on size.

Stage 2B Cervical Cancer
A subcategory of stage 2 cervical cancer where the cancer has grown into the parametrium surrounding the cervix and uterus.

Stage 3A Cervical Cancer
A subcategory of stage 3 cervical cancer where the tumor has grown into the lower third of the vagina.

Stage 3B Cervical Cancer
A subcategory of stage 3 cervical cancer where tumor growth reaches the pelvic wall or causes kidney swelling or dysfunction.

Stage 3C Cervical Cancer
A subcategory of stage 3 cervical cancer involving spread to pelvic lymph nodes or abdominal para-aortic lymph nodes.

Stage 4A Cervical Cancer
An advanced stage subcategory characterized by direct cancer spread to adjacent organs such as the bladder or rectum.

Stage 4B Cervical Cancer
A metastatic stage subcategory where cancer has spread to distant organs such as the liver, lungs, abdomen, or bone.<SEP>Metastatic cervical cancer characterized by distant spread or recurrence, where imaging monitors response to systemic therapy.

Cancer Care Plan
A tailored clinical document outlining treatment options, team members, side effects, and goals for cancer therapy.

Trachelectomy
A fertility-sparing surgical procedure that removes the cervix and upper part of the vagina while preserving the uterus.<SEP>A fertility-sparing surgical procedure to remove the cervix while leaving the uterus and ovaries intact, allowing potential future natural pregnancy.

Hysterectomy
A surgical operation removing the uterus, standardly recommended for early-stage cervical cancer when fertility preservation is not needed.<SEP>A surgical procedure that removes the uterus and cervix, along with portions of vaginal or cervical connective tissue, and potentially the ovaries causing surgical menopause.<SEP>A surgical procedure to remove the uterus and cervix, categorized into simple (extrafascial), modified radical, and radical types based on the extent of tissue removed.<SEP>Surgical removal of the uterus, which may be avoided if cervical cancer has spread beyond the cervix.

Dysplasia
Abnormal cell growth and precancerous cellular changes detected in cervical tissue during biopsy.

Minimally Invasive Surgery
Laparoscopic surgical techniques utilizing small incisions to reduce tissue trauma, post-operative pain, and recovery duration.

Extrafascial Hysterectomy
A simple hysterectomy procedure recommended for stage 1A1 cancer patients who do not seek fertility preservation.<SEP>A simple hysterectomy procedure that removes only the uterus and cervix, commonly indicated for stage IA1 cervical cancer.<SEP>A simple surgical procedure involving the removal of the uterus and cervix, recommended for low-risk stage 1A and 1B1 cervical cancers meeting specific criteria.

Modified Radical Hysterectomy
A surgical procedure that removes the uterus, cervix, adjacent parametrial connective tissue, and a small upper portion of the vagina via an abdominal incision.<SEP>A surgical procedure that removes the uterus, cervix, and adjacent tissue, recommended for stage 1A1 cancers with LVSI or when pre-cancer is found at cone margins.

Radical Hysterectomy
A surgical treatment option involving removal of reproductive organs, typically considered for carefully selected patients with local or regional cancer recurrence.<SEP>An extensive abdominal surgical procedure that removes the uterus, cervix, substantial surrounding parametrial tissue, and the upper quarter to third of the vagina.<SEP>An extensive surgical operation removing the uterus, cervix, parametrium, and upper vagina, used for stages 1B1 to 2A1 and higher-risk early-stage cases.

Ovary Preservation
A clinical surgical strategy to retain the ovaries during hysterectomy to prevent premature surgical menopause and hormonal loss.

Diagnostic Imaging
A class of medical diagnostic techniques used to produce detailed pictures of internal body structures to detect tumors and metastasis.<SEP>Radiological modalities including CT, MRI, PET, and transvaginal ultrasound used to evaluate the anatomical extent and staging of cancer.

Locally Advanced Cervical Cancer
A clinical classification of cervical cancer that has grown beyond the cervix or is larger than 4 cm (such as stages 1B3 to 4A) without distant metastasis.<SEP>A stage of cervical cancer where the tumor has grown beyond the cervix but has not spread to distant sites like the liver, lungs, or bones.<SEP>Cervical cancer that has spread beyond the cervix into surrounding tissues or nodes but has not metastasized to distant organs.

Metastatic Cervical Cancer
A classification of advanced cervical cancer that has spread to distant organs such as the liver, lungs, or bone, whether diagnosed initially or after treatment.<SEP>A stage of cervical cancer that has spread to distant sites such as liver, lungs, or bone, commonly managed with systemic therapies and supportive care.<SEP>Advanced cervical cancer that has spread to distant organs and tissues such as the liver, lungs, or bone.

Laparoscopic Surgical Staging
A minimally invasive surgical procedure used to access, remove, and evaluate pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes prior to treatment to guide therapy for advanced cancer.

Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy
An advanced conformal external beam radiation therapy technique using multiple beams of varying intensities to spare healthy tissues.<SEP>An advanced external radiation therapy technique that uses multiple beams of varying intensities, recommended for anal cancer.<SEP>An advanced radiation technique (IMRT) identified as the preferred method of radiation delivery for anal cancer.<SEP>An advanced technique of external beam radiation therapy that utilizes multiple beams of varying intensities to spare healthy organs while treating the tumor.<SEP>Intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) is an advanced high-precision radiation technique used to deliver targeted radiation doses to tumors while sparing healthy surrounding tissues.

Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy
A specialized form of external beam radiation therapy delivering high doses of highly focused radiation to metastatic tumors in five or fewer sessions.<SEP>A specialized, targeted form of external beam radiation therapy (SBRT) delivered over few sessions to treat tumors in organs like the liver, lungs, or bone.<SEP>A specialized, targeted form of radiation therapy (SBRT

Simulation
A clinical planning session involving scans and precise patient positioning conducted prior to external beam radiation therapy.<SEP>A preparation and planning session before radiation therapy where CT scans and positioning devices are used to establish precise treatment coordinates and doses.<SEP>A specialized planning session prior to radiation therapy where patient positioning, CT scans, and dose calculations are conducted.

Menopausal Hormone Therapy
Hormone treatment, historically called hormone replacement therapy (HRT), used to mitigate the symptoms and long-term effects of radiation-induced menopause.

Pelvic Lymph Nodes
Lymph nodes situated in the pelvis closest to the cervix, representing the initial site where cervical cancer typically spreads.

Para-Aortic Lymph Nodes
Lymph nodes located in the abdomen that can be involved in the spread of cervical cancer and are sometimes surgically excised for staging.

Premature Menopause
Early cessation of ovarian function and menopausal onset triggered by surgical removal or radiation exposure of the ovaries.

Intracavitary Brachytherapy
A common brachytherapy technique for cervical cancer where instruments holding radioactive material are inserted into the cervix, uterus, and vagina.

Interstitial Brachytherapy
A specialized brachytherapy technique where catheters are placed directly into the tumor or neighboring tissues, used for more advanced cancers involving the parametrium.

High Dose-Rate Brachytherapy
A form of brachytherapy (HDR) that delivers radiation in short bursts, commonly administered via specialized applicators over three to five sessions.

Recurrent Or Metastatic Cervical Cancer
A classification of cervical cancer that either returns after initial therapy or has spread to distant regions, often managed with systemic treatments.

Low Dose-Rate Brachytherapy
A form of brachytherapy (LDR) that delivers radiation continuously in long bursts over an extended period.

Tandem And Ring Applicator
A medical device applicator used for HDR brachytherapy consisting of a tandem tube inserted into the uterus and a ring placed in the vagina against the cervix.

Tandem And Ovoid Applicator
A specialized brachytherapy applicator apparatus featuring a tandem combined with hollow, rounded capsules inserted into the vaginal vault.

Early-Stage Cancer
A cancer stage classification typically managed with surgical interventions such as hysterectomy or trachelectomy.<SEP>Cervical cancers that are limited to the cervix (stage 1) or have spread to the upper vagina (stage 2A), typically treated with surgery or radiation.

Phase 1 Trial
An initial clinical trial phase studying the dosage, safety, side effects, and early signs of efficacy of an investigational drug or treatment.

Phase 2 Trial
A clinical research trial phase evaluating how effectively an investigational treatment works against a specific type of cancer.

Phase 3 Trial
A clinical trial phase testing an investigational drug or approach directly against standard treatment to achieve regulatory approval.

Phase 4 Trial
A post-marketing clinical trial studying the long-term safety and benefits of an FDA-approved cancer treatment.

Stage 1A1
An early microinvasive stage of cervical cancer categorized by microscopic stromal invasion, often treated based on the presence of LVSI.<SEP>An early substage of cervical cancer diagnosed typically by cone biopsy, manageable with fertility-sparing or non-fertility-sparing approaches.

Stage 1A2
A stage of cervical cancer characterized by slight depth of stromal invasion, managed through extrafascial or radical hysterectomy depending on risk factors.<SEP>A substage of cervical cancer evaluated with pelvic lymph node assessment and treated via cone biopsy or radical trachelectomy.

Stage 1B1
A substage of cervical cancer where tumor size dictates whether cone biopsy or radical trachelectomy with lymph node evaluation is recommended.<SEP>An early-stage invasive cervical cancer tumor measuring 2 cm or smaller, qualifying for extrafascial hysterectomy under strict low-risk criteria or radical hysterectomy.

Stage 1B2
A stage of cervical cancer measuring between 2 cm and 4 cm, typically managed with radical hysterectomy and pelvic lymph node evaluation.<SEP>An early substage of cervical cancer for which fertility-sparing surgery is uncommon due to larger tumor size.

Radical Trachelectomy
A surgical procedure to remove the cervix while leaving the uterus intact, offered as a fertility-sparing treatment in early-stage cervical cancer.

Lymphovascular Space Invasion
A pathological risk factor indicating tumor cells within blood vessels or lymph vessels, which increases the likelihood of spread to nearby lymph nodes.

Pelvic Lymph Node Evaluation
A diagnostic and surgical assessment performed to detect cancer spread to lymph nodes located in the pelvis.

Vaginal Brachytherapy
An internal radiation therapy modality administered locally into the vagina, sometimes alongside EBRT and chemotherapy.

Stage 1
A non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer stage where cancer has grown through the inner lining into the connective tissue layer.<SEP>An early stage of cervical cancer where the tumor has not spread beyond the cervix.

Stage 2A
A stage of cervical cancer indicating that the malignancy has spread to the upper vagina.

Pelvic Lymph Node Dissection
A surgical procedure to evaluate and remove lymph nodes within the pelvic basin to assess disease spread and determine staging.

Stage 1B3
A cervical cancer stage where the tumor is larger than 4 cm without extension beyond the cervix, treated as locally advanced with chemoradiation or surgery.

Stage 2A1
A cervical cancer stage involving the upper vagina measuring 4 cm or less, commonly treated with radical hysterectomy and lymph node evaluation.

Stage 2A2
A cervical cancer stage measuring larger than 4 cm that extends into the upper vagina, preferably treated with chemoradiation.

Stage 2B
A locally advanced cervical cancer stage defined by parametrial invasion, treated primarily with definitive chemoradiation and brachytherapy.

Stage 3
A locally advanced cervical cancer stage involving the lower vagina, pelvic wall, or causing hydronephrosis/kidney dysfunction, managed with chemoradiation.<SEP>A stage of bladder cancer that has grown through the wall into the surrounding fatty layer and potentially into nearby pelvic lymph nodes or organs.

Stage 4A
A locally advanced stage of cervical cancer where the tumor has invaded adjacent pelvic organs such as the bladder or rectum without distant metastasis.<SEP>A subgroup of Stage 4 bladder cancer characterized by invasion into the pelvis or abdominal wall, or spread to distant lymph nodes.

LVSI
Lymphovascular space invasion, a critical pathological risk factor whose presence dictates more extensive surgery or adjuvant chemoradiation.

data.entity_name: Small Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma Of The Cervix
data.content:
Small Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma Of The Cervix
A rare and aggressive type of cervical cancer subject to post-treatment surveillance and care protocols.

Physical Exams
Routine medical checkups conducted by oncologists to monitor for signs and symptoms of cancer recurrence post-treatment.

Pap Tests
Cervical or vaginal cytology screening tests performed annually after treatment to detect abnormal and precancerous cells.

Pelvic Recurrence
Local or regional return of cervical cancer within the pelvis following initial treatment.

Stages 2, 3, And 4A Cervical Cancer
Locally advanced stages of cervical cancer for which FDG-PET/CT or CT with contrast and pelvic MRI are recommended 3 to 6 months post-treatment.

CT With Contrast
Computed tomography scan using contrast dye, recommended as an imaging option for surveillance in advanced stages.

EBRT
External beam radiation therapy recommended after surgical resection in cases of local pelvic recurrence that have not been previously irradiated.

Exploratory Surgery
Surgical investigation to assess the full extent and spread of suspected recurrent cancer within the body.

Pelvic Exenteration
A radical surgical procedure involving the removal of multiple organs from the pelvis, including reproductive and potentially urinary or bowel organs, to treat recurrent pelvic cancer.<SEP>An extensive surgical procedure considered for local pelvic recurrence when prior radiation therapy precludes further radiation.

RET Gene Fusion
A rare genomic biomarker examined in cervical cancer to determine treatment pathways.

Cervical Sarcoma
A rare malignancy of the cervix specifically evaluated for NTRK gene fusions.

Cancer Survivor
An individual who has completed cancer treatment and participates in ongoing surveillance and survivorship care.

Stage 4B
A diagnostic cancer stage category designating cervical cancer that had already metastasized to distant organs at initial diagnosis.<SEP>A subgroup of Stage 4 representing metastatic bladder cancer that has spread to distant lymph nodes and distant organs such as bones, liver, or lungs.

Urinary Diversion
A category of surgical procedures, such as an ileal conduit or continent diversion (Indiana pouch), that redirect urine after the bladder is surgically removed.<SEP>A surgical procedure included with radical cystectomy designed to establish a new pathway for urine to leave the body.<SEP>Urinary diversion is a reconstructive surgical procedure performed alongside cystectomy to establish a new pathway for urine to exit the body.<SEP>Urinary diversion refers to surgical procedures that redirect the normal flow of urine out of the body, such as creating an Indiana pouch.

Double-Barreled Wet Colostomy
A surgical diversion procedure (DBWC) where both urine and stool exit through a single stoma when both the bladder and bowel are removed.

Ablative Therapies
A category of localized treatments using needles, probes, or electrodes to destroy cancerous tumors with minimal harm to adjacent normal tissues.

Local Or Regional Recurrence
A clinical condition where cancer returns in the same area or pelvic region after previous treatment.

Distant Recurrence
A clinical condition where cancer returns and metastasizes to distant organs after initial treatment.

Vaginal Reconstruction
A surgical procedure often performed after pelvic exenteration to create a neovagina, commonly using a muscle flap such as the rectus abdominis.

Ileal Conduit
An ileal conduit is a form of urinary diversion where a section of small intestine directs urine out through an abdominal stoma into an external ostomy bag.<SEP>An incontinent urinary diversion technique that uses a piece of the ileum to route urine from the kidneys to an external abdominal stoma and ostomy pouch.

Continent Urinary Diversion
A urinary diversion method, also called an artificial bladder or Indiana pouch, creating an internal intestinal reservoir catheterized through an abdominal stoma.

Immunotherapies
Cancer treatment modalities that stimulate or mobilize the body's immune system to attack cancer cells, guided by biomarker testing.

Resection
A surgical procedure aimed at removing part or all of a tumor, compared directly to an open biopsy in operative method.<SEP>A surgical procedure performed by a neurosurgeon to remove as much of a tumor as safely possible, serving as both treatment and diagnostic biopsy.<SEP>Surgical removal of new cancer growths, applicable in localized recurrence or selective metastatic settings.

Mediastinal Gray Zone Lymphoma
A rare lymphoma subtype (MGZL) characterized by overlapping features of primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma and Hodgkin lymphoma, usually presenting as a mediastinal mass.<SEP>Mediastinal gray zone lymphoma (MGZL) is a rare lymphoma showing features of both classical Hodgkin lymphoma and primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma, lacking a standard care consensus.

Primary Mediastinal B-Cell Lymphoma
A subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (PMBL) arising in the mediastinum, sharing morphological and clinical characteristics with mediastinal gray zone lymphoma.

Non-Mediastinal Gray Zone Lymphoma
A category of gray zone lymphoma presenting outside the mediastinum, typically in older patients with higher rates of extranodal and bone marrow involvement.

DLBCL-NOS
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (DLBCL-NOS) is a diagnostic category applied to lymphoma cases with extra-mediastinal presentation.<SEP>Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified; a lymphoma classification assigned to patients with gray zone disease features occurring outside the mediastinum.

Cancer Centers
Specialized medical and research facilities where clinical oncology practices, guidelines, and advanced biomarker evaluations are conducted.<SEP>Specialized medical facilities and hospitals that provide comprehensive cancer treatment, second opinions, and integrative oncology programs.<SEP>Specialized medical facilities and institutions equipped with experienced teams to manage and treat rare malignancies such as gray zone lymphomas.

Advance Care Planning
A structured process of communication and decision-making regarding future medical decisions and end-of-life care for patients with advanced disease.

Palliative Care
Specialized supportive medical care focusing on relief from symptoms, pain, and stress for individuals living with advanced or metastatic cancers.

Hospice Care
A model of compassionate, comfort-oriented end-of-life care provided as a component of supportive care when curative interventions are not viable.

First-Line Therapy
The initial systemic therapy regimen chosen to treat metastatic cancer, often selected based on specific biomarker profiles.

Second-Line Therapy
Subsequent systemic treatment options administered when first-line therapies fail or platinum-based chemotherapy cannot be tolerated.

Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma
A subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma (CHL) that shares pathological and clinical overlapping features with mediastinal gray zone lymphoma.<SEP>Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (CHL) is a subtype of lymphoma whose clinical and pathological features overlap with mediastinal gray zone lymphoma.

Hematopathologist
A medical specialist trained in diagnosing diseases of the blood and lymphoid tissues whose expert review is required to confirm gray zone lymphoma.<SEP>A medical specialist who evaluates blood smears, lymph nodes, and bone marrow samples under a microscope to detect signs of disease.<SEP>A medical specialist who is an expert at diagnosing cancers of blood and immune cells by examining blood, bone marrow, and lymph node samples.

Thyroid Cancer
A cancer of the thyroid gland, which in metastatic forms may be managed via monitoring, levothyroxine, targeted therapy, or clinical trials.<SEP>A category of cancer affecting the thyroid gland, treated via surgery, RAI therapy, targeted therapies, or radiation depending on its progression.<SEP>A malignancy originating in the thyroid gland that requires tailored surgical, diagnostic, and systemic treatment strategies.<SEP>Thyroid cancer is a malignancy of the thyroid gland, frequently diagnosed in young adults aged 18 to 33, with risks associated with radiation exposure and inherited syndromes.

Cowden Syndrome
Cowden syndrome, also called PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome (PHTS), is an inherited condition that increases the risk of follicular thyroid cancer and other malignancies.

Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia
Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) is a group of hereditary syndromes associated with an increased susceptibility to thyroid cancer.

Non-Hodgkin PMBL
Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma (PMBL) is a subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma that shares clinical and pathological features with mediastinal gray zone lymphoma.

Follicular Thyroid Cancer
A differentiated thyroid cancer subtype eligible for radioactive iodine therapy when distant metastases absorb iodine.<SEP>Follicular thyroid cancer is a distinct histologic subtype of thyroid cancer that can be caused by inherited genetic conditions such as Cowden syndrome.

Thyroid Nodules
Thyroid nodules are abnormal growths of tissue within the thyroid gland that are mostly benign but can occasionally be cancerous.

Hyperthyroidism
An endocrine disorder marked by an overactive thyroid and abnormally low TSH levels, often linked to hormone-producing nodules.<SEP>Hyperthyroidism, or an overactive thyroid, is a clinical condition characterized by high thyroid hormone levels and suppressed or low thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels.

Adolescent And Young Adult Cancer
Adolescent and young adult cancer refers to malignancies occurring in individuals aged 18 to 33, a demographic group where thyroid cancer is the most prevalent malignancy.

Chemoimmunotherapy
Chemoimmunotherapy is a cancer treatment modality combining standard chemotherapy with immunotherapy drugs, such as rituximab, used to treat mediastinal gray zone lymphoma.<SEP>Chemoimmunotherapy is an oncologic treatment approach combining chemotherapy and immunotherapy targeting specific biomarkers in CLL.

Involved-Site Radiation Therapy
Involved-site radiation therapy (ISRT) is a targeted radiation treatment method used for patients with localized mediastinal gray zone lymphoma.

TSH Test
A diagnostic blood test measuring thyroid-stimulating hormone levels to assess thyroid gland function and evaluate nodule activity.<SEP>The thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) test is a blood diagnostic test used to evaluate nodule hormone production and guide thyroid cancer evaluation.

Radioactive Iodine Uptake Test
A diagnostic evaluation ordered by a provider to assess thyroid nodule function and thyroid hormone production.<SEP>The radioactive iodine (RAI) uptake test is a diagnostic imaging assessment used to evaluate thyroid gland and nodule function.

Radiation Exposure
Radiation exposure, including therapeutic neck irradiation or environmental contamination, is a major established risk factor for developing thyroid cancer.

Catastrophic Event
A catastrophic event involving environmental radiation release represents a significant source of exposure that elevates thyroid cancer risk.

Papillary Carcinoma
The most common classification and type of thyroid cancer, categorized as a differentiated thyroid cancer.

Follicular Carcinoma
The second most common type of thyroid cancer, classified as one of the differentiated thyroid cancers.

Oncocytic Carcinoma
A specific classification of thyroid cancer grouped under differentiated thyroid cancers.<SEP>Oncocytic carcinoma, formerly known as Hürthle cell carcinoma (HCC), is an uncommon thyroid cancer more prone to spreading to lymph nodes and invading blood vessels.

Differentiated Thyroid Cancers
A broader category of slow-growing thyroid malignancies that includes papillary, follicular, and oncocytic carcinomas.<SEP>A group of thyroid cancers including papillary, follicular, and oncocytic carcinoma that generally grow slowly and have favorable treatment outcomes.

Medullary Thyroid Cancer
A distinct category of thyroid cancer for which radioactive iodine therapy is not effective.<SEP>A distinct subtype of thyroid cancer that may harbor RET gene fusions and requires specific diagnostic and therapeutic considerations.<SEP>The third most common form of thyroid cancer, which can have an inherited genetic component running in families.

Anaplastic Thyroid Cancer
An aggressive form of thyroid cancer for which external beam radiation therapy is commonly utilized.<SEP>An aggressive form of thyroid cancer that is not responsive to radioactive iodine therapy and is almost always treated with radiation therapy.<SEP>The least common and most aggressive type of thyroid cancer, often treated with combined chemotherapy and radiation therapy.<SEP>The most aggressive and rare category of thyroid cancer, which predominantly affects older adults.

Lobectomy
A surgical procedure involving the partial removal of the thyroid gland, evaluated as an option when cancer has not spread beyond the thyroid.<SEP>A surgical procedure involving the partial removal of the thyroid gland, requiring distinct surveillance methods compared to total thyroidectomy.<SEP>A surgical procedure performed under general anesthesia that removes the cancerous lobe and isthmus of the thyroid gland.<SEP>A surgical procedure removing part of the thyroid, suitable for small, low-risk, noninvasive cancers.

Total Thyroidectomy
A surgical procedure involving the complete removal of the thyroid gland, often preceding radioactive iodine therapy.<SEP>A surgical procedure involving the complete removal of the thyroid gland, recommended for tumors larger than 4 cm or those extending beyond the thyroid.<SEP>A surgical procedure involving the complete removal of the thyroid gland, requiring specific post-operative surveillance protocols including Tg testing.<SEP>A surgical procedure removing the entire thyroid gland, and sometimes adjacent lymph nodes, to treat thyroid cancer.<SEP>Surgical removal of the entire thyroid gland, used for larger, higher-risk, or invasive thyroid cancers.

Thyroid Hormone Replacement Therapy
A medical treatment using levothyroxine to replace thyroid hormones and maintain low or normal TSH levels following thyroid surgery.<SEP>A therapeutic category involving synthetic thyroid hormone (such as levothyroxine) used to restore hormone levels and suppress TSH to prevent cancer recurrence.<SEP>A therapeutic medical regimen using synthetic hormone replacement medications, such as levothyroxine, required after thyroid removal.<SEP>A treatment, often using levothyroxine, required after total thyroidectomy or certain lobectomies to replace hormones and regulate TSH levels.

Provider
A medical clinician or physician who evaluates patient nodules, orders laboratory and imaging tests, and directs cancer management plans.

Molecular Tests
Diagnostic genetic and molecular testing methods performed on biopsy specimens to assess malignancy risk and determine the necessity of surgery.

Neck Dissection
A surgical procedure performed during thyroidectomy to remove cervical lymph nodes known or suspected to contain cancer.

Hypoparathyroidism
An endocrine condition resulting in low blood calcium levels that can arise as a long-term complication of thyroid surgery.

Differentiated Thyroid Cancer
A broad classification of thyroid cancers that commonly responds to thyroid hormone suppression and radioactive iodine therapy.

Papillary Cancer
A common form of differentiated thyroid cancer for which external beam radiation therapy is rarely indicated.

Follicular Cancer
A form of differentiated thyroid cancer for which external beam radiation therapy is infrequently used.

Radioactive Iodine Therapy
A targeted cancer therapy using radioactive iodine-131 to destroy remaining thyroid cells and metastatic cancer following surgery.<SEP>A treatment (RAI therapy) used following thyroidectomy to eliminate residual cancer cells in the body.<SEP>A treatment (RAI) used in thyroid cancer management when cancer cells absorb iodine.<SEP>Radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy is a post-surgical medical treatment used to eliminate residual thyroid cancer cells in the body.

Whole-Body RAI Scan
A diagnostic nuclear medicine imaging procedure conducted before or after radioactive iodine therapy to locate residual thyroid tissue or cancer spread.

Endocrinologist
A medical specialist in hormone conditions who serves as part of the multidisciplinary thyroid cancer treatment team.

Nuclear Medicine Specialist
A medical physician specialized in radioactive materials who administers radioactive iodine treatments and scans.

Thyrotoxicosis
A clinical condition caused by an excess of thyroid hormone in the body, which can result from excessive levothyroxine dosage.

Remnant Ablation
A low-dose radioactive iodine-131 procedure performed shortly after thyroidectomy to eliminate remaining normal thyroid tissue.

Thyroidectomy
Surgical removal of all or part of the thyroid gland, often considered before radioactive iodine therapy.

U.S. FDA
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is the regulatory agency responsible for evaluating and approving investigational medical treatments tested in clinical trials.<SEP>The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is the regulatory authority responsible for approving investigational treatments evaluated in clinical trials.<SEP>The United States Food and Drug Administration is the regulatory agency responsible for reviewing and approving new cancer drugs, devices, and treatment approaches evaluated in clinical trials.

Kinase Inhibitors
A class of targeted therapy medications, mostly oral capsules, used to treat specific forms of thyroid cancer.

External Radiation
A specific form of radiation therapy delivered from an external machine to targeted areas like the neck to treat tumors and relieve cancer symptoms.

RAI Therapy
Radioactive iodine therapy used post-surgery to ablate residual thyroid tissue and treat iodine-avid recurrent or metastatic thyroid cancer.<SEP>Radioactive iodine therapy, a primary treatment option for thyroid cancer before alternative systemic or targeted therapies are considered.

Study Sponsor
An organization or entity funding clinical research and covering research-related costs such as investigational study drugs.

Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma
The most common type of thyroid cancer, often treated with lobectomy or total thyroidectomy, or managed through active surveillance in low-risk cases.

Follicular and Oncocytic Carcinoma
Subtypes of differentiated thyroid cancer that typically grow slowly and are treated surgically.

Completion Thyroidectomy
A secondary surgical procedure performed to remove the remaining portion of the thyroid gland following high-risk findings from an initial lobectomy.<SEP>A subsequent surgical procedure to remove the remainder of the thyroid following a previous lobectomy when high-risk or invasive features are identified.

Levothyroxine
A synthetic hormone medication used in lifelong thyroid hormone replacement therapy to keep thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels low or normal.<SEP>A thyroid hormone replacement drug taken by patients to replace thyroid function and suppress TSH levels to prevent cancer progression.

Classic Type Papillary Thyroid Cancer
The most frequently diagnosed subtype of papillary thyroid carcinoma.

data.entity_name: Follicular Variant of Papillary Thyroid Cancer
data.content:
Follicular Variant of Papillary Thyroid Cancer
A subtype of papillary thyroid cancer that may present different growth patterns compared to classic variants.

Tall-Cell/Columnar Cell Carcinoma
An aggressive subtype of papillary thyroid carcinoma characterized by faster growth and greater propensity to spread.

Hobnail Variant
A subtype of papillary thyroid cancer known to grow and spread more rapidly.

Diffuse Sclerosing Variant
A recognized subtype of papillary thyroid cancer that exhibits more aggressive spread.

Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma
Follicular thyroid carcinoma (FTC) is the second most common type of thyroid cancer, characterized by invasion into blood vessels or the outer tumor layer.

NIFTP
Noninvasive follicular thyroid neoplasm with papillary-like nuclear features (NIFTP) is a low-risk, noninvasive thyroid tumor formerly considered an encapsulated follicular variant of papillary thyroid cancer.

Papillary Thyroid Cancer
A common differentiated thyroid cancer subtype that is often treated with RAI therapy when metastatic disease exhibits iodine uptake.<SEP>A common type of thyroid cancer compared against follicular and oncocytic carcinomas, and historically linked to NIFTP.

Hürthle Cell Carcinoma
The former medical designation for oncocytic carcinoma, an uncommon and often more aggressive form of thyroid cancer.

Differentiated High-Grade Carcinoma
A specific diagnostic classification of malignant thyroid tumor characterized by differentiated features but aggressive, high-grade behavior.<SEP>An aggressive subtype of thyroid cancer that serves as an explicit indication for radioactive iodine therapy.

Neck Ultrasound
A non-invasive diagnostic imaging procedure used to inspect the neck for local recurrence of thyroid cancer following surgery.<SEP>A noninvasive post-operative imaging test recommended 6 to 12 months after total thyroidectomy for cancer surveillance.

Whole-Body RAI Imaging
A specialized follow-up nuclear medicine scan performed after radioactive iodine therapy to locate any residual thyroid cancer cells.

Recurrence
The return of cancer after a disease-free interval, which can occur locally at the anus, in regional lymph nodes, or at distant metastatic sites.<SEP>The return of thyroid cancer in the neck or distant areas following initial surgical and adjuvant treatment.

Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone
A pituitary hormone (TSH) monitored via blood testing to manage thyroid hormone replacement and evaluate thyroid disease status.

Thyroglobulin
A protein (Tg) produced exclusively by thyroid tissue, serving as a primary serum tumor marker for monitoring recurrence after total thyroidectomy.

Anti-Thyroglobulin Antibodies
Antibodies (Tg ab) produced against thyroglobulin that can interfere with Tg measurement and whose levels help assess treatment response.

No Evidence Of Disease
A clinical status (NED) indicating that follow-up exams, laboratory tests, and imaging show no signs of persistent or recurrent cancer.

Lenvatinib
An oral targeted multikinase inhibitor (marketed as Lenvima) designated as a preferred therapy for progressive, unresectable, radioactive iodine-refractory thyroid cancer.

Cabozantinib
A targeted multikinase inhibitor (marketed as Cabometyx) recommended as a subsequent therapy if cancer progresses after treatment with lenvatinib or sorafenib.

Oncocytic Thyroid Cancer
A subtype of thyroid cancer for which radioactive iodine therapy is indicated in metastatic disease that demonstrates iodine avidity.

Bone Cancer
A class of malignant disease affecting the skeletal system, primarily staged using the TNM classification system.<SEP>A group of malignancies originating in the bone or cartilage, distinguished as primary bone cancer or secondary metastatic cancer.<SEP>A group of malignant cancers originating in bone tissue that can disrupt normal bone formation and remodeling processes.<SEP>A malignancy of the bone, the diagnosis of which is confirmed through procedures like core needle or surgical biopsy.<SEP>A rare form of cancer and tumor disorders affecting the skeletal system, encompassing several distinct types such as osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, and chordoma.<SEP>A type of malignancy staged using T, N, M, and G criteria, which can also be a destination site for metastatic spread from primary liver cancer.

Osteosarcoma
A common primary bone sarcoma that arises in bone-forming cells, typically located in the metaphysis near growth plates.<SEP>A more common type of bone cancer typically managed through a combination of therapeutic modalities.

Ewing Sarcoma
A form of bone cancer characterized by chromosomal translocation and gene fusion, most commonly between chromosomes 11 and 22.<SEP>A type of bone cancer whose treatment protocol generally initiates with systemic therapy.<SEP>A type of bone sarcoma originating in the bone marrow, commonly affecting long bones or flat bones like the pelvis and scapula.

Chondrosarcoma
A primary bone cancer that originates in cells forming cartilage.<SEP>A specific type of bone cancer typically treated through surgical removal of the tumor.<SEP>A type of bone cancer whose patients are frequently prone to IDH1 gene mutations.

Chordoma
A rare bone tumor starting in notochordal cells that form the spine, typically occurring in the sacrum or skull base.<SEP>A type of bone cancer with treatment options typically including surgical resection or radiation therapy.

Giant Cell Tumor of Bone
A bone tumor characterized by cell overgrowth in the metaphysis extending into the epiphysis.<SEP>Also known as GCTB, a bone condition that is usually non-cancerous but requires aggressive medical treatment to prevent bone damage.

Multiple Myeloma
A cancer affecting plasma cells in the bone marrow, highlighted alongside other bone-related malignancies.<SEP>A cancer of plasma cells that weakens immune defenses, increasing susceptibility to anal cancer.

Primary Bone Cancer
Malignancies that originate directly in the bone or cartilage, most commonly classified as sarcomas.

Secondary Bone Malignancies
Metastatic cancers that originate in other organs such as the breast, lungs, or kidneys and spread to the bones.

Bone Sarcoma
A main group of sarcomas that originate within bone-forming cells, comprising cancers such as osteosarcoma.

Patients
Individuals diagnosed with conditions such as thyroid or bone cancer who make treatment decisions using educational guides.<SEP>Individuals diagnosed with or living with a glioma or brain tumor who experience symptoms, undergo testing, and receive treatments.

Cancer Experts
Respected medical oncologists and clinicians who formulate cancer care recommendations based on the latest scientific research.

Bone Cancer Staging
The diagnostic process of determining the extent, severity, and anatomical location of bone tumors within the body.

Surgical Biopsy
An open biopsy method requiring an operating room and an incision to remove a sample of a tumor.

Treating Surgeon
An experienced specialist responsible for performing surgical biopsies and subsequent cancer treatments at a specialized center.

Chromosomal Translocation
A genetic error where portions of two different chromosomes break off and switch locations, often causing gene fusions.

EWSR1 Gene
A gene located on chromosome 22 that commonly fuses with an ETS family gene in Ewing sarcoma.

FLI1 Gene
A member of the ETS gene family located on chromosome 11 that most commonly fuses with EWSR1 in Ewing sarcoma.

Tumor Mutational Burden-High (TMB-H)
A tumor classification indicating 10 or more mutations per million base pairs of tumor DNA.

IDH1 Mutation
A specific genetic mutation found in conditions such as chondrosarcoma that can be targeted by specific therapies.

Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS)
An advanced genetic sequencing method used to analyze DNA sequences and identify detailed mutations in genes.

Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)
A highly sensitive molecular testing technique used to make millions or billions of copies of DNA or RNA.

Sarcoma Cancer Center
Specialized medical facilities or hospitals equipped to diagnose, biopsy, and treat sarcoma and bone cancer.

Ossification
The biological process of new bone formation that starts in the womb and concludes during adolescence when skeletal growth ceases.

Bone Remodeling
A continuous physiological process that replaces mature bone by breaking down and rebuilding tissue to maintain calcium homeostasis.

Osteoblasts
Specialized bone-forming cells that synthesize bone tissue using calcium from the bloodstream.

Osteoclasts
Specialized bone cells responsible for breaking down bone tissue to release calcium into the bloodstream.

Epiphysis
An anatomical section at the end of a long bone, covered with cartilage to form a joint.

Metaphysis
The intermediate anatomical region of a bone located between the physis and diaphysis.

Diaphysis
The anatomical middle region of a long bone.<SEP>The main shaft or central middle region of a long bone.

Physis
The cartilaginous growth plate of a bone that forms a physeal line or scar following skeletal maturity.<SEP>The growth plate made of cartilage that enables bone elongation and forms a physeal scar after skeletal maturity.

T Category
A component of the TNM staging system that classifies the size, extent, and depth of the primary tumor across different anatomical regions.

N Category
A component of the TNM system indicating whether cancer has spread to nearby or regional lymph nodes.

M Category
A component of the TNM system designating whether bone cancer has spread to distant body sites, such as the lungs or other bones.

Appendicular Skeleton
An anatomical division consisting of 126 bones of the limbs and shoulder and pelvic girdles, used to define specific T-stage criteria.

Spine
An anatomical vertebral column including 24 flexible vertebrae, sacrum, and coccyx, featuring unique tumor staging designations.

Skeletal Maturity
A biological developmental milestone after which the growth plate ceases activity and leaves a physeal scar in the bone.

Shoulder Girdle
A group of bones connecting the upper arm limbs to the torso, forming part of the appendicular skeleton.

Pelvic Girdle
A group of bones connecting the lower leg limbs to the body, forming part of the appendicular skeleton.

Sacroiliac Joint
The anatomical articulation linking the pelvis to the lower spine, evaluated in high-stage T4 pelvic bone tumors.

Spinal Canal
The anatomical cavity within the vertebral column that houses the spinal cord, monitored for invasion by T4 spinal tumors.

Lung
A common distant visceral organ site for bone cancer metastasis, designated under subcategory M1a.

Primary Liver Cancer
A medical category encompassing cancers that originate directly in the liver, with hepatocellular carcinoma being the most prevalent type in adults.

Secondary Liver Cancer
A medical classification referring to cancers that originate in other organs, such as the colon, and spread or metastasize to the liver.

Hepatocellular Carcinoma
A specific category of liver cancer that forms the primary subject of diagnostic evaluation, risk monitoring, and screening programs.<SEP>The most common form of primary liver cancer in adults, often arising from underlying liver disease such as cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis infections.<SEP>The most common type of primary liver cancer in adults, which is the primary focus of patient guidelines and clinical management.

Fibrolamellar Hepatocellular Carcinoma
A rare subtype of hepatocellular carcinoma that typically occurs in younger individuals and affects a small patient population.

Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma
The second most common primary liver cancer in adults, arising specifically within the bile ducts inside the liver.

Metastatic Liver Cancer
Cancer that spreads from the liver to distant sites such as the lungs or bones, or secondary cancer originating elsewhere and spreading to the liver.<SEP>Liver cancer that has spread beyond the primary tumor to distant body sites, most frequently the lungs or bones.

Hepatobiliary System
A biological anatomical system consisting of the liver, gallbladder, and bile ducts that produces, stores, and transports bile.

Cancer Research UK
A cancer research and awareness charity, credited via CRUK for the anatomical diagram of the liver lobes and blood supply.

Wikimedia Commons
An online media repository hosting diagrammatic educational content regarding liver anatomy and blood supply.<SEP>An online open-access media repository cited as the host of medical diagram resources illustrating stomach cancer cells in lymph nodes.<SEP>An online repository and media platform hosting scientific and biomedical imagery.<SEP>An online repository providing open-access educational images and media referenced in medical literature.

Sarcoma Of The Liver
A rare form of primary liver cancer in adults that begins in the blood vessel cells of the liver.

Mixed-Type Liver Tumor
A rare form of primary liver malignancy composed of both hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma cells.

Gallbladder And Bile Duct Tumors
Malignancies developing in the gallbladder and biliary tract covered in specialized patient guidelines.

Hepatitis
An inflammatory liver condition listed as a major risk factor associated with liver cancer development.

GX Grade
A histological grading classification denoting that the degree of cellular differentiation cannot be assessed.

G1 Grade
A low-grade histological classification describing well-differentiated cancer cells that closely resemble normal cells.

G2 Grade
A high-grade histological classification describing moderately differentiated cancer cells.

G3 Grade
A high-grade histological classification describing poorly differentiated cancer cells that look very abnormal compared to normal cells.

Cirrhosis
A chronic liver condition classified as a key risk factor that warrants routine liver cancer screening.<SEP>A chronic liver disease characterized by the scarring of liver tissue, functioning as a primary risk factor for the development of liver cancer.

Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease
A liver condition occurring in individuals who drink little or no alcohol, linked to obesity, diabetes, and high cholesterol, which can progress to cirrhosis and liver cancer.

Genetic Hemochromatosis
An inherited medical disorder that causes the body and liver to store excessive amounts of iron from food, contributing to cirrhosis.

Liver Cancer Screening
A preventive medical routine involving ultrasound and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) testing every six months to detect liver cancer early in high-risk populations.<SEP>A routine testing process performed on asymptomatic individuals at risk, such as those with cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B, to detect cancer early.

Primary Biliary Cholangitis
A chronic liver disease that, particularly at Stage 4, causes progressive bile duct damage and serves as an established cause of liver cirrhosis.

Alpha-1-Antitrypsin Deficiency
A genetic disorder leading to a deficiency in the alpha-1-antitrypsin protein, which causes liver damage and acts as a risk factor for cirrhosis.

Alpha-Fetoprotein Test
A clinical blood test evaluating levels of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), an elevated marker indicating the possible presence of primary liver cancer.

Chronic Hepatitis B
A chronic viral infection of the liver recognized as a major risk factor requiring ongoing liver cancer screening.

Liver Cancer
A broad category of malignant tumors in the liver, commonly diagnosed using imaging tests and monitored through screening protocols.

Liver Disease
A broad medical category encompassing acute and chronic conditions affecting liver health, posing physical and emotional challenges.

Gastrointestinal Tract
An anatomical pathway within the digestive system comprising the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, colon, and rectum.

Dad
A cancer patient who was given a six-month prognosis in 2013 but achieved clinical cure through expert medical care and patient advocacy.

2013 Cancer Diagnosis
An event in 2013 where a patient received a critical cancer diagnosis with an initial prognosis of six months to live.

Intestinal Type
A major category of stomach adenocarcinoma where cells adhere to form tube- and gland-shaped structures, commonly carrying mutations treatable with targeted therapy.

Diffuse Type
A less common category of stomach adenocarcinoma where cells do not stick together and appear scattered across a broad area.

Early-Stage Stomach Cancer
A classification of stomach cancer characterized by tumors that have not spread beyond the innermost mucosa layer.<SEP>A clinical category of gastric cancer that has not grown beyond the first layer (mucosa) of the stomach wall, typically characterized by small tumors of 2 centimeters or less without lymph node involvement.

Narrator
The author and family caregiver who helped assemble a team of experts to navigate their father's terminal cancer prognosis and achieve a clinical cure.

Team of Experts
A multidisciplinary group of healthcare specialists formed by the narrator's family to navigate and treat the father's advanced cancer diagnosis.

Precancerous Changes
A category of early cellular abnormalities in the stomach mucosa that often develop slowly without symptoms prior to cancer onset.

Layers of the Stomach Wall
The anatomical classification of the five tissue layers composing the stomach: mucosa, submucosa, muscle layer, subserosa, and serosa.

Mucosa
The innermost layer category of the stomach wall, comprising the surface epithelium, lamina propria, and muscularis mucosae, where stomach cancers typically originate.

Submucosa
A structural layer category of connective tissue, blood vessels, nerve cells, and lymph channels situated beneath the mucosa.

Muscularis Propria
The muscle tissue layer category of the stomach wall responsible for churning and propelling food during digestion.

Subserosa
A supporting connective tissue layer category located directly underneath the serosa.

Serosa
The outermost membrane category covering the stomach wall that facilitates smooth movement against adjacent organs.

Digestive Organs
The anatomical category of organs involved in processing nutrients and waste, including the stomach, esophagus, liver, pancreas, intestines, and gallbladder.

Locoregional Stomach Cancer
A stage or category of stomach cancer that has invaded deeper layers of the stomach wall (submucosa and beyond) and may have spread to nearby lymph nodes or adjacent organs.

Metastatic Stomach Cancer
An advanced classification of gastric cancer where malignant cells have spread to distant areas of the body, such as the liver, peritoneum, distant lymph nodes, lungs, or bones.

Glioma
A broad category of brain tumors arising from glial cells, classified based on histology, grade, and molecular biomarkers.<SEP>A category of primary brain tumor originating in glial cells, discussed in terms of diagnosis, causes, types, and potential treatments.<SEP>A common type of malignant brain tumor originating from glial cells in the central nervous system, known for invading normal brain tissue.<SEP>A type of brain tumor that can cause symptoms such as sensory disturbances, vision problems, cognitive changes, weakness, and nausea.<SEP>A type of central nervous system tumor originating from glial cells in the brain or spinal cord, characterized by potential recurrence and disruption of brain function.

H. Pylori Tests
A diagnostic category focused on identifying Helicobacter pylori bacterial infection in the stomach.

H. Pylori Infection
A bacterial condition affecting the gastric lining that is relevant to patient medical history and gastric disease risk.

Support Person
A trusted peer, family member, or friend who assists the patient by providing transportation to visits, meals, note-taking, and emotional support.

Astrocytoma
A common type of glioma tumor composed of cells resembling star-shaped astrocytes, which maintain the chemical environment for nerve cell communication.<SEP>A subtype of glioma characterized by cells that resemble astrocytes, often identified alongside specific genetic mutations such as IDH.

Oligodendroglioma
A common type of glioma tumor formed from cells resembling oligodendrocytes, which protect electrical signaling in nerve cells.<SEP>A subtype of glioma characterized by cells that resemble oligodendrocytes under microscopic analysis.

Glioblastoma
The most common form of grade 4 glioma, marked by aggressive cellular growth and spread.<SEP>The most destructive and dangerous type of glioma tumor, developing from precursor cells that form astrocytes and oligodendrocytes.

Low-Grade Glioma
A classification encompassing Grade 1 and Grade 2 gliomas, characterized by slower growth and distinct prognosis.<SEP>A classification of glioma characterized by slower-growing tumor behavior.

High-Grade Glioma
A classification encompassing Grade 3 and Grade 4 gliomas, characterized by faster proliferation and invasiveness.<SEP>A classification of glioma characterized by rapid tumor growth and aggressive progression.

Glial Cells
A category of non-neuronal cells in the central nervous system that support the function of neurons and serve as the cells of origin for gliomas.<SEP>Supportive brain and spinal cord cells that assist nerve cell function and from which gliomas originate when mutations occur.<SEP>Supportive brain cells after which different varieties of gliomas are classified and named.

Cancer Cells
A category of abnormal cells that bypass regular cellular regulation, multiply rapidly, crowd out healthy cells, and resist programmed death.

Normal Cells
A category of healthy bodily cells that regulate growth according to bodily requirements and die when damaged or aged.

Specialized Brain Tumor Center
A medical facility or clinical institution with focused clinical experience and specialized expertise in diagnosing and managing brain tumors.

Astrocytomas
One of the three most common subtypes of glioma brain tumors.

Oligodendrogliomas
One of the three primary types of glioma brain tumors.

Glioblastomas
One of the most common and aggressive subtypes of glioma tumors.

Low-Grade Gliomas
A class of gliomas that typically grow slowly over years and may not immediately produce symptoms.

High-Grade Gliomas
An advanced classification of gliomas associated with serious complications, including blood clots in the legs and lungs.<SEP>An aggressive classification of gliomas that grow rapidly over weeks or months and produce noticeable symptoms.

Central Nervous System Tumors
Tumors located in the brain and spinal cord that disrupt normal neurological and cognitive functions.

Lab Testing
Diagnostic tests conducted to evaluate health parameters and tumor properties to guide treatment planning.

Headaches
A common early symptom of gliomas, often occurring in the morning or during the night and potentially accompanied by nausea.

Seizures
A frequent neurological symptom associated with brain tumors, often serving as an early indicator of low-grade gliomas.

Fatigue
A complex physical, cognitive, or emotional symptom characterized by exhaustion, influenced by tumors, medications, lifestyle, or environmental factors.<SEP>A frequent and debilitating symptom experienced by brain tumor patients that is not directly relieved by sleep.

Follow-Up Visits
Periodic medical checkups recommended after glioma treatment to monitor recurrence and assess disease stability.

Parietal Lobe
An anatomical brain region responsible for functions including intelligence, language, reading, sensation, and sensory perception.

Occipital Lobe
An anatomical brain region responsible for visual processing and color perception.

Blood Clots
A vascular complication in the legs and lungs linked to high-grade gliomas, causing swelling, chest pain, and breathing difficulties.

Neuropathologist
A medical specialist who analyzes brain tumor biopsy tissues under a microscope and conducts molecular testing to diagnose and classify tumors.<SEP>A medical specialist who examines tissue samples from tumors to identify specific biomarkers and provide diagnostic information about gliomas.

Biomarkers
Biological indicators, including gene and protein mutations, evaluated through neuropathology testing to classify gliomas and guide targeted treatments.<SEP>Molecular and genetic characteristics, such as IDH mutations, used to classify gliomas and predict their behavior.

Craniotomy
A surgical operation in which a section of the skull bone is temporarily removed to access the brain, performed during an open biopsy or resection.

Hospital Or Medical Center
A healthcare facility providing neurosurgical and pathology services for tumor diagnosis and management.

Astrocytes
A specific type of glial cell that astrocytoma tumor cells morphologically resemble.

Oligodendrocytes
A type of glial cell that oligodendroglioma tumor cells resemble under microscopic analysis.

IDH Gene Mutation
A specific genetic biomarker mutation identified during molecular testing to classify gliomas such as astrocytomas.

Astrocytoma IDH-Mutant Grade 2
An integrated diagnosis combining histology, biomarker status, and tumor grade.

Grade 1 Glioma
A slow-growing, typically benign classification of glioma tumor that is more common in children and often treated primarily with surgery.<SEP>A slow-growing, typically benign glioma type that is more common in children and often manageable with surgery alone.

Grade 2 Glioma
A slow-growing classification of glioma with somewhat abnormal cells that can invade normal tissue and may recur years later as a higher-grade tumor.<SEP>A slow-growing glioma with somewhat abnormal cells that can infiltrate normal brain tissue and potentially recur as a higher grade.

Grade 3 Glioma
A high-grade glioma category characterized by abnormal cells that multiply rapidly and invade nearby tissue, requiring therapies such as radiation and chemotherapy post-surgery.<SEP>A high-grade glioma subtype marked by abnormal cellular patterns and aggressive clinical behavior.

Grade 4 Glioma
The most aggressive classification of glioma with highly abnormal cells that grow and spread very rapidly.

Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma
A hematological condition closely related to chronic lymphocytic leukemia that affects the lymphatic system.<SEP>Small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) is the same disease as CLL, differing primarily in the primary location of the abnormal cells, which are mostly found in lymph nodes and the spleen.

Radiation
A cancer therapy utilizing high-energy rays, administered alongside chemotherapy following surgery for high-grade gliomas.<SEP>A cancer treatment modality that uses high-energy rays to treat cancer, capable of causing specific short- and long-term side effects.

High-Grade Tumors
A classification of aggressive gliomas comprising grades 3 and 4 that rapidly invade tissue and require multimodal post-surgical therapy.

DNA Mutation
An abnormal change in genetic code that alters cellular behavior and can lead to malignancies such as gliomas or chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

Richter Transformation
Richter transformation is a medical condition associated with lymphoma progression or transformation discussed in patient care materials.<SEP>Richter transformation is a rare complication and disease progression event where CLL develops into a more aggressive lymphoma.<SEP>Richter transformation is a significant medical complication and advanced condition that can develop in patients diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

Mantle Cell Lymphoma
Mantle cell lymphoma is a distinct type of lymphoma that lacks proteins such as CD200 and LEF1 found on CLL cells.

NIAID
The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) is a research organization credited in the source material for medical imagery regarding B cell surface markers.

Minimal Residual Disease
A post-treatment clinical condition where cancerous cells are reduced to minimal levels and blood cells are mostly healthy.

Anemia
A medical condition characterized by low levels of normal red blood cells, which can trigger the need for CLL treatment.

Blood Smear
A microscopic examination of a blood drop performed by a hematopathologist and oncologist to identify cancer cell morphology.<SEP>A microscopic laboratory examination of a drop of blood used to inspect the appearance of abnormal cells for clues about cancer.

CLL
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a type of blood cancer diagnosed by the presence of at least 5,000 monoclonal B lymphocytes per microliter of blood.

Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma (SLL)
Small lymphocytic lymphoma is a form of cancer closely related to CLL that is confirmed through lymph node examinations.

Hematologist-Oncologist
A medical specialist who focuses on blood cancers, evaluates diagnostic pathology reports, performs physical examinations, and coordinates cancer treatment plans.

Bone Marrow Aspiration
A clinical procedure performed on the back of the hip bone to extract liquid and cells from the bone marrow.

Beta-2 Microglobulin
A blood laboratory marker tested as part of the workup for planning CLL treatment.

DNA Sequencing
A molecular testing method used to analyze genetic sequences in blood cancer cells to guide treatment.<SEP>DNA sequencing is a laboratory molecular test used to detect genetic mutations in the TP53 and IGHV genes.

CpG-Stimulated Karyotype
A cytogenetic laboratory test assessing chromosome structure used in treatment planning for CLL.

Diagnostic CT Scan
Radiological imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis that may be used during treatment planning to check for internal lymph node and organ enlargement.

Direct Antiglobulin Test
Also known as the Coombs test, an optional laboratory test used during treatment planning for CLL patients.

Cutaneous B-Cell Lymphoma
Cutaneous B-cell lymphoma (CBCL) is a form of cancer that requires accurate blood tests, tissue tests, imaging, and biopsy to diagnose and establish a treatment plan.<SEP>Cutaneous B-cell lymphoma (CBCL) is a form of primary cutaneous lymphoma that starts in B-cell lymphocytes within the lymphatic system.<SEP>Cutaneous B-cell lymphoma (CBCL) is a subtype of primary cutaneous lymphoma that develops from abnormal B cells, typically presenting as skin nodules or papules.

Diagnostic CT
A medical imaging procedure that utilizes radiation and a contrast agent to detect enlarged lymph nodes and assess the extent of cancer prior to treatment.

CLL Specialist
A specialized medical practitioner who provides expert consultation, diagnosis, and treatment guidance for chronic lymphocytic leukemia patients.

Differential
A differential is a laboratory blood test that counts the most common types of white blood cells and checks their balance in the blood, often showing elevated counts in CLL.

17p Deletion
17p deletion is a specific chromosomal biomarker detected by FISH in CLL cells that helps determine disease prognosis and guide treatment selection.

Fertility Counselor
A specialized healthcare professional who counsels cancer patients on options and procedures for preserving fertility before starting treatment.

Radiology Department
A specialized hospital or clinical department equipped with scanners where diagnostic CT imaging is performed.

Consultation With A CLL Specialist
A clinical meeting between a patient and a chronic lymphocytic leukemia specialist to review diagnosis, test results, and treatment recommendations.

Primary Cutaneous Lymphomas
A clinical category of lymphomas arising in the skin, which encompasses cutaneous B-cell lymphoma.<SEP>Primary cutaneous lymphomas (PCL) are a rare group of non-Hodgkin lymphomas that originate in the skin from abnormal B or T lymphocytes.

Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphoma
Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) is a subtype of primary cutaneous lymphoma that develops from abnormal T lymphocytes, including forms like mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome.

Primary Cutaneous Marginal Zone Lymphoma
Primary cutaneous marginal zone lymphoma (PCMZL), also known as PCMZ lymphoproliferative disorder, is an indolent subtype of primary cutaneous B-cell lymphoma.

Primary Cutaneous Follicle Center Lymphoma
Primary cutaneous follicle center lymphoma (PCFCL) is an indolent subtype of primary cutaneous B-cell lymphoma.

data.entity_name: Primary Cutaneous Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma, Leg Type
data.content:
Primary Cutaneous Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma, Leg Type
Primary cutaneous diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, leg type (PC-DLBCL, leg type) is a specific subtype of primary cutaneous B-cell lymphoma.

Mycosis Fungoides
Mycosis fungoides is a specific type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL).

Sézary Syndrome
Sézary syndrome is an aggressive variant and clinical form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL).

Primary Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphoproliferative Disorders
Primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoproliferative disorders (PCLPDs) are a group of disorders related to cutaneous T-cell lymphomas.

Testing For CBCL
Testing for CBCL comprises a series of diagnostic evaluations—such as skin exams, blood tests, biopsies, imaging, and immunophenotyping—used to diagnose and determine a treatment plan for cutaneous B-cell lymphoma.

Doctor Visit
An in-person or telehealth clinical appointment where patients consult with healthcare providers, review diagnostic findings, and discuss treatment plans.

Follow-Up Testing
Routine diagnostic tests conducted over several years following cancer treatment to monitor and detect any recurrence of bladder cancer.

Medical History Assessment
A clinical evaluation process where a patient's past illnesses, injuries, treatments, medications, and supplements are documented to help determine optimal therapy.

Blood And Tissue Tests
A category of laboratory diagnostic evaluations performed on fluid and tissue specimens to identify and manage cutaneous B-cell lymphoma.

Urothelial Cancer
The most common form of bladder cancer that originates in the urothelial cells lining the urinary tract.<SEP>The primary and most common form of bladder cancer originating in urothelial cells, featuring multiple subtypes such as glandular, squamous cell, and micropapillary.

Hematuria
A medical symptom category characterized by the presence of blood in the urine, serving as the most common early sign of bladder cancer.

Non-Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer
A category of bladder cancer (stages 0 and 1) that has not invaded the deeper muscle layer of the bladder wall.<SEP>A clinical phase of bladder cancer where the tumor is confined to the inner urothelial layer and has not invaded the bladder muscle wall.<SEP>A specific form of bladder cancer that has not invaded the deeper muscle layer of the bladder wall and frequently requires post-treatment surveillance.

Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer
A category of bladder cancer (stages 2, 3, and 4) where cancer has penetrated into or beyond the bladder wall muscle layer, requiring more intensive treatment.<SEP>A more advanced stage of bladder cancer that has grown into the muscle layer of the bladder, requiring more intensive or complicated treatment.<SEP>An aggressive phase of bladder cancer where tumor cells have grown into the muscle layer of the bladder wall.<SEP>Bladder cancer encompassing stages 2, 3, and 4 where the tumor has invaded into or through the muscular layer of the bladder wall.<SEP>Muscle-invasive bladder cancer is an advanced stage of bladder malignancy that has penetrated into the muscle wall, typically requiring radical cystectomy.

Metastatic Bladder Cancer
Advanced bladder cancer that has spread beyond the pelvis to distant organs and lymph nodes, specifically designated as Stage 4B.<SEP>An advanced phase of bladder cancer characterized by the spread of cancer cells beyond the bladder to distant sites like lymph nodes, bones, lungs, or liver.<SEP>An advanced stage of bladder cancer that has spread beyond the bladder to other parts of the body, which is treatable with systemic therapies though typically not curable.

Chemical Exposure
An environmental and occupational risk factor category involving substances found in dyes, rubber, leather, printing, textiles, and paint that elevate bladder cancer risk.

Cancer of the Urothelium
A form of cancer that originates in the urothelial lining of the urinary tract, which includes the bladder, kidneys, ureters, and urethra.

Frequent Urination
A urinary symptom marked by needing to urinate more often than usual, which can indicate bladder cancer.

Urgency to Urinate
A medical symptom characterized by a sudden, intense need to urinate, associated with bladder cancer.

Painful Urination
A condition characterized by discomfort or burning during urination, presenting as a symptom of bladder cancer.

Back Pain
A physical discomfort in the back that can serve as a symptom of bladder cancer.

Urinalysis
A laboratory test performed on urine samples to identify microscopic blood and other abnormalities.

Urine Cytology
A diagnostic laboratory test examining urine samples under a microscope to detect abnormal or cancerous cells.<SEP>Urine cytology is a diagnostic laboratory test analyzing urine samples under a microscope to detect cancerous or precancerous cells.

Genetic Mutations
Abnormal alterations in cellular DNA instructions that cause normal cells to transform into cancerous cells.

Secondhand Smoke
