Environmental tobacco smoke exposure that increases an individual's risk of developing bladder cancer.<SEP>Passive tobacco smoke inhaled by family members and friends, raising their relative risk of developing bladder cancer.

Clinical Team
A group of doctors and medical specialists responsible for diagnosing, evaluating, and determining treatment options for bladder cancer patients.

Non-Invasive Bladder Cancer
An early phase of bladder cancer where the cancer cells have not penetrated into the deeper muscle tissue, often curable with treatment.

Cystoscopy And Biopsy
Diagnostic procedures used to visualize the inside of the bladder and extract tissue samples to confirm the diagnosis and extent of bladder cancer.

Medical And Family Histories
A diagnostic health assessment documenting past illnesses, treatments, medications, and hereditary disease patterns among blood relatives.

Blood And Urine Tests
Laboratory evaluations of fluid samples designed to identify disease signs and monitor organ performance in cancer patients.

Primary Care Doctor
A primary care doctor is a general physician who manages non-cancer medical care and helps patients communicate their treatment preferences to their oncology team.

Urologic Oncologist
A urologic oncologist is a surgeon specialized in diagnosing and treating urinary tract and male reproductive cancers using surgery and intravesical therapy.

Pharmacist
A healthcare professional who prepares chemotherapy and other oncology medications, and provides advice on drug treatments.

Advanced Practice Provider
Medical professionals including registered nurse practitioners and physician assistants who monitor patient health, manage care, and provide treatment within a healthcare team.

Resident and Fellow
Trainee physicians pursuing ongoing specialized medical education under supervision to become fully credentialed specialists.

Psychologist and Psychiatrist
Mental health clinicians who assist patients in managing psychological symptoms such as depression and anxiety related to their cancer diagnosis.

Liver Function Test
A diagnostic blood evaluation component of a CMP that measures hepatic enzymes, such as alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin, to check liver health.

Kidney Function Test
A diagnostic blood evaluation component of a CMP measuring waste products like creatinine and blood urea nitrogen to verify renal function prior to cancer treatment.

Biomarker Test
A diagnostic laboratory test detecting tumor markers or cellular clues in urine to assist in bladder cancer evaluation and surveillance.

Clinic Or Hospital
A healthcare facility and surgical setting where larger tumors found during examinations are removed in an operating room.

Ureteroscopy
A diagnostic procedure examining the upper parts of the urinary tract, including the ureters and inner kidneys, using a cystoscope.

Urogram
An imaging test using contrast solution alongside CT or MRI to evaluate the condition and lining of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder.<SEP>An imaging test using contrast with CT or MRI to evaluate the urinary tract lining and assess the extent of bladder cancer.

Renal Ultrasound
A non-surgical, painless imaging procedure utilizing sound waves to generate real-time images of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder.<SEP>A painless, non-surgical real-time imaging test producing black-and-white images of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder.

Blue Light Cystoscopy
An advanced cystoscopic imaging method that combines blue light and injected dye to detect bladder tumors more distinctly than standard white light.

Narrow-Band Imaging
An emerging endoscopic imaging technology that enhances tumor visibility during cystoscopy without requiring dye.

Lab
A laboratory facility responsible for testing and analyzing tissue samples collected during biopsies for the presence of cancer.

Tumor Removal
A surgical procedure conducted in an operating room at a clinic or hospital to excise cancerous growths identified in the bladder.

White Light Cystoscopy
The traditional standard method of examining the interior of the bladder using conventional white light illumination.

Post-Cystoscopy Side Effects
A group of common temporary complications following cystoscopy, including urethral bleeding, burning sensations during urination, and urinary frequency.

Pyelogram
An x-ray procedure using contrast solution to identify blockages such as tumors, stones, or blood clots in the ureters and kidneys.

Chest Imaging
A diagnostic imaging procedure utilizing CT or x-ray to determine if cancer has metastasized to the lungs.

Vaping
The use of e-cigarettes, which introduces nicotine and chemicals that hinder cancer treatments and increase complication risks.

FindAGeneticCounselor.com
A dedicated web directory assisting patients in locating qualified genetic counselors for hereditary cancer risk evaluation.

Upper Urinary Tract Cancer
Cancer located in the kidneys or ureters, which serves as a clinical indication for germline genetic testing.

Cancer Grading
A pathological assessment measuring how fast cancer cells are growing, categorizing tumors into low or high grades.<SEP>Cancer grading is a measure of the aggressiveness and rate of growth of cancer cells, categorized into low grade (slow growing) and high grade (fast growing).

Stage 0
The earliest stage of bladder cancer that affects only the inner urothelial lining, comprising subgroups Stage 0a and Stage 0is.

Stage 0a
A subgroup of Stage 0 bladder cancer describing cancer cells growing outward toward the hollow center of the bladder rather than into the bladder wall.

Stage 2
A muscle-invasive bladder cancer stage where tumor cells have grown into the bladder muscle layer without reaching the outer fatty layer or spreading.

Stage 3A
A subgroup of Stage 3 bladder cancer that has reached surrounding fatty tissue, potentially a single nearby lymph node, or nearby reproductive organs such as the prostate, uterus, or vagina.

Stage 3B
A subgroup of Stage 3 bladder cancer that has spread to multiple pelvic lymph nodes but not to distant organs or lymph nodes.

Stage 4
An advanced stage of bladder cancer where the cancer has grown through the bladder wall and may have spread to distant lymph nodes or distant organs.

Low Grade
A cancer grade classification (LG) indicating cancer cells that closely resemble normal cells and are slow-growing.<SEP>A grading classification (LG) indicating that bladder cancer cells appear relatively normal and are slow-growing.

High Grade
A cancer grade classification (HG) indicating cancer cells that look very abnormal and grow and spread quickly.<SEP>A grading classification (HG) indicating that bladder cancer cells look significantly abnormal, growing and spreading rapidly.

Urothelial Layer
The innermost lining of the bladder wall made of urothelial cells, where the majority of bladder cancers originate.

Connective Tissue Layer
The second anatomical layer of the bladder wall located between the inner urothelial lining and the muscle layer.

Muscle Layer
The muscular layer of the bladder wall; whether cancer has invaded this layer serves as the primary distinction between non-muscle-invasive and muscle-invasive disease.

Outer Fatty Layer
The outermost anatomical layer surrounding the bladder wall, involved when cancer advances to Stage 3.

TURBT
Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumor (TURBT) is a surgical procedure used to remove visible bladder tumors.<SEP>Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumor is a surgical procedure performed through the urethra to diagnose, stage, and resect bladder tumors.<SEP>Transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) is a surgical procedure that examines and removes tumors on the bladder wall, sometimes repeated for deeper biopsy or staging.<SEP>Transurethral resection of bladder tumor, a surgical procedure used to remove all visible cancer from the bladder prior to chemoradiation in trimodal therapy.

Intravesical Therapy
A local treatment method that involves filling the bladder with liquid medication to eliminate cancer cells, often combined with TURBT.<SEP>A localized cancer therapy administered directly into the bladder, which may cause bladder inflammation, pain, and urinary symptoms.<SEP>A localized cancer treatment method in which medication is instilled directly into the bladder via a catheter.<SEP>Intravesical therapy is a localized bladder treatment commonly performed in combination with TURBT.<SEP>Intravesical therapy is a medical procedure involving the instillation of liquid medication directly into the bladder via a catheter.

Glandular Subtype
A rare histological variant of urothelial cancer showing glandular cell features that may grow or advance faster than typical urothelial cancer.

Squamous Cell Subtype
A variant of urothelial cancer exhibiting squamous cell features, potentially requiring more aggressive treatment due to faster growth.

Micropapillary Subtype
An uncommon histological subtype of urothelial cancer known for potentially rapid disease advancement.

Plasmacytoid Subtype
A rare histological subtype of urothelial cancer characterized by distinctive morphological features and potentially aggressive behavior.

Sarcomatoid Subtype
A rare, aggressive variant of urothelial cancer presenting with spindle or sarcomatous cellular characteristics.

Nested Subtype
A recognized variant subtype of urothelial bladder carcinoma presenting with nested cell patterns.

Lymphoepithelioma-Like Subtype
A rare histological variant of urothelial carcinoma with morphological resemblance to lymphoepithelioma.

Microcystic And Tubular Subtype
A rare histological subtype of urothelial carcinoma characterized by microcystic and tubular cellular patterns.

Stage 0 Bladder Cancer
Non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer where abnormal cells have grown only on the inside lining of the bladder wall.

Stage 1 Bladder Cancer
Early-stage bladder cancer where a tumor has invaded the layer of connective tissue in the bladder wall without reaching the muscle layer.

Stage 3 Bladder Cancer
Advanced bladder cancer where the tumor has grown through the muscle layer into the surrounding fat layer, and potentially into nearby lymph nodes.

Stage 4 Bladder Cancer
Metastatic bladder cancer in which the disease has spread beyond the bladder to distant sites in the body.

Bladder Removal
A surgical procedure (cystectomy) involving the total removal of the bladder and sometimes adjacent organs to treat severe bladder cancer.

Indiana University
Indiana University is an academic institution whose surgeons developed the Indiana pouch urinary diversion technique.<SEP>Indiana University is an educational and research institution whose surgeons developed the Indiana pouch, a type of continent cutaneous urinary diversion.

Cystectomy
Cystectomy is a surgical procedure to remove all or part of the bladder, primarily utilized in treating bladder cancer.

Radical Cystectomy
A major surgical operation used for muscle-invasive bladder cancer that removes the bladder, nearby lymph nodes, and other pelvic organs.<SEP>A surgical procedure involving the complete removal of the bladder, which can be avoided in certain patients through trimodal preservation therapy.<SEP>Radical cystectomy is a major surgical procedure involving the removal of the entire bladder, nearby lymph nodes, and potentially other adjacent organs for muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

Partial Cystectomy
Partial cystectomy is a surgical operation that removes only a portion of the bladder, suitable for a small minority of bladder cancer patients.

Neobladder
A neobladder is an internal urinary diversion procedure that reconstructs a reservoir from the small intestine and connects it to the urethra, allowing urination along the normal pathway.

Continent Cutaneous Pouch
Continent cutaneous pouch, also known as an Indiana pouch, is a urinary diversion created from the large intestine with a stoma valve that is emptied via catheterization.

Urinary Incontinence
A medical condition characterized by loss of bladder control and unintended leakage of urine, often resulting from bladder surgery.<SEP>A post-surgical complication characterized by an inability to control the flow of urine.<SEP>Urinary incontinence is a medical condition characterized by involuntary leakage of urine, identified as a common occurrence following neobladder surgery.

Catheterization
Catheterization is the medical procedure of inserting a tube (catheter) through the urethra or a stoma to facilitate the drainage of urine from a reservoir.

BCG Shortage
The BCG shortage is an ongoing supply crisis in the United States and globally that restricts access to bacillus Calmette-Guérin therapy for bladder cancer patients.

Indiana Pouch
The Indiana pouch is a type of catheterizable continent urinary diversion created using a section of the small intestine connected to an abdominal stoma.

Intravesical BCG
Intravesical BCG is an immunotherapy treatment using weakened bacillus Calmette-Guérin bacteria instilled into the bladder to stimulate immune destruction of cancer cells.

Intravesical Chemotherapy
A localized cancer treatment category delivered directly inside the bladder rather than throughout the entire body.<SEP>Intravesical chemotherapy is a localized drug treatment instilled into the bladder to eradicate residual cancer cells and prevent recurrence.

Non–Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer
Non–muscle-invasive bladder cancer is a specific category of bladder cancer that has not invaded the deeper muscle layer of the bladder wall.

High-Grade Bladder Cancer
High-grade bladder cancer is an aggressive form of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer commonly treated with intravesical BCG.

Bladder Removal Surgery
A surgical treatment for bladder cancer involving the excision of the bladder, potentially causing bleeding, infections, incontinence, and sexual dysfunction.<SEP>Bladder removal surgery (cystectomy) is a surgical intervention considered for high-risk bladder cancer patients, particularly when BCG therapy is unavailable or ineffective.

FDA
The Food and Drug Administration is a regulatory agency responsible for approving treatments and drugs based on clinical trial results.<SEP>The Food and Drug Administration is a regulatory agency responsible for evaluating and approving safe and effective medical drugs, devices, and treatments based on clinical trial results.

Systemic Chemotherapy
A whole-body cancer treatment category involving drugs injected into the bloodstream to kill cancer cells throughout the body.

Trimodal Therapy
A bladder-preserving treatment protocol combining transurethral resection (TURBT) with concurrent chemotherapy and radiation therapy.

Phase 1 Clinical Trial
An initial research trial phase designed to evaluate the dose, safety, side effects, and preliminary efficacy of an investigational therapy.

Phase 2 Clinical Trial
A clinical research trial phase focused on assessing how well a treatment works against a specific type of cancer.

Phase 3 Clinical Trial
A clinical research phase that tests investigational therapies against standard-of-care treatments to support regulatory approval.

Phase 4 Clinical Trial
Post-approval research trials that assess the long-term safety, effectiveness, and benefits of therapies approved by regulatory agencies.

Dose-Dense Chemotherapy
A chemotherapy administration method that speeds up treatment by shortening the intervals between doses.

ddMVAC
A common systemic chemotherapy combination regimen consisting of dose-dense methotrexate, vinblastine, doxorubicin, and cisplatin used for bladder cancer.

Antibody-Drug Conjugate
A targeted therapy subcategory, such as enfortumab vedotin-ejfv, that binds to specific cancer cell surface proteins to deliver cytotoxic payloads.

Sexual Dysfunction
A complication of cancer and its treatments involving impaired physical sexual function or reduced sexual desire.

Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumor
A surgical procedure (TURBT) that examines and removes tumors located on the bladder wall.

Human Papillomavirus Infection
A widespread sexually transmitted infection (HPV) recognized as the primary risk factor for the development of anal cancer and other malignancies.

Anal Adenocarcinoma
A rare histological subtype of anal cancer originating from glandular cells rather than squamous cells.

Anal Melanoma
An uncommon form of anal malignancy that develops in melanocyte cells.

Pelvic Floor Exercises
Physical therapeutic exercises recommended to help patients regain urinary control following bladder surgery.

HPV16
A high-risk strain of human papillomavirus strongly associated with the development of anal and other anogenital cancers.<SEP>A specific high-risk strain of human papillomavirus that is strongly associated with the development of anal cancer and other malignancies.

Human Immunodeficiency Virus
A virus that weakens the immune system, hindering the body's ability to clear HPV infections and raising the risk of developing anal cancer.

Anal Dysplasia
A pre-cancerous condition characterized by abnormal cell lesions in or near the anus, categorized into LSIL, HSIL, and AIN.<SEP>Abnormal cell growth on the surface of the anal canal or perianal skin, representing an anal precancerous state.

Crohn's Disease
An autoimmune disorder identified as a potential risk factor contributing to an increased likelihood of anal cancer.

Superficially Invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma
The earliest, minimally invasive form of anal cancer, featuring microscopic lesions under 7 mm wide that are often detected incidentally.

High-Resolution Anoscopy
A specialized diagnostic examination procedure used to evaluate and detect abnormal tissue and anal cancer.<SEP>A specialized diagnostic procedure utilizing an anoscope, acetic acid, and a colposcope to examine the anal canal under magnification and take biopsies.<SEP>A specialized follow-up medical examination used to monitor and detect abnormalities or spread in anal tissue.

Anal Intraepithelial Neoplasia
Pre-cancerous abnormal changes in the lining of the anus, also classified under Stage 0 anal cancer or anal dysplasia.

Standard Anoscopy
An examination of the anal canal using an anoscope without colposcopic magnification, contrasted with high-resolution anoscopy.

Anal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
A form of invasive anal cancer diagnosed by biopsy that requires detailed testing, lymph node assessment, imaging, and staging.

SISCCA
Superficially invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the anus, an earlier and less advanced lesion than standard invasive anal cancer.

Precancer
Abnormal cell changes on the surface of the anal canal or perianal region that have not yet progressed to invasive cancer.

HPV
Human papillomavirus, a viral pathogen identified as the primary cause of almost all cervical cancers and linked to anal cancer.<SEP>Human papillomavirus, a widespread sexually transmitted virus identified as the risk factor most strongly linked with anal cancer.

Lymph Node Palpation
A physical examination technique where a doctor presses on the skin of the groin to feel for enlarged inguinal lymph nodes.

Gynecologic Exam
A clinical examination recommended for patients that includes cervical cancer and HPV screening.

Inguinal Lymph Nodes
Lymph nodes located in the groin region that are clinically relevant in pelvic and anal diseases.<SEP>Lymph nodes located in the groin where the thigh meets the abdomen, serving as common sites for anal cancer spread.

Michael
Michael is an anal cancer survivor who advocates for mentorship and mutual support among individuals undergoing and recovering from anal cancer treatment.

Anal Precancer
Anal precancer encompasses abnormal cell changes on the anal or perianal surface, including stage 0 anal cancer, anal dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, AIN, and HSIL.

Stage I Anal Cancer
Stage I anal cancer is a non-metastatic cancer stage defined by a primary tumor measuring 2 cm or smaller without spread to lymph nodes or distant sites.

Stage II Anal Cancer
Stage II anal cancer is a non-metastatic cancer stage subdivided into IIA (tumors larger than 2 cm up to 5 cm) and IIB (tumors larger than 5 cm) without spread to lymph nodes or distant sites.

Stage III Anal Cancer
Stage III anal cancer is an advanced non-metastatic stage subdivided into IIIA, IIIB, and IIIC, involving regional lymph node spread or invasion of nearby organs.

Stage IV Anal Cancer
Stage IV anal cancer is metastatic cancer that has spread beyond the pelvis to distant organs such as the liver or lungs.

Stage IIA Anal Cancer
A substage of stage II anal cancer characterized by tumors larger than 2 cm but not larger than 5 cm, with no spread to lymph nodes or distant sites (T2, N0, M0).

Stage IIB Anal Cancer
A substage of stage II anal cancer characterized by tumors larger than 5 cm without spread to nearby lymph nodes or distant metastases (T3, N0, M0).

Stage IIIA Anal Cancer
A substage of stage III anal cancer where the primary tumor is 5 cm or smaller and cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes (T1, N1, M0 or T2, N1, M0).

Stage IIIB Anal Cancer
A substage of stage III anal cancer where the tumor has invaded nearby organs like the vagina, urethra, or bladder without nodal spread (T4, N0, M0).

Stage IIIC Anal Cancer
A substage of stage III anal cancer where the tumor is larger than 5 cm or invades adjacent organs and has spread to regional lymph nodes (T3, N1, M0 or T4, N1, M0).

High-Grade Anal Intraepithelial Neoplasia
Also known as AIN, a form of severe precancerous lesion in the anal canal or perianal area with abnormal cells that may turn malignant.

High-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesions
Also known as HSIL, precancerous cellular abnormalities found in squamous tissue of the anal region.

Human Immunodeficiency Virus Infection
Commonly known as HIV infection, an immunocompromising viral condition identified as a key risk factor for anal cancer.

Infertility
A potential complication or side effect of pelvic cancer therapies resulting in the inability to conceive children.<SEP>The biological inability to conceive or produce children, frequently caused or contributed to by pelvic radiation therapy and chemotherapy.

Non-Metastatic Anal Cancer
Anal cancer classified as Stages I, II, or III, where the disease has not spread beyond the pelvis.

Metastatic Anal Cancer
A category of anal cancer where the disease has spread to distant body sites, such as the liver or lungs.<SEP>An advanced stage of cancer originating in the anus that has spread to distant body parts, managed with systemic and local therapies.<SEP>Metastatic anal cancer refers to anal cancer that has spread beyond the pelvis to distant organs, most commonly the liver or lungs.<SEP>Stage IV anal cancer, where the malignancy has spread beyond the pelvis and requires systemic therapy.

Anal Canal Cancer
A classification of cancer located within the anal canal, sharing chemoradiation and surveillance protocols with advanced perianal cancer.<SEP>A primary presentation of anal cancer that is predominantly treated with combined chemoradiation.<SEP>A specific form of anal cancer originating within the anal canal, categorized into non-metastatic (stages I–III) and metastatic forms.

Perianal Cancer
A form of cancer located in the perianal area, which can be nonmetastatic in stages I through III and managed via chemoradiation or local excision.<SEP>A specific classification of cancer affecting the perianal area, treated based on tumor grade, margins, and invasion depth.<SEP>A type of anal cancer that originates in the perianal region, surrounding the anal opening.

Digital Rectal Examination
A routine surveillance physical exam recommended every 3 to 6 months for 5 years after treatment to detect cancer return.<SEP>DRE, a clinical diagnostic evaluation procedure recommended after an initial cancer diagnosis.

Anoscopy
An endoscopic examination of the anal canal recommended every 6 to 12 months for 3 years post-treatment, when tolerated.<SEP>An examination of the anal canal and lower rectum recommended every 6 to 12 months for surveillance after recurrence treatment for patients without APR.<SEP>An examination procedure recommended after diagnosis to evaluate the anal canal.

HIV Testing
A diagnostic screening test recommended after diagnosis to check for human immunodeficiency virus infection.

Cervical Cancer Screening
A screening assessment recommended after an anal cancer diagnosis to check for co-occurring cervical cancer.

Aquaphor
An over-the-counter soothing ointment recommended to help alleviate skin irritation and breakdown caused by radiation therapy.

Silvadene
An over-the-counter healing cream suggested for use under the guidance of a radiation oncologist to treat skin damage from radiation.

Linear Accelerator
A large specialized machine used in external beam radiation therapy to deliver targeted high-energy x-rays.

Groin
The anatomical junction of the lower abdomen and the thigh containing vital lymph node basins.<SEP>The anatomical region where regional lymph nodes are located and targeted during radiation therapy for anal cancer.

Mitomycin
A chemotherapy drug commonly recommended in combination with capecitabine or 5-FU alongside radiation therapy for anal cancer.<SEP>An intravenous chemotherapy medicine administered on specific days in combination with capecitabine or 5-FU for anal cancer treatment.

5-FU
Fluorouracil (5-FU) is a chemotherapy drug given via continuous intravenous infusion over several days using a wearable pump and catheter.<SEP>Fluorouracil, a chemotherapy drug used in combination regimens with mitomycin or cisplatin alongside radiation for anal cancer.

PICC Line
A deep intravenous line placed in the arm as a temporary alternative to a chest port for continuous chemotherapy infusion.

Hand-Foot Syndrome
A dermatologic side effect associated with capecitabine treatment, causing redness, swelling, pain, and blistering on the palms and soles.

Surgical Margin
The edge of normal tissue removed around a tumor during local excision, evaluated for the absence of cancer cells.

Feedback Survey
An online feedback initiative conducted by NCCN to improve educational materials for cancer patients.

5-FU Infusion
A multi-day continuous intravenous administration event delivering 5-FU medication through a wearable pump.

Janet
Janet is an anal cancer survivor who advocates against stigma, emphasizing that anal cancer can affect anyone.

Complete Remission
A post-treatment diagnostic category indicating that there are no detectable signs of cancer remaining in the body.

Persistent Disease
A clinical category describing cancer that remains in the body after treatment but has not grown or spread.

Progressive Disease
A clinical category describing cancer that has continued to grow or spread following treatment.

G1 (Low Grade)
A grading category representing well-differentiated cancer cells eligible for local excision in perianal cancer cases.

G2 (Intermediate Grade)
A grading category representing moderately differentiated cancer cells eligible for local excision in perianal cancer cases.

G3 (High Grade)
A grading category representing poorly differentiated cancer cells that typically require chemoradiation rather than local excision.

G4 (High Grade)
A grading category representing undifferentiated cancer cells requiring intensive multimodal therapy like chemoradiation.

Follow-Up Examination
A clinical assessment with digital rectal examination and anoscopy recommended 8 to 12 weeks after chemoradiation to evaluate treatment efficacy.

Abdominoperineal Resection (APR)
A radical surgical procedure involving excision of the anus and perineum, indicated for locally progressive or recurrent anal cancer.

Stage I Cancer
A stage of cancer that, if high-grade and perianal, warrants chemoradiation rather than local excision.

Stage II Cancer
A stage of cancer that is recommended for chemoradiation if high-grade or if it has invaded the sphincter, and requires annual imaging surveillance.

Stage III Cancer
An advanced stage of nonmetastatic anal cancer that requires chemoradiation followed by surveillance, including regular imaging.

Re-Excision
A secondary surgical procedure performed when the initial excision margin is less than 1 cm or contains cancer cells.

Inguinal Lymph Node Exam
A physical examination of the groin lymph nodes conducted every 3 to 6 months for 5 years following treatment.

Recurrent Anal Cancer
Recurrent anal cancer is cancer that returns to the anal area or regional lymph nodes following initial treatment.

Permanent Colostomy
A permanent colostomy is a surgical creation of an opening (stoma) on the abdomen connecting to the colon to allow stool to exit into an external bag.

Groin Dissection
A groin dissection is a surgical procedure to remove cancerous lymph nodes located in the groin area.<SEP>A surgical procedure recommended if anal cancer recurs in the lymph nodes of the groin following prior radiation.

Muscle Flap Reconstruction
A surgical reconstruction technique using muscle tissue to fill pelvic and perineal defects after extensive tissue removal such as APR.<SEP>Muscle flap reconstruction is a reconstructive surgical technique using tissue from another area of the body, such as the rectus abdominis, to promote perineal wound healing.

Carboplatin and Paclitaxel
A chemotherapy regimen combining carboplatin and paclitaxel, recommended for treating recurrent anal cancer in lymph nodes and metastatic anal cancer.

5-FU and Cisplatin
A systemic chemotherapy regimen composed of 5-fluorouracil and cisplatin used in treating recurrent lymph node cancer and metastatic anal cancer.

FOLFCIS
A chemotherapy regimen consisting of 5-FU, leucovorin, and cisplatin recommended as an option for metastatic anal cancer.

Modified DCF
A modified chemotherapy regimen consisting of docetaxel, cisplatin, and fluorouracil used for metastatic anal cancer, typically not followed by chemoradiation.

Mitomycin and Capecitabine
A chemotherapy regimen utilized in combination with radiation therapy for recurrent groin lymph node disease in patients without prior radiation.

5-FU and Mitomycin
A chemotherapy regimen given alongside radiation therapy for recurrent inguinal lymph nodes in patients who received no prior radiation therapy.

Imaging Surveillance
Periodic radiological evaluations—including CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis or MRI—recommended annually for 3 years following treatment for cancer recurrence.

Thom
Thom is an anal cancer survivor who advocates for patient self-care, organization, note-taking, and active communication with healthcare teams.<SEP>Thom is an anal cancer survivor who shares words of encouragement about recovering from treatment and coping with life after cancer.

Melissa
Melissa is an anal cancer survivor who advocates finding an experienced oncology team specializing in rare cancers.

Survivorship
Survivorship is a phase of post-treatment cancer care addressing the physical, emotional, and long-term health needs of cancer survivors.

IMRT
Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy, an advanced radiation technique recommended for anal cancer that limits radiation exposure to adjacent healthy organs and tissues.

APR Surgery
Abdominoperineal resection, a surgical procedure to remove the anus and create a permanent colostomy when anal cancer recurs or fails initial treatment.

Survivorship Care Plan
A comprehensive written document created by an oncologist detailing treatment history, side effects, and follow-up schedules for post-treatment cancer management.

Anal Cancer Foundation
An advocacy and support organization dedicated to empowering patients, accelerating research, and providing resources for anal cancer.<SEP>The Anal Cancer Foundation is a non-profit patient advocacy organization providing support, education, and research funding for anal cancer.<SEP>The Anal Cancer Foundation is an organization providing support to anal cancer patients and caregivers, notably through its Peer-To-Peer Support Program.

Pelvic Floor Physical Therapy
A specialized therapy involving exercises and hands-on techniques to strengthen muscles supporting pelvic organs, assisting bowel, bladder, and sexual recovery.

Vaginal Dilator Therapy
A therapeutic intervention utilizing dilators of varying sizes to prevent and manage vaginal stenosis caused by pelvic radiation therapy.

Ostomy Care
A specialized branch of healthcare and patient self-management aimed at maintaining quality of life and active living for individuals with an ostomy.

Peer-To-Peer Support Program
A supportive initiative established by the Anal Cancer Foundation to pair patients and caregivers with trained peer volunteers.

Fecal Incontinence
A condition involving involuntary loss of bowel control, which can occur as a complication following anal cancer treatment.

Pelvic Floor
A group of muscles that supports the pelvic organs and plays a critical role in bowel and bladder control, as well as sexual function.

Kegel Exercises
At-home physical exercises designed to tighten and release the vaginal and anal muscles to improve pelvic floor strength.

Vaginal Stenosis
A condition causing shortening, narrowing, and scarring of the vaginal canal, frequently secondary to pelvic radiation or surgery.<SEP>The medical narrowing and shortening of the vagina that often results from pelvic radiation therapy, leading to pain or difficulty with intercourse and exams.

Cancer Screening
Preventive medical evaluations for detecting secondary malignancies such as breast, cervical, colorectal, and prostate cancers in cancer survivors.

Dietitian
Healthcare professionals specializing in oncology nutrition who provide dietary guidance to manage bowel changes after cancer therapy.

Sexual Health Therapist
Mental health and wellness practitioners specializing in helping cancer survivors address and overcome post-treatment sexual dysfunction.

Ostomy Nurse
A specialized healthcare provider trained in assisting and educating patients with stomas and ostomies.

Cancer Survivorship
A phase of cancer care focused on maintaining healthy living, managing long-term side effects, and addressing emotional and physical well-being after diagnosis and treatment.

Integrative Oncology
A medical approach to cancer care that combines conventional standard cancer treatments with evidence-based complementary and alternative therapies.

Complementary And Alternative Therapies
A collection of non-conventional health practices and products, such as acupuncture, meditation, and massage therapy, used to ease side effects and support cancer patients.

Shared Decision-Making
A collaborative communication process between cancer patients and their doctors to agree upon a treatment plan aligned with the patient's values and medical options.

Second Opinion
An evaluation obtained from an independent medical expert to verify a diagnosis or review proposed cancer treatment plans.<SEP>The practice of having another physician evaluate diagnosis and test results to suggest or validate a cancer treatment plan.

Bone Density Monitoring
A surveillance procedure used to assess pelvic bone strength and fracture risk following pelvic radiation therapy.

Smoking Cessation
The process of quitting tobacco use through physician-guided counseling and lifestyle interventions to reduce recurrence and secondary cancer risks.

Health Insurance Companies
Financial and healthcare organizations whose policies and coverage networks determine out-of-pocket costs for cancer treatments and second opinions.

Fertility Specialists
Medical experts consulted to discuss fertility preservation before initiating cancer treatments that may impair reproductive capability.

Acupuncture
A complementary therapeutic technique used to alleviate side effects and enhance comfort during and after cancer treatment.

Medical Marijuana
A complementary therapeutic product utilized in cancer care to alleviate symptoms and treatment-related discomfort.

Yoga
A mind-body complementary practice used in integrative oncology to promote patient well-being and symptom relief.

Meditation
A complementary mindfulness practice employed to manage emotional distress, anxiety, and side effects during cancer care.

American Cancer Society
A prominent health organization providing information, support, and resources on cancer, including anal cancer.<SEP>The American Cancer Society is a nationwide voluntary health organization dedicated to eliminating cancer and providing patient support and information.

Cancer Hope Network
A supportive care organization offering peer mentorship and resources for cancer patients and their families.<SEP>Cancer Hope Network is an organization providing free, confidential one-on-one peer support for cancer patients and their loved ones.

Cancer.Net
An oncologist-approved patient information resource offering comprehensive guides on cancer types, including anal cancer.<SEP>Cancer.Net is a comprehensive, oncologist-approved patient information resource offering guides and educational materials on various cancer types.

CancerCare
A national organization providing free, professional support services to anyone affected by cancer.<SEP>CancerCare is a national organization providing free professional support services, counseling, and financial assistance to people affected by cancer.

Cancer Support Community
A global non-profit network of cancer support dedicated to uplifting and strengthening people impacted by cancer.<SEP>Cancer Support Community is an international non-profit dedicated to providing support services, education, and hope to cancer patients and families.

Colorectal Cancer Alliance
A non-profit organization dedicated to ending colorectal cancer through patient support, research, and prevention.<SEP>The Colorectal Cancer Alliance is a non-profit dedicated to ending colorectal-related cancers through patient support, awareness, and research.

Fight Colorectal Cancer
An advocacy organization fighting colorectal cancer through research, education, and patient empowerment.<SEP>Fight Colorectal Cancer is an advocacy organization providing research, resources, and policy advocacy for patients with colorectal cancers.

HPV Cancers Alliance
An advocacy organization focused on raising awareness, prevention, and support for cancers caused by human papillomavirus.<SEP>HPV Cancers Alliance is an organization dedicated to raising awareness, education, and resources for cancers linked to the human papillomavirus.

Love Your Buns
An advocacy organization providing support and raising awareness for anal and rectal cancer.<SEP>Love Your Buns is an awareness and support organization focused on educating the public and supporting patients with rectal and anal cancers.

Pelvic Radiation
Radiation therapy administered specifically to the pelvic region, an important consideration when evaluating future chemoradiation regimens.

Follow-Up Care
Routine medical monitoring, surveillance testing, and healthcare visits conducted after completing cancer therapy to track late effects and detect recurrence.

Survivor Support Group
Support networks offering emotional support, peer guidance, and shared resources for cancer survivors post-treatment.

National Coalition for Cancer Survivorship
An advocacy organization advocating for quality cancer care for all people touched by cancer.

PAN Foundation
An independent charitable organization that helps federally insured individuals access healthcare and treatment.

The Anchor Study
A clinical research study evaluating prevention strategies and screening for anal cancer.

Anal Canal
A small section of the large intestine connecting the rectum and the anal opening.

Anal Sphincter
A ring-shaped muscle around the anal opening that regulates opening and closing for stool elimination.

Anus
The terminal opening of the large bowel through which digestive waste exits the human body.

Libido
Sexual desire or psychosexual energy, which may be affected by cancer and pelvic oncological treatments.

Perianal Region
The external surface and skin immediately surrounding the anal opening.
